- concurrent TL-UL and SPI side transactions
- sequential TL-UL (on CSB inactive) and SPI-TXn

  This double write is sent when the busy bit is set and it comprises
  of the first write setting the upper bits of the status register and
  the second write clearing the busy/wel bits.

The intr_state task now rather than making a read every X random
clk_cycles reads the intr_state every cycle through the backdoor and
if there are interrupts, then it does a front-door read to update the
predicted values in SCB. Otherwise, it may happen the TB doesn't
repopulate either half of the read buffer "early enough" leading to
memory mismatches.

subject: [dv,top_level] Fix chip_sw_sysrst_ctrl_ulp_z3_wakeup test
body:
The UVM code in the test sequence should not wait before updating
the phase memory location via backdoor when transitioning to phase
3, or the update can be too late and the test will fail.

More details: In phase 2 the SV side causes sysrst_ctrl to detect
the lid opened, which trigger a wakeup while the CPU is in deep
sleep. SV then calls sync_with_sw, which delays updating the phase
after the CPU enters test_main, and can cause phase 2 to rerun.
Normally this test passes, but the delay can be configured via
sim_dv runtime plusargs and set large enough for this to happen,
and that is what happens for this failure.

The wait in phase 2 is unnecessary since the chip is asleep and
opening the lid causes it to wakeup, so updating the phase can be
done anytime before the CPU restarts running the test code.

subject: [reggen,fpv] Fix array sizes in fpv_csr.sv.tpl
body:
Before and after this change, there are three arrays in this code that
are addressed by the index of an HRO register: regwen, access_policy
and exp_vals. The index of the HRO register comes from a variable
called hro_idx. Valid HRO registers get their position in the list of
such registers. Other values get a dummy value that is one greater.

Before this change, the exp_vals correctly had an extra element (to
represent this dummy hro_idx). The other two arrays did not.

This change makes things more uniform by adding the extra element to
those two arrays and initialising it to some default value. We should
no longer be able to access the arrays out of bounds.

body:
The previous change was mostly right, except for an off-by-one which
didn't get triggered with the HRO register count I was testing with.
If num_hro_regs = N, they will have indices 0, 1, ..., N-1. Then we'll
throw in an extra index for non-HRO registers, with value N.

To represent an arbitrary one of these indices, we need $clog2(N)
bits. My code was wrong and used $clog2(N+1) (because there are N+1
entries in the array).

It turns out that I was testing with a value of N where those two
calculations give the same result. But it doesn't work with N=3 (the
situation I have now).

subject: [crypto] Fix a bug in ECDSA-P256.
body:
Fixes the failing wycheproof ECDSA tests in #22322.

When computing the recovered x coordinate, we get a value that's reduced
modulo p (the coordinate field modulus) and we then need to reduce this
value modulo n (the curve order). This operation is almost always a
no-op, since p and n are very close together; there's roughly a 2^-130
probability of hitting this range by chance. However, the code
implementing the reduction was *always* a no-op. Essentially, by using
`bn.subm` instead of `bn.addm` here, the code was conditionally *adding*
the modulus n if `w19 - 0` underflowed, which it never would. Instead,
we need `bn.addm`, which will conditionally *subtract* the modulus n if
`w19 + 0` is greater than n.

subject: [i2c] Eliminate multi-item repeated start entry in ACQ FIFO
body:
Change recording of Start symbols to always accompany the address data,
instead of recording a separate R.Start, then Start+address. This helps
maintain certain availability invariants needed for reliable stretching
and NACK handling.

Note that a controller that chooses to do a Repeated Start and address a
*different* target is an unusual case, and it leads to a situation where
the transfer closing symbol won't appear until the Stop or a later
Repeated Start that *does* address this target. While this transaction
style is not explicitly forbidden in the I2C specification, it is not
typically supported in the wild. In any case, software should be able to
resolve this case, and a closing symbol will eventually appear.

Fix up the DV transaction generation to match the expected behavior.

Signed-off-by: Alexander Williams <awill@opentitan.org>

Add NackStop as an ACQ FIFO value to indicate the end of transactions
that had errors (generally, NACK'd transfers).

Fix up the glitch sequence to better handle the various states.

subject: [i2c] Add StretchAcqSetup state to preserve ACK setup time
body:
Add StretchAcqSetup state to follow the release of the hold from
StretchAcqFull after the ACQ FIFO gains the necessary space. Continue to
stretch SCL so the change to SDA doesn't violate setup time, then
proceed to the normal ACK setup state.

Remove the immediate write to the ACQ FIFO in the StretchAcqFull state
when we're proceeding to a normal ACK. This created extra ACQ FIFO
writes when it transitioned to the AcquireAckWait state, and the FSM
gets simpler and less error-prone if only error cases operate on FIFOs
outside of the non-stretch states.

subject: [dvsim,lint] Fix bug in duplicate detection in lint parser
body:
The code in extract_messages tries to avoid getting multiple hits at a
single location. The idea is that you might have two different buckets
that both match a particular string. For example, suppose we have
buckets with the following patterns:

  "This.*not.*bad"
  "This.*bad"

If the log that we're parsing contains "This is not bad", we want to
find a single hit (we probably want the one for the first pattern).

The code tries to do this by storing a partial map to compute "The
first pattern in the list that matches the string starting at the
given location".

This should work nicely! But I had messed up the Python side of things
and used m.pos instead of m.start. The pos field gives the pos
argument that got passed to find() (zero here) and the result is that
we find exactly one result, allocated to position zero. Oops!

Use m.start(), which gives the index of the first character that was
matched. Much cleaner!

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [lc_ctrl,dv] Fix width of coverage binding
body:
The existing binding expected a single object of type lc_tx_t, but the
thing that it was sampling changed type with commit fa447d0cdc9: it is
now NumRmaAckSigs different lc_tx_t objects.

VCS correctly complains at build time about the width mismatch. I
couldn't easily see how to name the instances sensibly and "bind

when building rv_dm. To see the current status, run:

  util/dvsim/dvsim.py hw/top_earlgrey/lint/top_earlgrey_lint_cfgs.hjson \
    --tool verilator --select-cfgs=rv_dm

Before this change, you got the following warnings:

    %Warning-WIDTHTRUNC: ../src/pulp-platform_riscv-dbg_0.1_0/pulp_riscv_dbg/src/dm_mem.sv:87:41: Operator VAR 'RomBaseAddr' expects 12 bits on the Initial value, but Initial value's VARREF 'HaltAddress' generates 64 bits.
                                                                                                : ... note: In instance 'rv_dm.u_dm_top.i_dm_mem'
       87 |   localparam logic [DbgAddressBits-1:0] RomBaseAddr   = dm::HaltAddress;
          |                                         ^~~~~~~~~~~
                         ... For warning description see https://verilator.org/warn/WIDTHTRUNC?v=5.020
                         ... Use "/* verilator lint_off WIDTHTRUNC */" and lint_on around source to disable this message.
    %Warning-WIDTHTRUNC: ../src/pulp-platform_riscv-dbg_0.1_0/pulp_riscv_dbg/src/dm_mem.sv:90:41: Operator VAR 'RomEndAddr' expects 12 bits on the Initial value, but Initial value's ADD generates 64 bits.
                                                                                                : ... note: In instance 'rv_dm.u_dm_top.i_dm_mem'
       90 |   localparam logic [DbgAddressBits-1:0] RomEndAddr    = dm::HaltAddress + 'h7FF;
          |                                         ^~~~~~~~~~
    %Warning-WIDTHEXPAND: ../src/pulp-platform_riscv-dbg_0.1_0/pulp_riscv_dbg/src/dm_mem.sv:92:59: Operator DIV expects 32 bits on the LHS, but LHS's VARREF 'ProgBufSize' generates 5 bits.
                                                                                                 : ... note: In instance 'rv_dm.u_dm_top.i_dm_mem'
       92 |   localparam int unsigned ProgBuf64Size = dm::ProgBufSize / 2;

  declared in `dm_pkg.sv` to be 64-bit variables. In `dm_mem.sv`,
  `DbgAddressBits` is a localparam equal to 12.

  32-bit value.

generates new entropy on both EDN0 and EDN1 but OTBN is only the user
of EDN1 so after the last OTBN request for entropy on the EDN1, a new

the command will queue forever and the test will hang when waiting

subject: [flash_ctrl] Enable firmware dealing with multi-bit ECC and ICV errors
body:
Before, these two errors types led to a fatal alert which is problematic
during firmware selection and verification. This commit changes the
design in the following way:
- The two relevant bits in the FAULT_STATUS CSR are made clearable by
  software. Other bits in this register remain sticky.
- The corresponding alert is no longer fatal.

This means the alert is only sent out until the two bits are cleared by
software. To be on the safe side, firmware can still classify the alert
as fatal on the receiver side (in the alert handler). For the other
error sources, the alert keeps getting triggered as before, i.e., it
remains fatal.

For more background information, refer to lowRISC/OpenTitan#21353.

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#21637.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

subject: [flash_ctrl] Pop read pipeline FIFOs for data and mask in sync
body:
This commit fixes a bug in the read pipeline where the data and the mask
storage FIFO could get out of sync in case of the mask computation
running behind the actual Flash read (e.g. due to back pressure in the
shared scrambling logic).

To avoid the FIFOs getting out of sync, the design now tracks whether
for reads that don't require descrambling, a mask was still computed.
This can happen if for scramble enabled locations that are being erased.
In case a mask computation has been started, the FIFOs are now only
popped if both the data and the mask FIFO contain a valid entry (i.e.
the mask computation for the data to be popped has finished).

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#22443

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

subject: [edn,rtl] Fix assertions
body:
The existing code wasn't quite right and actually causes a compilation
error when you try to push it through Jasper. For a bit more detail,
edn_enable_fo is the "edn enable fanout". This is indexed by entries
from FatalErr(=1) to LastEdnEntry-1, and doesn't have anything at
index zero. (This is what causes the compilation error)

In addition, one of the assertions no longer got disabled upon disabling
EDN. As a result, it would always fire after re-enabling EDN which
intentionally clears the FIFOs the assertion is checking.

These bugs got introduced by a974108, which removed an "enable_q" signal
from edn.sv. Looking at the assertions, I think the property that
we're talking about is "some of EDN is enabled". To get what I hope is
the intended behaviour, I've used a unary OR to combine together all
of the enable signals.

subject: [jtag_dmi_monitor,dv] Make monitor pickier about the DMI sequence
body:
It turns out that seeing a DmiOpOk JTAG response isn't *quite* enough
to conclude that the DMI is not busy. If you're a bit unlucky, it can
only realise that it's busy at the same time as it responds with
DmiOpOk the first time.

This change makes the monitor "safer" in this setting. It will only
conclude that a requested DMI operation has been sent after it has
seen another response since the original request.

Of course, there's still a question about what to do if we see a
request immediately after a request. The code here goes for the easy
option and fails instantly. We can fix the drivers to ensure they
don't do that!

subject: [i2c] Add ACK Control Mode
body:
Add an N-byte automatic ACK control so software may observe partial
command data and NACK the transaction in the middle of a transfer. The
counter begins at 0 for every transfer, and it decrements for every data
byte that is ACK'd. When the FSM reaches the (N)ACK phase, it stretches
the clock and awaits instructions from software (up to the stretch
timeout). Software can either program the Auto ACK Counter to a higher
number to ACK the pending byte (and subsequent ones, if the value
programmed is greater than 1), or it can explicitly NACK that byte and
the rest of the transaction.

Show the pending data byte in a separate CSR, away from the ACQ FIFO,
and change the "ACQ FIFO full" interrupt into a generic "stretching on
ACQuisition" interrupt, with the particular reason shown in the STATUS
CSR. When ACK Control Mode is disabled, that interrupt becomes purely an
"ACQ FIFO full" interrupt again.

A mechanism for mid-transfer NACKing is required for SMBus protocol
support.

subject: [prim,fpv] Rephrase some "backwards" assertions in prim_count
body:
In this module, we have forwards assertions that say "If an input
happens then we change accordingly" and we have backwards assertions
that say "If we change then an input must have been asserted".

We've got several different inputs that might change the
count (incr/decr/set/clear). The existing backwards assertions were
quite strong and asked for a change that definitely wasn't caused by a
different input. For example, ClrBkwd_A said "If we change and it
wasn't caused by incr, decr or set, then we must have seen clear".

This is fine, but it creates a cover property to see a change that
isn't caused by the other inputs. We might not be able to hit
that! In particular, in the alert_handler_esc_timer module, we weren't
every seeing set_i without incr.

But we don't really care! This commit generalises the backward
assertion. This should give the same level of confidence, but avoids
the vacuity that Jasper reports as a coverage hole otherwise.

subject: cert: make sure fake CA matches TPM certificates' Issuer
body:
For openssl x509 certificate chain verification to succeed
subject/issuer key ID and subject/issuer Distinguished Name fields
must match. Moreover, the Distinguished name components must match
literally, i.e. not just the component values, but also the components
layout in the certificate.

The country name field must be exactly two characters (US for the USA).

The hjson cert parser seems to be changing the order of the DN
components listed in the input files, changing the openssl
configuration file allows to create a CSR which results in the
expected layout of the generated certificate's DN field.

After these changes the generated certificates can be successfully
verified, i.e.
 $ openssl verify -CAfile fake_ca.pem tpm_ek.full.pem
 tpm_ek.full.pem: OK

This width wasn't quite right for u_prim_count_esc_cnt in the
design (and Jasper correctly points out that we can't get to the
maximal count value).

We pick a target to ping by incrementing that target's index every
time we went around the FSM that drove the pings. Of course, there are
only finitely many targets (N_ESC_SEV of them) and we wrap at
N_ESC_SEV-1.

With the current code (before or after this commit), this is done by
driving an esc_cnt_clr signal. Before we switched to use
prim_count (in commit b5eb150), the wrapping was implemented directly
in this file.

The switch to prim_count was reasonable, but instantiated the counter
with a width of PING_CNT_DW, which is 16, instead of the number of
bits needed to represent N_ESC_SEV-1 = 3, which is just 2.

subject: [ot_certs] Rework Name handling
body:
Names were previously represented as maps but this is problematic
for two reasons:
- order is not preserved,
- it cannot represente multi-valued RDNs (although they are are).

This commit changes the representation to an array of maps so that
it maps cleanly to the ASN1 representation (sequence of sets). In
particular the order in the array preserved while the order in the
map/set is arbitrary (this matches the expected X501 behaviour).
This makes the hjson a little bit more ugly but it's not too terrible.
One issue that arises from this change is that although it is very
easy to modify the builder to handle multi-valued RDNs, the openssl
parser cannot reconstruct them because the openssl-sys binding
misses a function (see FIXME in the code). Since multi-valued RDNs
are rare and not used in our codebase presently, we simply assume
single-valued RDNs are the moment.

- Writes cannot overwrite contents already written or most likely
  some bit will not be able to flip from 0 to 1. This maintains
  a collection of addresses that have been already written to
  avoid overwrites.
- A bug is fixed for writes that span multiple program windows
  (aligned at 64 bytes): the dv code was replacing the sequence
  of writes by repeated writes to the start of the program window.

subject: [kmac/rtl] Fix four problems in error handling
body:
This commit fixes four problems in KMAC's error handling:

1) App interface done after SW has processed error

   Before this commit, when the FSM in `kmac_app` was in its `StError`
   state and SW acknowledged the error by writing the `err_processed`
   bit in the `CFG_SHADOWED` CSR, the FSM would go back to the `StIdle`
   state.  If the active HW app interface had not provided all data
   before this SW-induced transition to the `StIdle` state, KMAC was no
   longer ready to absorb the remaining data, thereby stalling the HW
   app interface.

   This commit extends the FSM in `kmac_app` so that when an error
   happens it doesn't matter whether SW acknowledges the error before or
   after the HW app interface has provided all data.  In both cases, the
   FSM now waits for SW to acknowledge *and* the HW app interface to
   provide all data before it returns to `StIdle`.

   To implement this, two new states (`StErrorAwaitSw` and
   `StErrorAwaitApp`) get added.

   In block-level DV, `kmac_key_error_vseq` waited for the *first* data
   item instead of the *last* before stopping to send items on the
   active HW app interface and continuing with the vseq (acknowledging
   the error from SW and going to the next iteration).  This no longer
   works because KMAC now remains in `StError` until the HW app
   interface has send the last data item, so that vseq now correctly
   sends all data items including the last on the HW app interface.

   This may raise a new issue: If the HW app interface misbehaves, KMAC
   will remain in the error state until it gets reset.  To remediate
   this, we could add a mechanism for SW to clear KMAC's state
   regardless of the state of the HW app interface.

2) SHA3 core not told to process

   Before this commit, when the FSM in `kmac_app` went through the
   `StError` state, it would not tell the SHA3 core to process the data
   so that its internal state would get flushed.

   This commit extends the FSM in `kmac_app` so that `CmdProcess` is
   signaled on `cmd_o` to the SHA3 core when the error is handled, and
   lets the FSM wait for the completion of SHA3 (`absorbed_i` input)
   before returning to idle.  To implement this, a new state
   (`StErrorWaitAbsorbed`) is added.

3) Signaling completion to SW when an error has occurred in SW mode

   Before this commit, when an error would occur in SW mode (`mux_sel ==
   SelSw`), the `absorbed_o` output, which in turn triggers the
   `kmac_done` IRQ would not be raised.  This case could not happen
   because no errors were raised in SW mode (such errors will get raised
   with the next commit), but it's still wrong.

   This commit extends the FSM in `kmac_app` with a side-band state bit
   (`err_during_sw_q`) and uses that to set `absorbed_o` when an error
   that occurred during SW mode got handled.

4) Clearing of `kmac_errchk`

   Before this commit, the state of the `kmac_errchk` would not get
   cleared after the error has been handled.  Thus the next invocation
   of KMAC could start with a residual state in `kmac_errchk` and
   incorrectly fail.

   This commits adds a MuBi-encoded signal from `kmac_app` to
   `kmac_errchk` through which the former can clear the latter after an
   error.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [kmac/rtl] Abort when sideload key is invalid during operation
body:
The KMAC HW IP block features an option to load keys from Key Manager
via a HW key sideload interface.  Prior to this commit, KMAC would:
- when used via the SW application interface: *not check at all* if the
  sideload key is valid (issue #10704, #16855);
- when used via a HW application interface: check if the sideload key is
  valid *only for a single cycle* when the application interface gets
  configured (state `StAppCfg` in `kmac_app`).

This could lead to cases where KMAC would use an invalid sideload key.

This commit fixes the problem by checking whether the sideload key is
valid in *every* FSM state in which the sideload key is used.  If the
sideload key is invalid even for a single cycle (the FSM cannot know
whether the key is being used in this exact cycle or not), `kmac_app`'s
FSM goes into the `StKeyMgrErrKeyNotValid` state.  In that state, the
FSM signals the `keymgr_pkg::ErrKeyNotValid` error code in KMAC's
`err_code` CSR.  The FSM then transitions to the `StError` state, where
it drains data from the HW application interface by keeping
`app_o.ready` high.  The digest output remains all-zero (it can only
take a non-zero value in the `StAppWait` state).  The FSM exits the
`StError` state after SW has signalled that it has processed the error
by writing the `processed` bit in the `CFG_SHADOWED` CSR *and* the
active HW app interface has sent the last data item.

This commit resolves #10704 and implements the RTL part of #16855.
Covering this in DV remains open, although the existing tests (which
don't cover this) keep their previous pass rates.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

scrambling is acceptable.

subject: [i2c] Prevent transmission until the bus is free
body:
Consolidate start/stop detection, bus idle timeouts, and transaction
boundary checking in a separate bus monitor module. Also move counting
of the bus free time to the bus monitor, and use all of these inputs to
determine when a bus is free, ready for the controller's next
transmission.

Adjust the controller FSM to respond to the bus monitor's "bus free"
status signal.

Remove the "SDA is low in Idle" check from the SDA interference
interrupt. There are various single-controller scenarios where this may
trigger uselessly, and it isn't compatible with multi-controller
scenarios. If a user wishes to know if SDA is low when the RTL's comment
literally indicated, merely around the time when the controller is first
enabled, then software may probe the RX oversample CSR for the current
value.

subject: [i2c] Add clock low / SMBus bus timeout feature
body:
Add an option to switch the main TIMEOUT_CTRL from a "stretch timeout"
to a general "bus timeout." Since they are the same value in SMBus,
these timeouts do not need to be active simultaneously.

A stretch timeout only triggers when this IP's controller has released
SCL, but it doesn't reach a high state within the duration specified by
the CSR. By contrast, a bus timeout triggers whenever SCL is held low
continuously for the duration specified by the CSR, no matter the
source. A bus timeout affects both the target module and the controller
module, and transactions are aborted with error/NACK reporting.

Signed-off-by: Alexander Williams <awill@opentitan.org>

subject: [i2c] Handle initialization of bus monitor
body:

pins on the i2c block may be held low, due to pinmux defaults. Avoid

timeouts enabled for single-controller setups.

Add a multi-controller mode to the bus monitor so it *can* begin in the
busy state, and require that at least the host idle timeout be defined.
If multi-controller mode is disabled, report that the bus is always
free, so the controller FSM is not gated by it.

locked.  This did not cause problems because keymgr currently does not
raise an error and go into the Invalid state.  This behavior of keymgr
will be changed/fixed in a subsequent commit, so this commit fixes the
`entropy_src_edn_reqs_test` so that it doesn't fail when keymgr gets

subject: [keymgr/rtl] Abort into Invalid when Creator Root Key not valid
body:
Prior to this commit, keymgr could be initialized and would open itself
to operations even if the Creator Root Key shares provided by OTP in the
`root_key_i` input were invalid (although keymgr did write all-zeros and
all-ones instead of the input from OTP into its key shares if that was
the case).  However, the specification dictates that kemygr must signal
an invalid operation, though it did not specify the next state.

This commit fixes the problem by letting keymgr raise an *invalid
operation* error in this case and then transition to the terminal
Invalid state (going through a wipe state to clear any secrets with
entropy).  The rationale for this implementation is that the Creator
Root Key is meant to be static after reset, so SW doesn't have to be
able to retry the initialization.  Letting keymgr abort into a terminal
state thus is an additional HW security countermeasure to deter FI
attacks aimed at loading a manipulated Creator Root Key.

This closes #17776.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [keymgr/rtl] Raise error for any operation in Invalid state

Invalid state.  Prior to this commit, keymgr did not raise an *invalid

`ERR_CODE` CSRs.

This commit fixes keymgr to do all these things.

generate an exception causing chip reset, which will reset not only the
watchdog, but other IP blocks that the owner code wanted retained across
the period of sleep.

Also, do not re-configure pinmux or attempt to read SW_BOOTSTRAP pins if
waking from sleep.

subject: [keymgr] Change reseed counter to count PRNG updates instead of cycles
body:
Previously, the reseed counter was counting clock cycles which was
problematic for the following reasons:
- Once started, the counter couldn't be stopped anymore and keymgr would
  repeatedly request entropy even if being completely idle. This is bad
  for power.
- The number of clock cycles since the last reseed operation is no good
  indication for the seed lifetime.

Therefore, this commit changes the design to only advance the counter
when the PRNG is updated. Such updates only happen while keymgr is busy
and the number of PRNG updates is a more accurate measure for the seed
lifetime.

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#22877.

subject: [opentitantool] Re-attach kernel driver
body:
Sometimes, tools using libusb may ask that the kernel driver for a
particular USB interface be "detached" from that interface, such that
libusb can be used to control which data transfers to make.  At Google,
"servod" is one such tool, which has a habit of detaching the kernel
serial port driver from C2D2 or uServo debuggers, meaning that the
/dev/ttyUSBn devices would not be present.

This CL adds logic to make sure that the kernel serial driver is
attached to any HyperDebug USB interface, before searching for the
proper devUSBn.

subject: [opentitantool] Claim USB interface before using
body:
When establihsing connection to a HyperDebug device, opentitantool will
send a request on the CMSIS-DAP USB interface to ask about the
capabilities of HyperDebug.  If the USB interface is later used for GPIO
bitbanging or similar, opentitantool will "claim" it before doing actual
communication.  We want to let openocd have the option of claiming the
interface as well, for JTAG debugging.

The querying of capabilities leads to a kernel warning about
opentitantool accessing an interface without claiming it first.  This CL
adds code to briefly claim then release the interface, on startup.  This
still allows openocd to later establish connection for JTAG, but it
could interfere with the ability to invoke opentitantool while JTAG
debugging is ongoing.  (I do not think it could have worked before, as
the kernel would probably have refused opentitantool's request to send
bulk data to an interface already claimed by another process.  And even
if not, the USB protocol has no way of multiplexing requests from
multiple sources.)

Change-Id: I5c4ec0f1aa09b668a7fd5597b4f801dbaf137dd4
Signed-off-by: Jes B. Klinke <jbk@chromium.org>

subject: [prim_diff_decode] Use `prim_xnor2` to detect integrity issue

otherwise a signal integrity issue exists.  Such issues can be detected

behavioral RTL code, which could allow some synthesis tools to perform
undesired optimizations for the complementary differential signals.

This commit changes the implementation to a `prim_xnor2` instance, so
that synthesis tools cannot change that logic.

subject: [i2c] Halt subsequent read if prior read failed
body:
Add a CSR to report fault events that occurred during a read, and gate
the next read (stretch clock at the first bit) until the event latch is
cleared. This is for reads to this IP's target module.

The gate helps prevent stale data from emerging from the FIFO.

Also roll in some of the functionality the TXRST_ON_COND CSR was meant
to provide, and make this a catch-all gate for releasing the TX FIFO on
a read instead. The prior mechanism had some corner cases that produced
races with software, such as software being able to inadvertently write
a new (yet stale) byte of data after the clear yet before being notified
that the command completed. The separate gating CSR helps avoid such
races by not allowing software's normal write path to bypass event
handling.

subject: [edn/dv] This commit fixes the deadlock in edn_disable_auto_req_mode

Currently there is a deadlock in the edn_disable_auto_req_mode test.
This deadlock occurs whenever the EDN is disabled during the initialization
of auto mode. The config variable cfg.abort_sw_cmd is used to signal to
the base vseq that the EDN will be disabled. However, this variable is not
taken into consideration in all of the apropriate places. Furthermore,
the variable is not being looked at during spinwaits. For this reason
reset_asserted() needs to be called to tell the csr_utils_pkg that there
is an incoming re-enablement (even though we are not resetting and this
still works and I prefer this option over adding an additional function to
csr_utils_pkg for re-enablements).
This commit makes sure that for edn_disable_auto_req_mode, the EDN is only
disabled, when no csr acceses are outstanding (which if IIUC is the intention
behind cfg.abort_sw_cmd).

subject: [otbn,dv] Ensure an error in opcode corrupting otbn_ctrl_redun_vseq
body:
In this branch (if err_type is picked to be 2), the sequence tries to
corrupt the opcode in the bignum ALU. The existing code correctly
waited until the ALU had a valid operation, and then wrote a different
value to the opcode.

But the "valid" flag might be high when the operation was "None". If
that happened and we wrote another invalid operation (also ignored)
then the corruption wouldn't actually do anything. Oops!

With this patch, we wait for the operation_valid_i flag as before, but
also wait until the opcode specifies a valid operation. That way,
corrupting it should cause something to happen.

subject: [chip,dv] Wait for JTAG connection in chip_sw_base_vseq
body:
The wait_lc_status() task does a DMI read over JTAG to figure out the
current state of lc_ctrl. This requires pinmux to route the JTAG
signals to LC_CTRL and things get rather confused if we run this task
before the routing has happened.

In normal use, the JTAG driver will send an IR command to switch
address to the DMI address. Then it will send a DR command to do the
DMI read/write. On the next DMI command, it can avoid the silly extra
IR command because it knows we're already pointing at the DMI address.

Of course, this doesn't work if the JTAG signals got squashed. In that
case, it will not know that IR hasn't changed, so it will send
repeated DR commands expecting to see a particular lc_ctrl status come
out. But that won't happen because we're not actually looking at the
DMI register at all. Oops!

This commit adds a wait to make sure that JTAG has actually been
connected up.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [rv_dm,dv] Tidy up halt_resume_whereto vseq
body:
This sequence is currently failing, after some changes I made to the
DMI driver/monitor a few weeks ago. It turns out that the problem is
caused by the fact that the vseq was doing a DMI operation by directly
driving the JTAG signals (instead of using the DMI driver).

Fixing this was reasonably easy but I realised that the sequence
itself didn't give much confidence about what it was doing. This
commit replaces magic hex constants and adds lots of comments to
explain what it is actually doing. The behaviour should be mostly
unchanged.

The hex constants were a little tricky to interpret! Indeed, figuring
out the exact abstract command that was running in this sequence was a
bit hard: we were just writing the hex constant 'h5C00021102 to the
"dmi" register.

I decoded this with the RISC-V debug specification. Firstly (section
6.1.5), the constant splits into fields as

    address = 'h17
    data    = 'h00008440
    op      = 2'b10 = 2

op = 2 means the operation is "write data to address". address = 'h17
is "command" (the abstract command register)

The abstract command register is documented in section 3.12.7 of the
same specification and has fields cmdtype, control. The 'h8440
constant splits up as:

    cmdtype = 8'h00
    control = 24'h008440

A cmdtype of zero means "Access register command". Then constant in
control is decoded as

    aarsize          = 2
    aarpostincrement = 0
    postexec         = 1
    transfer         = 0
    write            = 0
    regno            = 16'h40 (CSR 64)

After this commit, the code should do the same thing but it will
hopefully be a bit easier to understand.

The only extra change that I've made is to add an extra busy check to
the end of the vseq, which should make this all a bit more
symmetrical. I've added the check to the testpoint to keep things in
sync.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [jtag,dv] Move host_cb back to negedge of tck
body:
This clocking block was moved to the negedge of tck in 2022 with
commit 143ebe944b7. The reasoning there was it fixed an rv_dm issue on
the closed source side.

Two days later, commit d4d8a647513 moved back to the posedge. The
message for that commit doesn't discuss the change, so I have a strong
suspicion that it was a rebasing issue. This commit also didn't remove
the documentation comment on the line above that still claims we're
using the negedge!

This commit moves us back to negedge. The logic is that we can then
deal better with a situation where we want to drive a value to TDI
when the clock is currently stopped. The jtag driver might have
something like:

    `HOST_CB.tdi <= tdi;
    @(`HOST_CB);

Suppose the JTAG clock is currently paused (with tck_en=0) and tck is
high. When host_cb is on the posedge of tck, the write gets missed by
the design code because the write sits waiting in the clocking block
until the posedge and the design ends up sampling the previous value.
The sequence of events is:

  - Clock pauses for a bit (tck=1)
  - Clock is enabled.
  - We write to TDI through the clocking block
  - tck=0
  - tck=1
  - Design samples the value that's currently on TDI
  - The write makes it through the clocking block

Moving the driver to the negedge ensures that this "write just after
unpausing TCK" gets seen correctly by the design, because we end up
with the following sequence of events:

  - Clock pauses for a bit (tck=1)
  - Clock is enabled.
  - We write to TDI through the clocking block
  - tck=0
  - The write makes it through the clocking block
  - tck=1
  - Design samples the value that's currently on TDI

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

Previously the code preserves both the `pattern` and `backdoor` fields
when we scramble main SRAM. The `pattern` field is the one that we
expect to be scrambled and trigger ECC errors. In DV-sim environments
the `backdoor` field is magically corrected so that it's scrambled with

number of ECC errors was doubled.

subject: [i2c] Add bus arbitration support for the controller
body:
Detect when the controller is transmitting SDA high, but the value on
the wire is low, resulting in lost arbitration in a multi-controller
environment.

Proceed immediately to Idle, set a bit in CONTROLLER_EVENTS for lost
arbitration, and halt at Idle until that bit is cleared. This allows
software to respond and prepare the FMT FIFO for the next transmission,
which may be a retry.

Add a parameter for the top-level input delay between cio_sda_o and
cio_sda_i, and avoid triggering bus errors during that period.
Internally, the detection window will also be reduced by the rise time
for SCL, so this parameter only represents the worst case delay from the
output flop's output to the pad plus the pad back to the first input
flop's input.

Set InputDelayCycles to 1 for earlgrey. Assume a 50 ns glitch filter
contributing to input delay and that the delay above the 24 MHz clock's
period isn't enough to push the sampling point into the next clock cycle
(i.e. past the second edge after the output edge).

Signed-off-by: Alexander Williams <awill@opentitan.org>

subject: [i2c] Add bus arbitration for the target
body:
If the target "transmits" a high SDA, but SDA is low while SCL is high,
the target loses arbitration. In such cases, report that the transaction
is "NACK'd" and handle like any other NACK'd transfer.

This behavior would generally only apply in the case of broadcast read
commands that elicit responses from multiple targets (e.g. SMBus ARP's
general Get UDID command).

Signed-off-by: Alexander Williams <awill@opentitan.org>

subject: [i2c] Add clock synchronization for the controller
body:

early by comparing the value of SCL on the prior cycle. Immediately make

negedge.

Signed-off-by: Alexander Williams <awill@opentitan.org>

subject: [i2c] Harmonize fault cases with multi-controller
body:
Remove SDA interference triggering during SCL low, and fold the three
fault cases into multi-controller types:

- SDA interference represents lost arbitration due to the controller
  "transmitting" high SDA, but seeing low while SCL is high.
- SDA unstable represents unexpected Stop or Start conditions occuring
  while SCL is high.
- SCL interference is simply clock synchronization in a multi-controller
  environment. In single-controller environments, it's not expected, but
  in multi-controller cases, the interrupt should be disabled.

Signed-off-by: Alexander Williams <awill@opentitan.org>

subject: [i2c] Fix up simulation timing and reporting of fault cases
body:

subject: [i2c] Monitor stretching and lost arbitration for control symbols
body:
The control symbols were overlooked for clock stretching and
arbitration. SCL can be stretched on (repeated) Start and Stop symbols
like any other, and in the multi-controller context, SCL can be pulled
low early as well. If SCL is pulled low before the controller intended,
treat it as clock synchronization if SDA had already reached its desired
level first, and treat it as lost arbitration if SDA did not.

Categorize any SCL pulse that is shorter than the round-trip time as a
runt pulse. Add SCL interference events for runt SCL pulses detected by
the bus monitor, and treat these as arbitration loss, since the SCL
movement is too fast to satisfy any of the timing requirements.

Signed-off-by: Alexander Williams <awill@opentitan.org>

subject: [cryptolib] Also poll CSRNG command ready bit for additional data
body:
Previously, the command register ready bit was only polled for the
additional data when writing commands to the SW register of EDN.

When writing commands to CSRNG instead, not polling the command ready
bit could cause CSRNG to drop additional data provided by software while
handling a hardware command. Once the hardware command was handled, the
software instance would win arbitration and CSRNG would wait for
software to provide the dropped additional data, thereby stalling the
entire entropy complex. This would happen for example if a HW instance
request would collide with a software request. Since the software
command FIFO is only 2 entries deep, it can only be guaranteed to absorb
2 words if the software interface doesn't win arbitration immediately.

This is related to lowRISC/OpenTitan#22209 and lowRISC/OpenTitan#22210.

subject: [pattgen/rtl] Flop outputs to prevent glitches
body:
Prior to this commit, both `pcl_o` and `pda_o` were driven from
combinational logic.  In case of `pcl_o`, that logic was one mux (using
`polarity_q` as selector) that switched between the `pcl_int_q` and its
inverse.  In case of `pda_o`, that logic was a mux (using `!enable`,
where `enable` comes from a CSR field) that selected between 0 and
`data_q[bit_cnt_q]`.  Especially the latter term can be problematic,
because during the `[bit_cnt_q]` indexing the different bits of
`bit_cnt_q` can have different propagation delays to the mux structure
that selects one bit from `data_q`, which has a significant probability
of causing glitches on `pda_o`.

This commit prevents glitches by flopping both signals before outputting
them.

subject: [opentitantool] Factor JSON configuration files
body:
Third-party developers, such as Chrome OS, who use Teacup boards for
development and testing, will want to use how pins of HyperDebug are
routed to pins of the OpenTitan chip as declared in
hyperdebug_teacup.json.  However, depending on their test suites, they
may want HyperDebug to drive e.g. IOA4 as a UART, as GPIO with some
default level, or not drive in the "default" state prior to test
execution.  Even within OpenTitan repository, one could imagine separate
test suites wanting different default state.

In order to accomodate such differences, while still allowing re-use of
the lengthy list of how e.g. IOA4 is connected to CN8_10 on the board
(which will necessarily apply to all users of the Teacup board), this PR
factors `hyperdebug_teacup.json` into two files.  All users will
continue to use `hyperdebug_teacup.json`, which declares the signal
routing.  Tests in OpenTitan repo will additionally use the new
`hyperdebug_teacup_default.json` which sets up defaults on particular
pins.  Other users will combine the former with their own configuration
files.

feed has completed when it got told to stop.  This is problematic
because its `msg_feed_complete_o` signal is used by `prim_sha2` to
determine when to stop waiting for more data from the message FIFO.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [hmac/rtl] Wait for digest of complete block when stopping
body:
Prior to this commit, when HMAC was told to stop, it would wait for the
completion of a complete block based on its message length counter.
However, the relevant message length counter for this is inside
`prim_sha2` and depends on the digest size, leading to problems such as
issue #23163.

This commit fixes these problems by letting `prim_sha2` signal when it
is computing a digest for a complete block and by taking that signal
into account in `hmac`'s `done_state` FSM.

This resolves #23163.

Co-authored-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>
Signed-off-by: Martin Velay <mvelay@lowrisc.org>

subject: [hmac/rtl] Fix idle_o when told to stop
body:
Prior to this commit, `hmac_core` and thus the entire `hmac` module
would not raise the `idle_o` output when it got told to stop (#23036).
This is problematic because then HMAC cannot be clock-gated during
context switch (save & restore feature).  Clock gating would only work
when a message stream is fully processed (after the *process* command).

This commit fixes the problem by keeping track of idleness inside
`hmac_core`.  In addition to the conditions that existed before, this
tracker goes to idle when a *stop* command is received and the current
message block is completely processed.

This fixes #23036.

happened using a call stack as one or both of the compare operands when
the stack was empty. Whilst OTBN raises an error due to the use of the
empty stack the branch result goes to X (as the comparison inputs are
X) which produces Xs on the imem request interface.

With this change output from the stack gets squashed to 0 when its
empty.

subject: [otbn, rtl] Fix X-propagation issue in prefetch stage
body:
When executing near Xs in imem it's possible for Xs to be received on
the incoming imem data. The prefetcher looks at the incoming data to see
if its a branch instruction.

Previous to this change this branch check took priority over a check
related to looping which altered the request going to imem. So when the
incoming imem data was X, when simulation propagated Xs though ifs we
end up with an X on the imem request address.

With this change the check for the branch happens regardless of whether
or not the looping related logic activates and the branch logic itself
does not alter the imem request so it avoids generating Xs on the
external (to OTBN core) imem request interface.

subject: [sram_ctrl] Add readback feature
body:
When enabled with the SRAM_CTRL.READBACK CSR, the SRAM readback mode
checks each read and write to the SRAM.

On a read, the readback mode issues a second read to the same address
to check, whether the correct data was fetched from memory. On a write,
the readback mode issues a read to check, whether the data was actually
written into the memory. To avoid that the holding register is read,
the readback is delayed by one cycle.

On a mismatch, a fatal error is triggered and the STATUS.READBACK_ERROR
register is set.

To avoid RTL changes as much as possible, the readback mode is
implemented in the tlul_sram_byte module. In this module, after the
initial read or write was executed, the bus interface to the host is
stalled and the readback is performed. Due to the bus stalling, a
performance impact is expected.

subject: [rom] More comprehensive ROM_EXT version selection
body:

version number in selecting which slot to boot:

- If equal, select the slot with the greater minor version.
- If equal, select slot A.

policies where a newer ROM_EXT can be qualified in a testing/staging
fleet before committing to an anti-rollback event.

subject: [opentitantool] Advanced bitbanging
body:
This CL enhances the existing FTDI-inspired bitbanging supported by
HyperDebug.  In particular, it adds means of specifying that generation
of the waveform should be put on "pause" at a certain point, until a
certain logic level is seen on particular pins.

This feature allows generating I2C waveforms, while allowing the I2C
device to stretch the clock.  Or generating an edge on a GPIO pin at a
very precise time after OT has toggled some other pin, in order for a
test case to attempt to trigger a race condition.

subject: [opentitantool] Non-blocking bitbanging trait
body:
In order to make best use of the new advanced bit-banging support, one
should be able to perform other operations with opentitantool and
HyperDebug, while a bit-banging waveform is waiting for a trigger
condition.

This CL makes it such that while the `opentitantool gpio bitbang ...`
command still returns only when the waveform is complete, the underlying
opentitanlib methods are changed such that they must be repeatedly
polled.  This works well with `opentitansession`, in that the session
daemon process being single-threaded will be able to respond to the
repeated queries, while also serving requests from other invocations of
`opentitantool` in between.

Signed-off-by: Jes B. Klinke <jbk@chromium.org>

subject: [rv_dm,dv] Return more quickly on reset in rv_dm_tap_fsm_vseq
body:
This is fixing two separate problems. Firstly, the rv_dm_tap_fsm_vseq
sequence takes quite a while, issuing back-to-back CSR accesses. The
code in wait_to_issue_reset fails as a result, because it can't find a
good time to inject one. To avoid that happening, we notice when
wait_to_issue_reset is waiting and wait a few cycles without doing a
CSR access to give it a chance.

The second failure mode is more confusing! Here, we are running the
vseq multiple times, and issuing resets after each one. A run might
look like this:

    Start vseq 0
    Issue reset
    Disable fork
    Start vseq 1
    Issue reset
    Disable fork
    ...

The problem is that vseq 0 might not have stopped because of the first
reset. We start vseq 1, but it stays queued because vseq 0 is still
running. We then do the "disable fork" for the second time, killing
the process that had queued up vseq 1. This causes quite a cryptic
error from uvm_sequencer_base:

  The task responsible for requesting a wait_for_grant on sequencer
  'uvm_test_top.env.m_jtag_agent.sequencer' for sequence
  'uvm_test_top.env.virtual_sequencer.rv_dm_tap_fsm_vseq' has been
  killed, to avoid a deadlock the sequence will be removed from the
  arbitration queues

That turns out to be reasonable! We killed the process for something
that was awaiting arbitration, so there's no way to start its
sequence.

Returning more quickly should fix this.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [pwrmgr] Don't lock CONTROL until observing core_sleep
body:
To avoid race conditions with WFI and locking the CONTROL CSR
prematurely, wait until the transition out of FastPwrStateActive that
begins low power entry before locking the CONTROL CSR.

This allows software to clear CONTROL.LOW_POWER_HINT if an early
interrupt caused the "core_sleep" pulse to be too short for pwrmgr to
capture. Then, subsequent WFI instructions may still choose between full
power and a low power mode.

When software wakes up, it must attempt to clear CONTROL.LOW_POWER_HINT,
then busy-poll until it reads its value as 0. If pwrmgr triggered low
power entry, the CPU will poll until pwrmgr completes the low power
sequence. If pwrmgr did not trigger low power entry, the CPU's write
will succeed, and the read will immediately return 0.

Signed-off-by: Alexander Williams <awill@opentitan.org>

individual instances after enabling and then lock down instances

This commit thus adds a per-instance internal state read enable on top

state of all instances can be read and firmware can disable read access

subject: [flash_ctrl/rtl] Host data XOR address infection
body:
This commit adds the data XOR address infection mechanism. The goal
of this countermeasure is to detect faults on read addresses targeting
the flash controller.

On a host flash read, the address used for accessing the data is XORed
inside the flash_phy_rd module to the fetched data.

The address then is removed in the u_tl_adapter_eflash where the core has
a TL-UL interface to the flash memory. Here, the buffered address from the
incoming TL-UL read request is taken.

When a FI attack manipulates an address, data would be fetched from the
wrong address in the flash memory. But inside the flash_phy_rd module,
this manipulated address is XORed to the data. Now, when removing the
address by using the original address, and there is a difference from
a FI, the data would be faulty and the subsequent integrity check detects
the attack.

happen as a result of a flash ECC error. When this type of exception is
generated, the exception handler overwrites function argument registers

subject: [rv_dm] Fix RDC and DFT issue with resets
body:

in the core clock domain, placing them on the D input of the first flop
of the prim_flop_2sync, instead of the reset inputs of both flops. This
removes the asynchronous reset assertion that may cause RDC issues, and
it restores scan reset as the only reset for those 2 flops.

Note that prim_fifo_async_simple guarantees that a prior transaction in
flight will at least maintain its data values, since the holding
register is *not* reset. This mechanism does not guarantee that the
request will be squashed, but it *does* guarantee that the request will
not be malformed by the reset. In addition, if the JTAG reset is held
for long enough (i.e. >= the round-trip delay), the response for any
previously in-flight request will be dropped.

subject: [otbn,dv] Disable FI checks in DMEM req fifos
body:
These currently cause spurious errors in the otbn_sec_cm test. The
problem is that the count in the request fifo gets forced from 0 to 1.
This spits out a bogus TL request, and also causes an alert to be
raised by the sram adapter.

The alert is good: it's exactly what is supposed to happen.
Unfortunately, the request that goes out might be X (because the fifo
has never not been empty). Unfortunately, the TL response ends up
polluted with X and this ends up polluting the start/stop control FSM,
causing it to get stuck in the X state.

The end result is that we see a fatal alert with no corresponding
status change, causing a DV check to fail (because we always expect
OTBN to lock up after it generates a fatal alert).

This change disables fault injection on these particular FIFO
counters, side-stepping the issue.

subject: [i2c,dv] Split out Reference Model from Scoreboard
body:
The current state of the I2C DV environment is not great. Very little of the
hardware is modelled, sequence items are used to represent vastly different
things in different contexts, and checking in the scoreboard is deliberately
limited to a subset of fields we believe to have modelled correctly. The vseq's
frequently intertwine stimulus and checking, and often reach into other parts of
the DV environment (e.g. agent's monitor, scoreboard) to reset state when our
modelling is insufficient. This is not great.

This change begins to setup a new, principled foundation for DV by tackling the
scoreboard. Currently, as often is done in OpenTitan DV, the scoreboard performs
two functions, both the intended checking component, but also acts as a
reference model to try and predict future DUT behaviour. This leads to a very
dense and overloaded module, and makes it difficult to modify while maintaining
a clean seperation.
This commit splits the modelling components of the existing scoreboard into a
seperate component "i2c_reference_model" (aka predictor), leaving the scoreboard
as a more bare-bones comparator. The scoreboard maintains a handle to the
reference model, and is responsible for calling "process_tl_access()" based on
observed TL-UL bus activity. Ideally the reference model would communicate with
the scoreboard only via TLM ports/fifo, but this is not yet implemented.

This change also routes stimulus seq_items, generated by the vseq's to drive the
agent (particularly for DUT-Target tests), first into the reference model and
then onto the scoreboard. In some cases the items are passed-on unchanged to the
scoreboard, but sometimes we make modifications. This architecture is maybe not
ideal, but does clean up what we have currently, and could be iterated on.

Additional/Related Changes
- Cleanup i2c_monitor tran_id to start counting from 0.

Signed-off-by: Harry Callahan <hcallahan@lowrisc.org>

This was due to some undefined bits that were propagating through
CSRNG after a signal is forced. The forced signal caused a FIFO to
push in some undefined bits. This caused assertions to fail and
eventually the tlul interface to throw an error due to unexpected
data. This commit fixes the above issue by forcing all of the input
bits of the downstream FIFO to zero. This way no undefined bits will
propagate.

Something similar happens for the sfifo_gbencack_err. This commit
also fixes the sfifo_gbencack_err test by forcing adstage_glast to 0.
This ensures that no request to the downstream arbiter is made, which
used to trigger some assertions.

data, a call to 'csr_rd' will block until the D-channel response is

This causes issues when checking if the BUSY bit is unset, since it
can happen the flash_status write cleared the BUSY bit, but since the
D-channel response took long to be output by that time the BUSY bit
may have been set again.

So, if the BUSY bit is unset early due to backpressure, we don't check
that it's still set at a later point, since that can mean the BUSY bit
has been set again after being unset.

subject: [jtag,dv] Keep TCK running a short time after a transaction
body:
This handles a rather confusing situation in the DMI frontdoor. The
problem is that a DMI request has to travel from dmi_jtag to
dm_top (involving a CDC from TCK to the main clock) and then back
again (involving a CDC from the main clock back to TCK).

If we stop sending JTAG operations in that time, the CDC doesn't
actually get anywhere. The wait is jtag_agent_cfg_h.vif.wait_tck(10),
which ends up waiting based on elapsed time rather than clock edges.

The result is that when we send another JTAG operation to find out the
result of the operation, the "busy" status only makes it through the
CDC *after* the JTAG operation has finished and reported that the dm
is idle.

subject: [opentitantool] Arbitrary waveform generation via HyperDebug
body:
HyperDebug has fast DACs, meaning that we can have them generate
arbitrary waveforms on the analog output pins.

This is useful for verifying that the OpenTitan ADC filters have been
configured as intended, by simulating e.g. USB-PD negotiation going on
"on top of" the steady state CC voltage levels.

This feature builds on the existing support for streaming binary data
for bit-banging, and handling it on HyperDebug via a timer interrupt.

Current HyperDebug firmware supports short bursts of up to 2000 samples
at up to 1Msps, or streamed generation of arbitrary lengths at up to
around 80ksps.  (If necessary, HyperDebug firmware could be modified to
allocate larger buffers, such that more than 2000 samples could be
emitted at the maximum speed.)

subject: [entropy_src/rtl] Delay the main_sm_done signal
body:

signal arrived one cycle too early in the single lane mode. This

This in turn caused the issue that the last word from the precon
FIFO is not absorbed properly by SHA3.
This commit fixes this by delaying the main_sm_done signal by 1 cycle
in the single lane mode. The ht_error signal has to be delayed by 1
cycle as well to guarantee that the error signal arrives at the same
time as the main_sm_done signal.

factor in the `ack_i` signal coming from the Flash macro. While the open
source simulation model never really de-asserts `ack_i`, some real

buffers. This effectively halves the number of usable read buffers which
may have a negative impact on performance.

actual Flash macro request handshake for doing allocations.

subject: [otbn,dv] Avoid killing during TL read in otbn_stack_addr_integ_chk
body:
Diagnosing this took me ages! In this situation (with err_type = 1),
the vseq works forking into two processes. One injects an error on
every stack write. The other waits until it sees a read from the
stack, which should trigger an alert, and then tells the model to
go into a locked state.

Once the latter process finishes, we can release our forced signals
and wait until the RTL and the model raise an alert at the same time.
At this point, we use "disable fork"

The first process waited for reads from the stack using the
wait_for_flag() task which, in turn, used wait_for_run_completion() to
detect the end of a run (at which point, we weren't going to see the
flag change, so should stop early).

Unfortunately, wait_for_run_completion would sometimes wait for the
end of the run by polling the STATUS register. Doing so would normally
involve a TL transaction. The test was failing because we started a TL
transaction to read STATUS and then killed a process that was inside
the sequencer, in wait_for_item_done(). This meant that the
transaction blocked forever and we never passed the response back to
the sequence. As a result, the csr_rd task timed out and the test
failed.

The fix is rather simple in the end: if you want your process to be
disabled, don't do a front-door TL transaction.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

sometimes didn't make it across the initial EDN and CSRNG re-config
section. The reason is that the RNG inside AST produces raw entropy
at a lower rate while the entropy consuming part of AST still consumes
a reasonable amount of entropy. As a result and depending on the EDN
config, the esfinal FIFO would never fill up and the reconfiguration
section would never finish.

To fix this, this commit adds a timeout for the esfinal FIFO: If the
FIFO hasn't filled up within 32 ms (under normal conditions, this should
suffice to fill the FIFO easily), we proceed without a full FIFO.

This fixes lowRISC/OpenTitan#23606.

the conditioner is never active without a valid handshake on the CS AES
Halt interface.

interrupt might never finish and eventually time out.

interrupt to 2 health test windows per interrupt routine. The Observe
FIFO may run full afterwards but our DV environment can handle this and
having the FIFO run full between extracting contiguous entropy bits is
an actually relevant scenario.

d_ready to speed up the actual read out in the max rate test.

subject: [i2c,dv] Consolidate I2C item to model at transfer-level, use monitor output for expectations
body:
This large commit fixes a number of fundamental flaws and confusing design
decisions around the way we model TLM transactions using the i2c_item.

The major flaw this change initally set out to fix was that scoreboard
expectations were being formed by passing the generated stimulus from the
virtual sequences directly to the model/scoreboard. This is against UVM design
patterns, and severely limits the ability to predict behaviour when the effect
of the driver are fundamentally bypassed and unpredictable. In I2C, the receiver
in any transaction can alter the progression of the traffic by choosing to ACK
or to stretch SCL. In our I2C environment, where both endpoints are
operated/tested as both Controllers and Targets, this means any reactivity
in the Agent cannot be predictable, and sequences are therefore reduced to only
a very small subset of behaviour. This problem was partially circumvented by a
slew of configuration variables used to hold bits of state and signal events to other
components, but this is unclean and inconvenient.

To fix this problem, another intermediate issue needed to be addressed. The
i2c_item was grossly overloaded in the way it was used to represent different
things to different people across the testbench and agent. For read transfers,
the seq_item was used to capture the entire transfer (data_q[$] held all the
bytes of data), but for writes we would capture one item per entry in the
ACQFIFO CSR to signal an I2C transaction was taking place. Different fields in
the item were used for each use-case, and some were re-used with different
meanings for each case.
> There is also a third use of the i2c_item, again using different fields (with
> some overlap), which is to control the i2c_driver in discrete steps depending
> on the value of a control enum variable 'drv_type'. This use case remains, but
> should definitely be removed in the future.
To model at a transfer level, new fields 'rstart_front' and 'rstart_back' were
added to the item, which indicate if the start or the end of the transaction was
signalled using RSTARTS instead of STARTs and STOPs. The previous 'rstart' field
would be ambiguous when used for modelling at a transfer-level.

Additionally, this commit also importantly changes the way mis-addressed
transfers are captured and checked. Previously, the i2c_agent contained copies
of the DUT's configured Target-Mode addresses, and used these to change the way
it captured observations and generated stimulus based on if the address given
was known ahead of time to match the DUT. This is clearly a badly-designed
dependence between the modules, and by removing this pre-filtering of
transaction items, we now generate and check items which do not match the
targets address. These items are effectively the I2C-Controller shouting into
the void, which is a valid i2c transfer in terms of signalling, but in a single
controller, single target system, a wholly uninteresting one.

In short, this commit achieves the following:
- Reworks the i2c_item to model full 'i2c_transfers', and updates the
  i2c_monitor to generate seq_items at this level of abstraction, for both reads
  and writes.
- Change the reference_model/scoreboard to gather observations in this new
  format from the monitor only (connections to the vseqr are now removed)
- The i2c_monitor now generates valid transfer items for mis-addressed stimulus,
  easily observed by checking if the ITEM_T.addr_ack field is equal to i2c_pkg::NACK.
- Replaces the stimulus generation routines in the i2c_base_vseq with new,
  concise versions that no longer need to generate transaction items to send to
  the model/scoreboard. The previous code here was verbose, unclear and
  difficult to modify.
  - create_txn()/fetch_txn() now replaced by a single call to
  generate_agent_controller_stimulus(), which makes better use of types,
  targeted subroutines and randomization to achieve the same goal in a clear and
  simpler way.
- Renames variables across the env/agent cfgs, moved variables from the
  class-scope into task/function scope where possible, and used user-defined
  types where appropriate to aid readability.

Signed-off-by: Harry Callahan <hcallahan@lowrisc.org>

subject: [i2c,dv] Spawn i2c_agent base_seq driving hooks as background tasks
body:
The way that the i2c_agent drives the interface reactively currently has a small
race condition. We watch the in-progress transfer field 'inp_xfer.state' to know
when the transfer has progressed to a new state, but sometimes the previous
driving hook returns on the same timestep as the state variable changes. This
causes the agent to miss the state-change and hence miss it's hook for when the
bus should be driven.

I think this architecture could be iterated on in the future, but for now a
solution is to schedule bus driving events into background processes and to not
await them to finish before going back to wait on the next state change. These
hooks should not overlap in practice. Since we do not change i2c_agent sequences
on-the-fly during testcases, these background threads can all complete in their
own time.

subject: [i2c,dv,chip] Fixup the chip_sw_i2c_device vseq to use xfer-level TLM
body:
This builds upon changes from a number of previous PRs and commits to collect
and drive Agent Stimulus using the transfer-level item abstractions. This
sequence previously made use of create_txn()/fetch_txn() routines inspired by
the previous i2c_base_vseq code, which had a much looser model of what each
sequence item represented. That model was re-worked in #23911, and so this
sequence also needs to collect and drive transaction data at this new level of
abstraction.

Firstly, this sequence got a cleanup pass, removing unnecessary code, adding
comments and some minor refactors such as moving the i2c_agent timing parameter
configuration into a separate routine.

Secondly and more substantially, the code responsible for generating
stimulus `send_i2c_host_rx_data()` has been replaced with a new but equivalent
routine `drive_i2c_agent_stimulus()`, which now works at the transfer-level.
The driven stimulus is still the same, comprising of:
- An Agent-Controller READ transfer
- An Agent-Controller WRITE transfer, writing the same data received in the read
payload.
Transfer read data is captured via a TLM fifo in the chip sequencer
'i2c_rd_fifos', which needs to be connected to the monitor's
'controller_mode_rd_item_port'. This is another required change based on
previous monitor reworks.

Note. the routine convert_i2c_txn_to_drv_q() has been copied from the block
level base_vseq, which is responsible for converting transfer-level items into a
quirky queue of items which is how we currently interface with the driver. This
behaviour will eventually be replaced, at which point this duplicate code can be
removed. However, that task is a future improvement.

subject: [flash_ctrl/doc] Document ECC/scrambling require 64-bit aligned accesses
body:
The minimum granularity of host and controller interface accesses is
32 bits while the Flash word size is 64 bits. Internally, invalid Flash
words (uninitialized) or sub words (resulting from unaligned
program operations) are marked and detected using all-one vectors.

As reliability ECC and scrambling both operate on full 64-bit Flash
words, the detection of uninitialized sub words no longer works whenever
ECC and/or scrambling are enabled. In this case, operations should
always be made using 64-bit aligned addresses. This commit documents
this requirement in the design spec and programmer's guide.

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#13429.

subject: [i2c,dv] Integrate i2c monitor data into reference model predictions
body:
This is part of a larger push to improve the i2c_reference_model to start making
better and more granular predictions.

This commit achieves the following:
- Connects the i2c_monitor's target-mode transfer ports and in-progress ports
through to the reference model.
- Creates a local queue of predicted controller-mode transfers based on CSR
access stimulus that defines the transfers. Rather than pushing these items
directly to the scoreboard, we need to keep an in-order list to fuse
with bus observations from the i2c monitor.
  - Create a separate queue of both read and write transfers (prev_item[$])
  together, as determination of the next transfer always depends on the
  ending conditions of the previous one, no matter if it was a read or a write.
- Fuses observed ACK/NACK bits from the bus with the predictions from the CSR
accesses. This is not yet particularly interesting, but will be crucial for
better modelling mid-transfer inputs in the future.

When a new word is being pushed into the observe FIFO while we are in the
address phase of reading the observe_fifo_depth register, the prediction
will be off by one cycle. The reason for this is that the prediction can't
be done while the register is being read, so the prediction has to wait until
the register is not busy anymore. This commit adds two additional variables
that allow for accurate prediction even in this edge case.

subject: [i2v,dv] Move TP:target_error_intr / i2c_target_unexp_stop to V3
body:
This test is currently broken, and the feature is unused by any test software or
mentioned in the programmers guide. It's purpose was to detect invalid bus
driving by the I2C-Controller, when a STOP condition was received at an earlier
point that expected during a READ transfer.

Due to previous RTL changes to enable multi-controller support, new logic has
been added to explicitly allow bus arbitration. This logic fundamentally aims
to detect another I2C bus-device driving the bus when we (the DUT) expect to be
driving it.

In the context of an unexpected STOP condition during a READ, any attempt for
the I2C-Controller device to drive a STOP will cause the target-mode logic to
detect an arbitration failure, and to back-off the transfer, awaiting the next
STOP condition. (Due to the open-drain bus signalling scheme, drive-conflicts
and hence arbitration failures can only be detected when a party that has
released the bus high observes another party driving it low. To signal a stop
condition, a low-to-high transition on SDA is required, and hence a
drive-conflict and arbitration loss is detected when the other endpoint pulls
SDA low, before it can even signal the stop condition).

This arbitration failure and back-off happens before the logic that creates the
'UnexpStop' interrupt fires, and hence this interrupt can no longer be triggered.

I think this testpoint may possibly be re-written to confirm we can identify an
unexpected STOP condition via the arbitration-lost signalling, but it may end up
getting dropped altogether. For now, move it to V3.

Signed-off-by: Harry Callahan <hcallahan@lowrisc.org>

subject: [i2c,dv] Fixup test failures in the i2c_target_hrst_vseq
body:
This test falls squarely under the 'needs improvement' category, so this commit
takes the opportunity to remove & clarify some of its worse aspects while
getting things going again after previous changes caused it to regress.

- This test's name and description is confusing, to start with. I think 'hrst'
may have been an acronym for 'host-reset', but this test does not do that. It's
description talks about introducing 'glitches', but really it introduces
unexpected, non-protocol START and STOP conditions which cause a transfer to end
early. These aren't really 'glitches' at all, as it is valid to send a S or P at
any time.
- The test constrains stimulus to only use 'WRITE-transfers', and then points to
"glitches" in READ-transfer being covered by the i2c_glitch_vseq. As a result,
all of the code in this vseq relating to generating READ-transfer stimulus is
dead. Which is about 30% of the whole module. All this code has been removed,
and the existing implementation simplified to reflect this.
- The task "stop_target_interrupt_handler()" just duplicates the base class
implementation. Removed.
- The vseq tried to keep the scoreboard/env alive after introducing each
"glitch" by reaching out and clearing state in the i2c_agent's monitor and also
the env's scoreboard. This is deeply unpleasant, and added a whole bunch of code
to both of those modules just for this particular testcase. There is in-fact a
much easier way to do this, which is now possible after previous refactors to
make the i2c_item model a single i2c-transfer at a TLM level. An early START or
STOP condition just signals an early end-of-transfer, and we simply need to
ensure the monitor will end the transfer when it sees this condition. This logic
has already been added to most routines inside the monitor, but it was not added
to the routine which captures the address+direction byte, so it has been added
now. All of the sideband 'cfg.monitor_rst' mechanism has been removed, as has
the code which reaches in and artificially ends the transfer early. This is no
longer needed, now that we just properly model the S/P condition ending the
current transfer.
  - This also removes the need to mess around with 'skipping-starts' and other
  changes to stimulus, as the monitor will automatically start capturing a new
  transfer if the "glitch" stimulus event is a START (i.e. an RSTART in this context).

Signed-off-by: Harry Callahan <hcallahan@lowrisc.org>

subject: [i2c,dv] Fixup failures in the 'i2c_host_fifo_full_vseq' test
body:
This test just needed some small tweaks to align stimulus with the new
abstractions. I also gave it a cleanup while I was here.

Note. There was an icebox comment (#18979) that I have removed while here. In
essence, it described a more directed testcase that just checked the fifo_full
status bit when in response to overfilling and then emptying the fifo.

I think this is not required for the following reasons:
1. This sort of directed testcase mostly just re-verifies the hookup of the
   standard fifo status signals, which have been verified at a primative level to
   be correct in isolation, and get test coverage across many blocks in OpenTitan.
2. Instead of a directed testcase, we should just model the fifo(s) in the
   i2c_reference_model(), and use that to predict levels/status signals. This way
   we get checking across all possible stimulus, and re-use of the checking in any
   environment where the i2c_env components can be instantiated (one day at
   top-level too).
3. We shouldn't encourage directed tests when modelling the behaviour in a
   predictor is not that hard. With the recent changes to standardize the i2c_item
   as an TLM-representation of an i2c-transfer, this really shouldn't be difficult to
   model. I think the inconsistent DV architecture made this difficult in the past,
   and under those circumstances a directed tests certainly would have been quicker
   to implement.

while waiting for entropy. After this point, the scoreboard would no
longer perform any checks on the command FIFO, no longer update the
internal state, and no longer compare the generated bits of the
corresponding app. This is bad in two ways: either it can go completely
unnoticed or lead to failing checks when comparing internal states
between the scoreboard and the DUT using check_internal_state().

Luckily, the fix is easy. We can just replace the `return` keyword by
a `continue` to drop the current item of the queue and start over in case

subject: [sw,lib] Add compile-time check for log argument size
body:
When an argument (to be formatted via format specifiers in a given string) is passed to the
`LOG` function either directly or indirectly, this value is listed as a variable argument,
and then read from the va_list. In the case of DV logging via the backdoor, this is always
read as a `uint32_t`. In the case of core logging (on Ibex), this is either `uint32_t`,
`size_t`, `uintptr_t` or `status_t` (a struct storing an `int32_t`).

As a result, when a 64 bit integer is passed into some debug logging functionality without
appropriate explicit casting, no implicit casting is performed as may be expected by a
programmer, and instead the 64 bit integer argument is read as a 32 bit variable argument.

As per N1570 7.16.1.1 paragraph 2: "... if type is not compatible with the type of the
actual next argument (as promoted according to the default argument promotions), the
behaviour is undefined, except for the following cases:
    - one type is a singed integer type, the other type is the corresponding unsigned
    integer type, and the value is representable in both types.
    - one type is pointer to void and the other is a pointer to a character type."

Because there is no implicit cast, any such invocations of debug printing functionality
without casting 64 bit arguments are undefined behaviour, and may cause unreliable and
unexpected behaviour in logging. This can compound and mislead separate debugging efforts,
and so should not be allowed to occur.

This commit introduces additional macro functionality in order to check the type of each
of these variable arguments at compile time. As a result, any code that provides an
incorrect argument to e.g. the `LOG_INFO` function will result in the code not compiling
with an appropriate error message pointing out the line and a suggestion for how to fix
the problem. As this is all done via `_Generic` and `static_assert`, no additional
runtime cost is added to perform these checks.

As part of this functionality, this commit expands the base library of macros to include
generic macros for invoking a macro per each argument in a variable list, as well as
checking the size of a given argument.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

(any functions like `CHECK` or `LOG_INFO` that call LOG).

This can be verified by running

```
./bazelisk.sh build -t- --keep_going --define bitstream=skip
	//util/... //sw/...
```

All fixes simply involve performing an appropriate cast from a 64
