subject: [fpga,rom] Speed up ROM splicing by omitting contiguous addresses
body:
We take a reasonable assumption from the UpdateMEM documentation and
intuiton that UpdateMEM's runtime scales in some way with the number of
addresses (i.e. "non-contiguous writes", even if the data is contiguous)
in the ROM to splice.

Currently, when generating an UpdateMEM-compatible MEM file for the ROM
(unlike the OTP), we omit an address for each individual ROM word. This
is despite the fact that, for the majority of widths, the number of
characters per word will be such that data is written to contiguous
addresses.

Introduce logic to check whether ROM word addresses are contiguous, and,
if so, omit the redundant address from the generated MEM file. UpdateMEM
will then produce identical bitstreams with the new ROM file, but basic
empirical testing suggests that ROM splicing speeds up by up to 4-5x.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [tl,dv] Document, rename and fix chk_prot_mask_in_enabled_lanes
body:
This behaviour actually changes slightly because we base the
calculation of active lanes on DataWidth instead of SizeWidth. The
latter is TL_SZW.

For a 32-bit bus, TL_DW is 32. As such, byte lane zero is all
addresses that are multiples of 32/8 = 4.

In the existing code:

 a_addr[SizeWidth-1:0]    is the index of the lowest active lane.
 (a_mask >> ..)           is the mask, shifted to put the lowest
                          active lane to the start.
 (.. >> (1 << a_size))    is the mask shifted by another 2^a_size bits.

This checks that none of the lanes above the active lanes have a
nonzero mask.

In the new code:

 (1 << a_size) - 1            is a pattern of the bits for active
                              lanes, starting at index zero.
 .. << a_addr[SizeWidth-1:0]  is the pattern of active lanes, starting
                              in the right place.
 ~(...)                       is the pattern of nonactive lanes
 a_mask & ...                 is the pattern of inactive lanes that
                              are HIGH in the mask.

This should behave the same for the lanes above the active lanes but
should also require the mask to be zero for lanes below the active lanes.

The other change is a minor tweak, and changes discussion of "enabled"
lanes to talk about "active" lanes (matching the terminology in the
spec).

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [dv, alert_receiver_driver] Driver refactor for correct alert handshake
body:
Similarly to the monitor, the driver has been refactor so it tackles either
alerts or pings.

The driver now has the capability to retract a ping if it sees an alert before
the ping is driven.

In addition, the queues holding alert and pings are cleared during reaset, just
so if the driver has sent a ping/alert before reset and the handshake is not
completed the driver won't assume the handshake needs to continue after reset.

Finally, the driver can be configured via the config object by setting
'drive_ping' to zero so it doesn't drive pings. This is particularly useful
since the alert escalation agent has a ping sequence in the run_phase which runs
forever. Said sequence may interfere with other TB checks if a ping is driven
when the checks aren't expecting any alert such as at the end of a VSEQ.

Signed-off-by: Antonio Martinez Zambrana <amz@lowrisc.org>

subject: [reggen] Undetectable zero assignment
body:
While doing FPV analysis on rv_plic, we realised that two variables'
initial assignment to zero could never have an effect. This is because
every bit of the variables gets explicitly written in a continuous
assignment just below.

For example, addr_hit is sized to have indices ${len(regs_flat)}-1:0
and then its bits are assigned in a loop over regs_flat, ensuring all
indices will be assigned.

reg_we_check is sized the same and assigned with an equivalent loop.

subject: [RACL] Fix RACL ranges.
body:
A previous commit changed RACL ranges from a parameter to a signal,
however the topgen templates were not updated.

This commit fixes RACL ranges up such that they are working again with
topgen:

* RACL range support was added to bus_interfaces.py such that the
  template can know which interface uses RACL ranges.

* The parameter RaclPolicySelRangesRamNum was removed from the ip hjson
  and its name aligned with what the template previously generated.
  The template now also generates the necessary default value if RACL
  ranges are disabled.

* toplevel_racl.tpl was split into two files to allow generating the
  necessary parameters and signals:
  toplevel_racl_parameters.tpl and toplevel_racl_signals.tpl

* The toplevel_racl_pg.sv.tpl has been updated to only emit RACL range
  parameters for interfaces that support it. And the format was slightly
  adjusted to not generate lines that are too long.

the otp secret1 partition holds flash_ctrl keys. Darjeeling has no flash
and has no keys in otp.

Detect this examining the content of the otp rather than using an
ipgen_param.  This assumes the flash keys are in the secret1 partition,
and are named "flash*key_seed" (case doesn't matter). If in some future
otp mmap the location of these keys changes we can revisit this
detection.

subject: [test,flash_ctrl_idle_low_power_test] Correct check for sleep abort
body:
The test expects the sleep to abort because of the inflight flash
transaction. Currently, this is done by calling looking at the reset
reason stored in retentation by the ROM. This is incorrect since
if the device wrongly enter (shallow) low-power sleep then it would
not reset so the ROM will not run and rstmgr will play not role.
Instead, the correct way to check this is to ask the pwrmgr's wakeup
info and check for the aborted type.

Note that the test by itself was still performing as expected because
the aon_timer is configured in a way that if the device ever entered
sleep then it would reset due to an watchdog bite and this would
cause the test to fail anyway. But it would not catch other types
of errors such as the pwrmgr entering sleep and waking up unexpectedly.

Signed-off-by: Amaury Pouly <amaury.pouly@lowrisc.org>

subject: [otlib] Improve serial port RX buffer clearing
body:
When clearing the uart RX buffers, there are two buffers to take
care of: the host buffers and the device buffers. The host buffers
are taken care of, but in the case of CW310 (which uses the SAM3x),
the code is not currently doing anything for the device buffers.
This is different on other backands such as hyperdebug which have
a dedicated usb request to achieve.

This commit changes the behaviour of the default "serial port uart"
implementation to both clear host buffers and try to read from the
device until we get no more data (or a timeout expires). This change
will primarily affect the cw310 (sam3x) backend. On hyperdebug, since
we first clear the device buffers and then the host buffers, reading
from the device will not yield any data and this change will only
result in a short (5ms) delay.

subject: [pentest] Add ASM trigger high/low
body:
Until now, we've used the pentest_set_trigger_high/low functions.
However, this is problematic as:
- These functions are calling multiple other sub-functions which
  contain a lot of code. Hence, executing this function takes
  a lot of time.
- This is bad for the pentest_set_trigger_high as, once the
  trigger raises, the function still executes for a couple
  of cycles. In these cycles we assume that we are already
  executing our FI target code sequence but instead we
  still execute the trigger function. Hence, we could
  land up attacking the trigger function.
- Similar, for the pentest_set_trigger_low, it takes
  actually quite some time until the trigger falls down.
- As these functions are function calls, they mess around
  with the registers. Hence, we need to initialize the
  registers after the trigger high function. Again, with
  this we could land up attacking the register init.

As measuring this cycle delay is quite challenging, we've
decided to implement an optimized trigger function that
purely consists of ASM instructions. Hence, we also
can move the register initialization before the trigger
as we know which registers are getting touched by the
trigger set macro.

Use with caution as it is not guaranteed that this will
work in future OpenTitan versions.

Signed-off-by: Pascal Nasahl <nasahlpa@lowrisc.org>
Co-authored-by: Siemen Dhooghe <sdhooghe@google.com>

subject: [dv] Simplify use of dv_base_reg::atomic_en_shadow_wr
body:
This code was trying to ensure that the semaphore had exactly one
token in it. Knowing that it would only ever have at most one token,
the code worked by trying to get that token if there was one and then
putting a new token in.

Casting the result of the try_get() function to void causes a lint
error from Verissimo. And there's a simpler way to get the same
behaviour: just make a new semaphore!

This would be a problem if anything took a reference to the old
semaphore (leaving a "dangling pointer") but a quick grep shows that
this doesn't happen.

subject: [sw,silicon_creator,rom] Add a ROM state API
body:
The ROM state API allows for defining a set of ROM states and their
associated hooks and callback. Each state is defined by its run
callback, and two hooks: the pre-run hook is executed prior to the run
callback while the post-run one runs after.
The rom_state_fsm() function walks through the ROM states, as each state
run callback returns the next ROM state to transition to.

ROM state hooks can be overridden by silicon creator implementations,
through an external, potentially closed source, code repository.

subject: [mdbook] Add patch for .mdbookignore
body:
Mdbook has no way to ignore files when copying the website. There
is an unmerged PR (https://github.com/rust-lang/mdBook/pull/1908)
which adds a .mdbookignore file to do that. This commit cherry
picks this PR as a patch. This is not entirely straightforward
however:
- the PR modifies files which are not found in the release source
  (like the documentation)
- the PR modifies Cargo.toml but the git's version differs from
  the crates.io version (which normalizes Cargo.toml)
- the PR applies on the latest version, but we use version 0.4.43

For this reason, the patch is a trimmed down and manually edit
version of the PR. Furthermore, there is another difficulty:
the patch makes `ignore` a required dependency when previously
mdbook only had it as an optional (and not enabled) dependency,
it also bumps the version. For this reason, this commit manually
adds the required version of `ignore` to the Cargo.toml and uses
rules_rust crate annotations to add a dependency from mdbook to
this version of `ignore`.

subject: [rtl,sec] Define more precise version of ASSERT_ERROR_TRIGGER_ALERT
body:
Existing properties like ASSERT_PRIM_COUNT_ERROR_TRIGGER_ALERT aren't
actually true in a formal setting! The problem is that they measure
the time between a bad thing happening and the alert_p signal going
high. But there is a stateful interface between the alert sender and
receiver, so that time depends on the behaviour of the alert receiver.

I started thinking about how to reason carefully about this, but
realised (with help...) that it was silly! We actually have formal
verification of the alert machinery (for example, see the
lowrisc:fpv:prim_alert_rxtx_fpv core). As such, it probably makes more
sense to be checking that after the bad thing happens, the error is
passed to the alert system. Then the existing (shared) DV for the
alert system will check that the alert_tx_o signal is updated
accordingly.

body:
Adds a word-offset of 1 to the index of the second decoy in `hardened_memcpy`
so that we have more possible source/destination pairs. Otherwise, there would
only be 4 possible unique pairs; 4 word-sized increments after `decoy[3] =
decoy[7]` would be `decoy[7] = decoy[3]`. Adding an offset results in more
unique pairs for minimal overhead.

This doesn't really have an effect on `hardened_memeq` since all the decoys
have to be equal there, but I changed it there anyway just to keep the pattern
consistent.

subject: [rom_ctrl,rtl] Weaken an assertion to make it true!
body:
In the main FSM, there is an edge from ReadingLow to ReadingHigh which
is supposed to be taken when we pass the last word to KMAC.

Originally, it was encoded as this:

    if (counter_lnt && kmac_rom_rdy_i && kmac_rom_vld_o) begin
      state_d = ReadingHigh;
    end

which means "if we are sending the last word (so counter_lnt is true)
and the transfer goes through (rdy & vld), then we should jump to the
ReadingHigh state.

We noticed that you never see it when kmac_rom_vld_o is false and
realised that this *can't* happen. The counter_lnt signal says that we
presented the last word to KMAC on the previous cycle (and the valid
signal was definitely high).

The code changed to

    if (counter_lnt && kmac_rom_rdy_i) begin
      state_d = ReadingHigh;
    end

which is slightly simpler and (to make sure we didn't get it wrong),
we added the CounterLntImpliesKmacRomVldO_A assertion. These changes
happened in bbc658ebfa4.

Unfortunately, the assertion isn't necessarily true! This is because
it doesn't also assume we're in the ReadingLow state (the only time it
matters). Make the precondition more precise. It is now provable with
Jasper (and the assertion still covers the check we need).

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

the flop directly for forcing. This meant that the forcing would delay

subject: [uartdpi] Exit string for simulator exit
body:
This adds an option to the UART DPI to define an exit string that when
seen will exit the simulator. This is useful as a way for software to
exit the simulator where there are no other ways to exit the simulator.

By default this exit methodology is disabled so should be safe to
integrate into OpenTitan. It is a more general implementation for the
exit methodology already used in Sonata:
https://github.com/lowRISC/sonata-system/blob/a9142361a190da2a196556b658f516cb9abe90b6/vendor/patches/lowrisc_ip/uartdpi/0002-Simulator-Exit-Condition.patch

subject: [dtgen] Add ipgen extension to expose ipconfig parameters
body:
This extension will look at the ipconfig parameters and automatically
generate code for those parameters marked with `dtgen`. The format
of the `dtgen` dictionary is currently as follows:
- `type`: type of the data exposed by the dt API. Only `uint8` is
  currently supported but the code is architectured in a way that
  it can easily support any scalar type
- `name` (optional): name to use (otherwise the parameter name)
  This controls the API which will be named `dt_<ip>_<name>()`
- `doc`: optional documentation of the parameter.

The most important part of the generated code is a new dt function
for each attribute of the form:

subject: [rv_dm/rtl] Disable DMI/JTAG TAP when HW Debug goes off outside reset
body:
Life Cycle Controller (lc_ctrl) enables or disables HW Debug functions
of OpenTitan through its `lc_hw_debug_en_o` output.  This signal gets
flopped (in `rv_dm_dmi_gate` when the top-level design uses a
TL-UL-based Debug Module Interface (DMI) or in `pinmux_strap_sampling`
when the top-level design uses a JTAG-based Test Access Port (TAP)). The
respective flop is *not* reset during non-debug-module (NDM) resets, so
that a DMI or JTAG connection survives an NDM reset.  lc_ctrl itself
*is* reset during an NDM reset.

There are two mechanisms for clearing these flops and hence disabling
the DMI or JTAG TAP (apart from resetting the flops, of course):
* lc_ctrl's `lc_escalate_en_o` output, which is On when lc_ctrl signals
  a fatal escalation that locks the chip up;
* lc_ctrl's `lc_check_byp_en_o` output, which is On whenever a life
  cycle transition is initiated, so that the flops gating the DMI or
  JTAG TAP get a new value dependent on whether HW Debug is enabled in
  the new life cycle or not.

However, there is a third scenario in which these flops should be
cleared: in lc_ctrl's `PostTransSt` state.  This terminal FSM state is
reached when `lc_ctrl` could not successfully complete a life cycle
transition.  In this case, `lc_ctrl_signal_decode` sets
`lc_hw_debug_en_o` to Off, which essentially disables everything the
Debug Module can do, but the DMI/JTAG connection is left intact.  One
can no longer do anything through this DMI/JTAG connection other than
accessing the Debug Module, but for consistency and to add another
safety net, this access should be disabled as well.

This commit adds a new output to `lc_ctrl`, `lc_hw_debug_clr_o`, which
is set to On in the aforementioned third scenario.  `rv_dm_dmi_gate` and
`pinmux_strap_sampling`, respectively, get connected to this new signal
and use it to clear their flops storing the `lc_hw_debug_en` value.

Version implications:
All three involved CIPs, `lc_ctrl`, `pinmux`, and `rv_dm`, have their
patch version incremented because this is a HW change that is not
visible to SW through CSRs.

Verification stage implications:
* The verification stage of `pinmux` is kept constant because the
  existing FPV covers the new `lc_hw_debug_clr_i` input (through an
  assertion on `u_pinmux_strap_sampling.pinmux_hw_debug_en_q`).
* The verification stage of `rv_dm` is decremented to V1 because the new
  `lc_hw_debug_clr_i` input isn't covered by the existing DV.  This is
  tracked in issue #27435.  The renewal of the V2S sign-off is tracked
  in issue #27437.
* The verification stage of `lc_ctrl` is decremented to V1 because the
  new `lc_hw_debug_clr_o` output isn't covered by the existing DV.  This
  is tracked in issue #27436.  The renewal of the V2S sign-off is
  tracked in issue #27438.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [prim, rtl] Deadcode else statement when state_q is IsStd
body:
diff_check_ok true means that we have differential pairs 2 cycles
ago (with some amount of random cdc delay). We further flop the
output of the 2sync flop to diff_pq and diff_nq. If diff_check_ok
is false, this means the the pairs are no longer differential
atleast 2 cycles before. But since we flop the synchronized output
to diff_xq registers, means that the synchronized output pairs on
last cycle were differential.

With the above explanation, in state IsStd when diff_check_ok is
no longer true, we look for diff_n_edge and diff_p_edge and they
must be differential. This leads state_d to jump into IsSkewed.
So, this is impossible to jump into SigInt when the state is
IsStd.

The reason why we care about this change is jasper analyzed the
coverage of this else block as dead. This PR tweak the case for
state is IsStd, to just look for diff_check_ok and it is false
then jump into IsSkewed.

This change has also got checked through an assertion saying
if state_q is in IsStd then we can either have diff_check_ok or
diff_p_edge and diff_n_edge are differential.

Signed-off-by: Kinza Qamar <kqzaman@lowrisc.org>

with sideloaded keys from the keymgr, but directly compared the output

subject: [usbdev] Conditional update of rxenable_out register
body:
Avoid a sw-hw race in which the USB device may disable OUT packet
reception on an endpoint - because of the set_nak_out functionality -
and software then re-enables OUT packet on that endpoint when it
was simply trying to re-enable OUT packet reception on another
active endpoint.

This is achieved by including 'preserve' bits in the upper half of
word writes to the rxenable_out register; software may then update
only the endpoint(s) it wants to affect.

The use of 'preserve' bits, along with the priority of software writes
over hardware clears achieves backwards compatibility whilst allowing
firmware to be simplified on future versions of the USB device.

subject: [imm_section] Do not record the codebase clean/modified status
body:
We cannot record clean/modified status because this affects build
reproducibility during ROM_EXT signing.

During a signing ceremony:
- First we generate pre-signing artifacts, typically in a clean codebase.
- Next, we take hashes of the pre-signing artifacts offline and sign them
  with our signing infrastructure.
- Finally, we bring the offline signatures back to the codebase and land
  them in an appropriate `signatures` subdirectory.  This modifies the
  codebase, which then causes a change in the build_status value, which
  causes bazel to rebuild pre-signing artifacts, which invalidates the
  signatures.

(cherry picked from commit 4e75543236e9a943094dc2b4c1848e6a2b726574)

subject: [doc] Remove requirement to enable/disable CSRNG and ENTROPY_SRC in sync
body:
This requirement got added by c6d92ff95156897cb3b98a9e103d87cd6856372c
and was required as the handshake interfaces between previous versions
of ENTROPY_SRC and CSRNG were erroneously not stateless (for details,
see lowRISC/OpenTitan#17941). This issue got fixed before the
Earlgrey production tapeout (see lowRISC/OpenTitan#21787). In the
meantime, it has been successfully verified on silicon that ENTROPY_SRC
can be disabled/re-enabled while CSRNG remains running. However, the
interfaces between CSRNG and the EDNs are still not stateless and
therefore, the EDNs can only be disabled and re-enabled together with
CSRNG.

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#26779.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

subject: [edn/doc] Document how to uninstantiate a CSRNG instance through EDN
body:
If firmware just disables EDN, there is a high risk of leaving the
associated CSRNG instance in an undetermined state. Getting out of this
state means disabling and re-enabling and thus reconfiguring both EDNs
and all CSRNG instances which is non-ideal.

This document, how firmware can safely uninstantiate a CSRNG instance
through EDN without to enable reconfiguring individual EDNs.

This is related to lowRISC/OpenTitan#26781.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

subject: [doc] Document how to disable ENTROPY_SRC while CSRNG/EDN remain running
body:
Disabling ENTROPY_SRC (as well as the analog noise source) once all
CSRNG instances have been seeded helps saving power. At the same time,
CSRNG can remain powered to keep serving entropy using the current
seeds. Not having to disable/re-enable the entire entropy complex is
beneficial from a programmer's perspective.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

This change adds the ability to provide an HJSON testcase file to the
OTBN standalone simulation runner.

The standalone runner will:

- Load initial register values (provided as a dictionary of label-to-integer

allowing for more targeted testing and debugging.

by 100, and the Hyperdebug firmware then performs the corresponding
multiplication to retrieve the original baud rate. Perform the
calculation on the host as well and check that the decompressed value
matches the initial value, emitting a warning if some data has been
lost.

Probably in practice no baud rate that can be used with Hyperdebug will
face this issue, but it's still better to encode for this edge case than
rely on it implicitly working.

subject: [build] Introduce OTP emulation images.
body:
This change is in preparation for managing the SiVal silicon
configuration using a separate OTP scaffolding. The
`//sw/ip/otp_ctrl/data/earlgrey_skus/emulation` targets will contain
OTP images used for simulation as well as FPGA emulation. FPGA emulation

subject: [rules,rom] Mark legacy_rom_targets targets with compatible info
body:
Currently, opentitan_binary creates a single target for all platforms
(cw310, cw340, sim_dv, etc). This is in contrast to opentitan_test which
creates one per platform. This creates a difficulty when building the
(test) ROM: we have a single target but we want to extract, say, the
CW310 VMEM for splicing. This is done by the legacy_rom_targets macro
which mimics per-platform targets which used to exists with the old
build rules.

Unfortunately, with multi-top this causes some issues. Taking the
test_rom target as an example: this target is marked as compatible
with all tops, but note that the Earlgrey target has a CW310 VMEM
whereas the Darjeeling does not. As a result, trying to build a
target created by legacy_rom_targets for the CW310 will try to extract
the CW310 VMEM, even for a Darjeeling build. Obviously, such a VMEM
does not exist so trying to expand this target somewhere will fail.

The solution adopted by this commit is to mark target created by
legacy_rom_targets with compatibility information based on the top.
This can be done by passing extend information to the macro so that
it knows, for example, that building a CW310 VMEM is only compatible
with Earlgrey. Fortunately, this problem had already arised with
opentitan_test so most of the infrastructure to figure this out is
already there.

subject: [rom_ctrl,rtl] Add a flop between rom_ctrl and kmac
body:
This injects a clock edge between data coming out of the ROM and data
going into KMAC to be hashed. Inserting the delay is pretty trivial:
we just use a prim_fifo_sync.

There *is* an area vs. efficiency question. Because there is no
pass-through, a prim_fifo_sync with depth 1 will have half throughput,
because it has to alternate between taking an item and passing it on.
Although, there's the bandwidth to do both on the same cycle, breaking
the combinatorial path means that we can't pass the KMAC block's
"ready" signal all the way back to the ROM.

This works perfectly well, but takes twice as long as you might hope.

A lazy workaround is to use Depth = 2. This is a little silly, because
it uses twice as much area as necessary. But it's very easy from a
coding perspective!

work around short transient network failures and rate-limiting issues
that we occasionally encounter in our CI environment.

We need to manually implement a basic exponential-backoff scheme for the
toolchain download itself (compared to the initial query), because there
is still the possibility for mid-stream failures after a successful HTTP
status code. `urllib3` cannot handle this natively, so we wrap in
additional logic to handle this case.

This is implemented manually wrapping `urllib` rather than using the
`urllib3` dependency because the Python interpreter that the bitstreams
workspace is currently interpreted with has no additional packages
installed, only the standard library.

This should reduce any flakiness in the bitstream cache due to transient
network failures or rate limits.

subject: [ci] Retry CI Curl downloads on failure
body:
We sometimes see transient networking failures causing mid-stream errors
that cannot be easily handled when downloading e.g. Verilator or
Verible. These are often caused by issues connecting with Github
servers.

This commit wraps these `curl` commands with a mechanism that retries,
with exponential backoff, to handle some of these transient failures.
This means that after the first failure, the script will wait 2s and
retry, then 4s, then 8s and finally 16s. If the 5th attempt still fails,
then the download will fail.

A preferable long-term mechanism would be to mirror our dependencies to
a more reliable download source, but this change is intended to make CI
more robust to transient failures in the meantime (and we could still
get transient networking errors even with a mirror).

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

nanoseconds respectively, despite the fact that these two values are
dependent on physical characteristics. Specifically the signal rise time
is dependent upon the capacitance and physical design of the I2C bus,

execution environments (kDeviceType). This commit refactors the

subject: [ottf_console] buffer SPI console data in SW
body:
When using the spi_device transport for the OTTF console, a header is
attached to every data payload before writing the data payload to the
spi_device flash buffer (to be later read out by the host). This creates
a large overhead (12-bytes) when the data payload is small (e.g., only a
single character).

Moreover, the way the UJSON message transmit macros are implemented,
results in writing several small strings, or even single characters, to
the printf (console) sink function. This created an unncessarily large
number of SPI console frames when sending the `perso_blob_t` UJSON
struct to the host.

This commit adds a SW buffering mechanism to the OTTF SPI console to
collect all small strings / single character writes into a single large
SPI console transaction. This greatly improves the efficiency in sending
large UJSON structs over the SPI OTTF console.

Signed-off-by: Tim Trippel <ttrippel@google.com>

subject: [entropy_src/dv] Prevent accidental locking of invalid configurations
body:
Before locking down write access to configuration CSRs via the SW_REGUPD
CSR, we need to make sure there has been enough time for signaling and
detecting a recoverable alert (e.g. because of writing invalid MuBis).
Upon receiving an alert, the calling task will abort the configuration
task thereby preventing the locking. But without sufficient time, DV may
lock an invalid configuration which would require resetting the DUT.

This change is required due to 60959f9c17de6c6f5a323cd0421793237dbe8005
which correctly inserted a delay in the function waiting for alert
triggers to account for ongoing alert pings.

Without this change, the crucial entropy_src_rng vseq had a failure rate
of around 50% which massively impacts functional coverage for the
ENTROPY_SRC block.

subject: [crypto/rsa_keygen] Refactor `run_rsa_keygen` DMEM layout
body:
Unlike other OTBN apps, the `run_rsa_keygen` app hard-coded its DMEM
memory layout within its implementation (in `rsa_keygen.s`) leading to
tests having to declare their own separate DMEM locations for test
vectors and other artifacts. This cohabitation of application data
together with test data has worked out so far as the available memory
sufficed to host both types. A situation that is likely to change as
hardening the RSA routines will incur a hefty memory overhead that
does not allow for any application-unrelated data to be loaded as
well. Moreover, having to handle both app data and test concurrently
is both cumbersome and error-prone. In a nutshell, there should never
be any application-unrelated data in the OTBN DMEM as the application
itself should be able to use all the available memory. This commit
unfolds in two stages:

  1. Make the `run_rsa_keygen` memory layout explicit by removing the
  hard-coded symbols, see `run_rsa_keygen_mem.s`. All subroutines of
  `run_rsa_keygen` inherit thereon from this layout.
  2. Completely remove all test artifacts that polluted the DMEM
  through the usage of the `testcase` feature of the OTBN simulator
  which allows for test data to be injected into the DMEM at
  runtime. For some reason, this very handy feature is well-hidden in
  the OTBN simulator and has only been used once for a single
  unrelated test.

Addresses: #27847

body:
With more seeds some edge cases were exposed in the DV:

- Aborting immediately after setting Go can prevent completion
  of the final word write, so do not check the request in this
  case.

- Aborting/panicking must allow any outstanding SRAM writes
  to complete before proceeding with the next transaction,
  because otherwise the write responses may be accepted into
  the DUT logic and lead to TL-UL assertion failures.

  The DUT is built to ignore these responses because it has
  a zero-valued count of outstanding requests, but only
  provided that it has not been restarted.

2 independent of the configuration. This size is not appropriate for
the Darjeeling configuration and leads to lots of entropy drops, causing
various block-level DV issues. This commit changes the simulation config
to use the same parameters used by the instantiations in Earlgrey and
Darjeeling.

from 4 to 3. This results in an RTL but this doesn't have an impact on
the system. Both Earlgrey and Darjeeling are anyway instantiation the
ENTROPY_SRC with a esfinal FIFO depth of 3. Changing default parameter
just ensures we simulate the proper configuration in block-level DV.

subject: [dv] Add an access lock to dv_base_reg
body:
This can be used to avoid two different processes trying to read/write
a register at the same time.

This took me... quite a long time... to track down! The problem is
visible if you have processes A, B and C all trying to write a
register at the same time.

 - Suppose A wins the race. Then uvm_reg::write() will grab the
   m_atomic semaphore (and processes B and C will block).

 - The uvm_reg::write() method then callls uvm_reg::do_write(), which
   tries to take the semaphore again. Interestingly, the UVM authors
   added a special case to skip doing so if we already have the lock.
   Bizarrely, I distinctly remember reading programming textbooks
   teaching me not to do this when I was a teenager!

 - Once A has finished the bus access, uvm_reg::do_write() calls put
   on the semaphore.

 - At this point, the semaphore is granted to process B.

 - This doesn't actually make process A yield, so it carries on,
   returning to the uvm_reg::write() method.

 - This then calls put on the semaphore again, clearing process B's
   lock.

 - Now the semaphore is granted to process C.

Voila! Now processes B and C are running concurrently through the
critical section.

There's a pretty obvious fix: add a counter to uvm_reg.svh. Indeed,
version 2020-2.0 of UVM actually does that. Phew! Unfortunately, EDA
tools aren't particularly prompt at taking UVM versions, and OpenTitan
doesn't currently depend on versions of the tools that have a recent
enough version of UVM.

Since we don't ship our own version of UVM, this bodge will work
around the problem.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [entropy_src/rtl] Fix bucket test result aggregation for Darjeeling
body:
Before this commit, the max bin counter values of the individual
NumBucketHtInst groups (each testing BucketHtDataWidth channels) got
added together. This is not meaningful as it attenuates outliers
observed in individual groups, meaning systematic health test failures
in some channels or groups get buried in noise. This makes it also
harder to come up with useful threshold values as the threshold is not
compared against this final result, but to the results of the individual
NumBucketHtInst groups.

This commit changes the design to instead return the max value of all
NumBucketHtInst groups. This value is most meaningful for defining the
thresholds to be provided by firmware.

proportion, the bucket and the Markov health tests was broken. As a
result, the important entropy_src_rng and entropy_src_rng_max_rate tests

ENTROPY_SRC hardware pipeline (from the conditioner onward) as the
final processing of the conditioner is only triggered if a window passes
the health checks. Because of the wrong thresholds, practically all
health tests constantly failed for these three health tests.

This commit fixes the computation of the thresholds and improves the
documentation of the corresponding functions.

subject: [otp_ctrl/rtl] Read zeroization marker always without checking integrity
body:
Prior to this commit, a DAI read of the zeroization marker field of a
partition could result in an integrity error if the partition had been
zeroized but `otp_ctrl` hadn't been reset since the zeroization (which
would cause a reinitialization and, as part of that, the zeroization
state of the partition would have been updated in `otp_ctrl`).

This was problematic because SW couldn't just unconditionally go through
the zeroization markers of all partitions to determine which have been
zeroized and which haven't: if one partition had been zeroized without a
reset of `otp_ctrl`, reading the zeroization marker of that partition
would have caused a fatal integrity error, locking `otp_ctrl` up.

This commit fixes that by always using *raw* reads (i.e., reads that
ignore integrity checks) for the zeroization marker fields.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [chip, dv] Made rstmgr_rst_cnsty_escalation working on Xcelium
body:
This test pokes a consistency fault in rstmgr. Just before doing so,
the test writes to NMI_ENABLE register and expects NMI_STATE.Alert
to be raised. The way it works is by injecting fault into the path
that was registered inside the queue of proxies for rstmgr. In
return, u_alert_handler in top_earlgrey sends an escalation request
to u_rv_core_ibex.Inside the list of proxies, there are two paths
registered for fault injection for rstmgr as follows:

1) *u_rstmgr_aon.u_d0_spi_host_0.leaf_rst_o (generates a consistency
fault)
2) *u_rstmgr_aon.u_d0_spi_host_0.state_o (generates an FSM fault)

To grab the path from the list, the vseq chip_sw_fault_base_vseq
uses find_sec_cm_if_proxy function present in sec_cm_pkg. This
function contains a call to find_first() to find the first entry
that matches with the pattern *u_rstmgr_aon.u_d0_spi_host_0* inside
the list of proxies. Both VCS and Xcelium registers the above two
entries with different order. So, Xcelium gets the entry that turns
out to generate a non-consistency fault. But this test somehow
expects to generate a consistency fault. This is the reason why
u_alert_handler in top_earlgrey never sends an escalation request to
the core and as a result never writes to NMI_STATE.Alert.

Signed-off-by: Kinza Qamar <kqzaman@lowrisc.org>

subject: [tlul,dv] Rephrase some sequences to make them simpler

were supposed to model the case where e.g. the host asserts a_valid on
the A channel and then changes the address without the original
transaction being accepted.

With the old sequences, we wanted to see valid but not ready and then
have a different value of e.g. a_addr on the next cycle where valid
was true.

I've simplified things a bit by saying that I'm only interested in
situations where the signal changes without valid dropping in the
middle.

My logic is that the aValidNotAccepted_S and dValidNotAccepted_S
sequences already capture the looser case where we're allowing valid
to drop in the middle, but this coverage target should probably want
the "most pesky" situation anyway, which is what you get from the

subject: [crypto] Protect HMAC against FI
body:
This commit adds fault injection protection to the HMAC cryptolib
implementation.

When `security_level == kOtcryptoKeySecurityLevelLow`, no protection
is provided, similar until now.

When `seucrity_level == kOtcryptoKeySecurityLevelMedium`, the CL
now calls the CL-internal `hmac_hmac_sha256()` function twice. By
comparing both tag outputs, an ongoing FI attack can be mitigated.

When `security_level == kOtcryptoKeySecurityLevelHigh`, the CL
now calls once the CL-internal `hmac_hmac_sha256()` function as well
as the new `hmac_hmac_sha256_redundant()` function. Both functions
again calculate the same tag and the CL compares both tages. However,
the second implementation uses an alternative HMAC implementation
that does not use the HMAC core itself but constructs HMAC over the
SHA core. The idea is that two identical faults affect both
implementations differently, which can be detected.

Impact on the runtime for HMAC SHA256, 13 bytes message:
otcrypto_hmac() runtime with security_level low: 6026 cycles
otcrypto_hmac() runtime with security_level medium: 11852 cycles
otcrypto_hmac() runtime with security_level high: 14975 cycles

Signed-off-by: Pascal Nasahl <nasahlpa@lowrisc.org>

subject: [HARDENED_TRY] Harden HARDENED_TRY
body:
The HARDENED_TRY macro currently only does a redundant branch in case the status is ok, but misses a redundant branch for the error limb.

Adapt the macro such that it performs a redundant branch on each case. In order to save code size, a new configuration is used.
For example, use the fact that error statuses are negative values.

The assembly has the following pattern:

j function
addi a0, a0, -1849 // This is done to branch on zero to save code size
beqz a0, continue_branch
addi a0, a0, 1849
bltz a0, return_branch
unimp
...
continue_branch:
beqz a0, rest_of_the_code
unimp

Finally, running //sw/device/tests/crypto:otcrypto_export_size, code size goes from ~84k to ~83k.

In order to accomodate a HARDENED_TRY with asm volatile instructions using the RISC-V instruction set, the macro is now also checked in status_functest.

subject: [rv_timer,dv] Fix subtly broken fork/join tree
body:
With the previous version, we had something of this form:

  fork
    for (...) begin
      fork
        something_or_other();
      join_none
    end
    wait fork;
  join

This means the "wait fork" ends up starting in parallel with the thing
that was supposed to start sub-processes. This was all rather
confusing when I ran things with Xcelium because we end up with the
"wait fork" completing immediately, but then the something_or_other
process starting afterwards (no longer being waited for). This gets
followed by a "disable fork", leaving a process being killed when it
is trying to get a sequencer, causing a failure a cycle later.

I think the author probably intended something like this:

  begin
    for (...) begin
      fork
        something_or_other();
      join_none
    end
    wait fork;
  end

(where the outer begin/end is necessary to make this a single item in
a surrounding fork).

The only other change is to pull out a complicated expression, which
lets us indent it properly.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

Secondly, I realised that if delay is large and spinwait_timeout_ns is

subject: [p256] Harden bn.sel and rshi
body:
Harden the OTBN code for p256 against side-channel analysis.
- Remove the second load of shifting w7 (was not needed)
- Shift the second share of the scalar with randomness instead of with zeros
- Perform bn.sel without unmasking the scalar

Solutions include
- decision on xor: L ? a : b = L1 ? (L0 ? b : a) : (L0 ? a : b)
- decision on or: L ? a : b = L0 ? a : (L1 ? a : b)

Note that in p256.c you can view the instruction count difference.

wishing to use the UART bitbanging decoding interface can interface with

This performs the necessary optimisations to avoid needlessly sampling

whilst the UART is idle.

subject: [opentitanlib] Handle unexpected starts in UART RX monitoring
body:
In the UART bitbanging RX decoding logic, where a GPIO monitoring
interface is used for the UART RX signal, it may be the case that we
started monitoring the pin either when (a) RX had not yet been pulled up
by the other UART, so the line starts floating / low or (b)
mid-transaction, meaning that we will start reading garbage, and the
decoder may stay out of sync if the UART does not return idle for some
time.

To avoid these issues, introduce additional sampling/decoding logic to
handle both these cases. Check that the first edge is a falling edge,
and skip to the next edge if not. Before waiting for this falling edge,
first wait for some "stable state" where we can take a consistent number
of samples longer than a UART frame. These can all be logical low (break
condition) or high (idle), as we just care that the UART is not
mid-transmission when we start decoding.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [entropy_src] Lock up Ack SM upon fatal local events, align scoreboard
body:
This commit modifies the RTL to move the Ack SM into the terminal error
state whenever a fatal local event is observed. Previously, the Ack SM
would only move to this state upon observing one particular fatal error
event, namely the counter error event. As the fatal alert was signaled
already before, this is not a very critical issue. But the new behavior
is more desirable as it means the ENTROPY_SRC immediately stops serving entropy whenever
a fatal local event is observed.

In addition, the modeling in the scoreboard is re-aligned with the
actual RTL implementation which fixes a notable amount of test failures.

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#24410.

subject: [entropy_src/rtl] Absorb full window before triggering SHA3 processing
body:
It can happen that a health test window ends while the conditioner is
busy. Before this commit, the final processing of the conditioner got
triggered whenever testing the last symbol of a health test window and
independent of the fill status of the various FIFOs before the
conditioner. As a result, it could happen that the conditioner got
triggered before absorbing the last couple of symbols belonging to the
health test window.

To avoid this, this commit modifies the RTL to monitor the fill status
of the distribution and preconditioner FIFOs, and to delay the process
command accordingly.

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#24085.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

pipeline capacity needs to be aligned with this granularity.

subject: [entropy_src/rtl] Move alert counter clearing to end of HT window
body:
This commit fixes an RTL bug that can occur when interfacing noise
sources operating at high rates. In particular, this commit ensures that
the point when alert counters get cleared is moved to right after
testing the last symbol belonging to the current health test window.

Prior to this commit, the clearing of the alert counters was controlled
by the main state machine which is operating on delayed versions of the
health test done / failed pulses where the amount of delay depends on
the exact configuration of the ENTROPY_SRC. As a result, it could happen
that the clearing pulse collided with the any_fail_pulse triggered
by the failure of one of the continuous health tests failing (repcnt and
repcnts). This could lead to continuous health test failures getting
ignored / not counting towards the total alert threshold.

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#24159.

subject: [bazel/otbn] Assemble source files into a single .o file
body:
By passing multiple .s files to `riscv32-unknown-elf-as`, instead of
producing one .o file per .s, it is possible to make use of
conditional compilation using the `.set` directive. This is similar to
the preprocessor macros in C.

The Bazel build targets can be rewritten to having multiple source
inputs instead of declaring dependencies, e.g.,

```
otbn_sim_test(
    name = "rsa_512_dec_test",
    srcs = [
        "rsa_512_dec_test.s",
        "//sw/otbn/crypto:modexp.s",
        "//sw/otbn/crypto:montmul.s",
        "//sw/otbn/crypto:run_rsa_modexp_mem,s",
    ],
    testcase = "rsa_512_dec_test.hjson",
)
```

The main application for this feature is the conditional
enabling/disabling of hardening countermeasures. With the above test
this could look like this:

```
// rsa_512_dec_test.s
.set RSA_MODEXP_ENABLE_MESSAGE_BLINDING, 1

// modexp.s
.ifdef RSA_MODEXP_ENABLE_MESSAGE_BLINDING
  // Code with blinding
.else
  // Code without blinding
.endif
```

exponentiation with a hardened, constant-time Montgomery ladder. The
hardening approach is two-pronged:

subject: [crypto/rsa] Hardened RSA key generation
body:
This commit is a complete rewrite of the RSA key generation OTBN
implementation in an effort to render it more secure. It consists of
the following changes:

  1. Use the previously hardened `modexp` routine as the center piece
  of the Fermat and Miller-Rabin primality tests. The sequence of
  Fermat and Miller-Rabin tests replaces the previous trial divisions
  followed by a Miller-Rabin sequence.

  2. Mask the computation of the GCD during the derivation of the
  secret exponent d.

  3. Merge RSA sign/enc and key generation into a single hardened OTBN
  app (`run_rsa`). Move the orthogonal RSA key from cofactor routine
  into a separate app (`run_rsa_key_from_cofactor`). This merge
  results in some cosmetic changes in the cryptolib C API.

  4. Adapt all the existing OTBN assembler tests to the new RSA key
  generation algorithm.

The implementation is compliant with FIPS 186-5.

subject: [csrng/rtl] Simplify main state machine
body:
Before this commit, the main state machine had a separate prepare and
request state for each command. The prepare states could be grouped into
two categories by whether fresh entropy gets requested before moving to
the respective request state, or not.

Each request state, however, only differed by asserting a different
request signal towards csrng_core, which then got OR-combined without
any additional security countermeasures.

Hence, this commit reduces all request states to a single one (and a
single request signal towards csrng_core), and all prepare states to
two, one where entropy is requested, and one where this is not done.

Furthermore, the commit changes the interaction between main state
machine, the command stages and the ctr_drbg_cmd module to be based
on proper valid/ready handshakes.

subject: [sw,cryptolib] Hardened bn.sel for internal point mult
body:
This commit adds hardening for the internal scalar point
multiplication.
Before the shares would be combined in the main loop to decide
whether 0, P or 2P should be added.
This commit determines this without combining the shares.
If the MSB of both shares are both 1 we want to add 2P.
If only one bit is 1 we want to add P.
If both bits are 0 we want to add 0.

In a simplified way this is done as explained below.

In a first step we pick P if MSB(d0) ^ MSB(d1) is 1 and 2P otherwise.
This is done as follows:
p_temp0 = d0 ? (d1 ? 2P : P) : (d1 ? P : 2P)

In a second step we pick between p_temp and 0.
If MSB(d0) | MSB(d1) = 1 then we pick p_temp otherwise we pick 0.
This is done as follows:
p_temp1 = d0 ? p_temp0 : 0
p_temp2 = d1 ? p_temp0 : p_temp1

Signed-off-by: Hakim Filali <hfilali@lowrisc.org>

subject: [keymgr/keymgr_dpe,rtl] Fix wrong cast
body:
`rom_digest_i[k].data` is casted to `MaxWidth`. In SV, the cast fills
up the MSBs with 0. This means that an all-1 vector is no  longer an
all-1 vector after the cast. E.g., when casting 8'hFF to 16-bits, we
would get 16'h00ff.

This is problematic as we use the casted value in the `valid_chk`
function. This function checks if the value is an all-1 or all-0
vector.

So far this was not problematic as `MaxWidth` and `rom_digest_i[k].data`
are both 256-bits. However, we should still fix this by using
`prim_msb_extend`.

This issue has been flagged by Muhammad Hafiz Abu Hassan from the Malaysian
Cryptology Technology and Management Centre during the HACK@CHES'25 event.

body:
A part-select (defined in section 11.5.1 of IEEE 1800-2012) can either
be indexed on non-indexed. The code that was here before used a
non-indexed part-selects, which are defined as having the syntax
"vect[msb_expr:lsb_expr]". Rather confusingly, "msb" here means "the
left-most bit in the vector (as defined by it's data type). (see
section 6.9.1 of the same reference).

As such, the msb of a variable defined as "bit [0:10] foo" is the one
at index 0, not 10. Accessing foo[3:0] will seemingly work, but the
EDA tool might throw a warning about the fact that 3 can't be an MSB
if 0 is the LSB.

This is all rather mysterious! But we can cheat and make things easy
for ourselves by using an indexed part-select instead. The [0 +: AW]
range is equivalent to what we had before, but doesn't really care
about the order of the LSB/MSB in the type of the integral variables
that are being sliced.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [opentitantool] Correct the SHA256 hash ordering
body:
Opentitanlib was computing the SHA256 hash and storing it in a fixed-sized
bigint.  This led to various problems dealing with the endianness of the
resulting digest, including emitting digest in "little-endian" order.
A SHA256 digest _is not_ an integer; it is a sequence of bytes.

1. Eliminate the bigint representation of the SHA256 digest.  Give the
   digest struct serialization, display and parsing traits to eliminate
   the need for dealing with conversions for those ues cases.  Add
   `to_vec` and `to_vec_rev` to produce the raw bytes when needed.
2. Add a `--spx-hash-reversal-bug` switch to opentitantool spx commands
   for cases where firmware erroneously uses a reversed digest.
3. Eliminate the copious digest reversals present in hsmtool.  Add a
   `Sha256HashReversed` input format for cases where
   firmware erroneously uses a reversed digest.
4. Fix the signing rules to use the reversed format only for keys
   tied to a firmware implementation with the reversal bug.

subject: [csrng/rtl] Add unified CTR_DRBG data path module
body:
This commit adds the unified csrng_ctr_drbg module which replaces the
csrng_ctr_drbg_{cmd, gen, upd} modules. It combines all required data
path elements from the aforementioned modules and introduces a newly
designed FSM which creates all necessary control- and handshake signals.

This step allows for significant reduction of both circuit area and
design complexity. The unified module splits the response ports up:
Previously, writes to the state db, the genbits FIFOs in the command
stages, and signalling commands as completed to main and command stages
FSM were done on a single handshake channel. This is now done with three
independent channels which allows for a more streamlined data path and
does away with buffering and pipeline stages previously required.

Note that some of the response handshake channels do not feature a ready
signal, since the respective responders (state db, genbits FIFOs) are
always ready by construction.

Furthermore, csrng_ctr_drbg reworks the v-counter logic to perform all
v-increments inside the hardened prim_count. Before, when loading v from
the state db, the first increment was done outside of the prim_count as
part of its `set` value, potentially harming the overall hardening of v.

Signed-off-by: Florian Glaser <glaserf@lowrisc.org>

subject: [csrng/rtl] Instantiate the unified CTR_DRBG module
body:
This commit instantiates the unified csrng_ctr_drbg data path module in
csrng_core and removes the csrng_ctr_drbg_{cmd,gen,upd} modules from the
code base. This either requires or enables the following steps as well:

- Remove several assertions that reference removed parts of the design
- Remove/tweak data types from csrng_pkg
- Remove the flopped status_ack interface from the state db
- Remove the no longer needed cmdid FIFO from csrng_block_encrypt

subject: [alert,dv] Substantial tweaks in alert_monitor
body:
This was all actually prompted by a mistake I had made locally where
alert_receiver_ping_seq was being a bit too enthusiastic and sending
LOTS of ping requests, almost "back-to-back".

But there's not really any reason that alert_monitor *shouldn't* be
able to cope with this. The whole setup is quite fiddly to reason
about (because of the way pings and alert transactions use the same
wires), so I went through the code very carefully, adding lots of
comments.

Significant changes:

  - The way that resets and initialisation were tracked was rather
    confusing (and I misunderstood it more than once!). The genuine
    reset signal (rst_n) is now tracked with
    alert_esc_base_monitor::reset_thread (rather than overriding it),
    and run_phase is now split into an on_reset function (which runs
    when reset is asserted) and a run_between_resets task (which does
    the "normal job" of run_phase).

  - Now initialisation can happen "just after reset" with very simple
    code: it just gets called first in run_between_resets.

  - In general, the code is a little bit more hierarchical. Most
    functions (including run_between_resets) don't care about tracking
    under_reset. Similarly, many functions don't track
    cfg.en_alert_lpg. That tracking gets done by "the guy that called
    them" each time.

  - I think the forever @(...) logic in the thread arbiter inside the
    old alert_and_ping_thread wasn't quite right. I think it would
    work, so long as e.g. active_alert got cleared before active_ping
    was set. But that seems rather too complicated. I also had to add
    a "first_time" flag to work properly if the set of flags get set
    at the same time as we started thread_arbiter, but the code
    setting the flags happened to get queued first.

  - The monitor_ping task now gets an argument to tell it what the
    value of ping_p was on the cycle before. If your ping sequence is
    very trigger happy, it can change the value of ping_p on the cycle
    that you start monitor_ping, and that's ok! But monitor_ping needs
    to know that it happened.

  - I have removed the timeout from monitor_alert_handshake. I think
    that the original design of this machinery allowed timeouts for
    alerts as well. I'm not sure what that could be used for, and
    perhaps the design team agreed, so they specialised to just pings.
    The DV here wasn't quite updated correctly (it should have dropped
    the timeout entirely, but instead reported a ping timeout).

Minor / cosmetic changes:

  - Lots of virtual tasks and functions are now local: they were only
    used in alert_monitor anyway.

  - There are quite a few places where the code was doing a while loop
    and checking some variable from a clocking block. See wait_ack for
    example. But this can be much easier: because the variable is in
    the clocking block, wait(...) will terminate at the right time.

  - Since almost everything became local, I've moved
    monitor_ready_to_end (which isn't) further up in the file, to make
    sure that all the public stuff was at the top.

  - I have renamed wait_ping_thread to report_ping_requests. This is
    mainly because I couldn't work out what it was for until missing
    it made my alert_handler tests fail. In hindsight, when you are
    testing something that sends pings, you're going to have to get
    your testbench to notice them...

    There's no significant change to the task (except for it now
    handling resets in the same way as the other nearby tasks), but
    I've put quite a bit of documentation around it, and have named it
    something that's more different from "ping_thread".

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [sram-exec] Avoid using compressed instructions when loading sp.
body:
This changes solves an issue that caused larger programs to return the
following linker error:

```
relocation truncated to fit: R_RISCV_GPREL_I against symbol `_stack_end' defined in .sram_start
```

Using the `norelax` option avoids the use of compressed instructions

body:
This interface adds considerable design and verification complexity
without substantial gain: The two crypto primitives serialized by this
interface (unmasked AES core inside CSRNG, unmasked SHA3 inside
ENTROPY_SRC) amount to less than 40 kGE together. Much more logic than
this got removed through the CSRNG restructuring effort.

At the same time, the interface is the main source of back pressure
inside the ENTROPY_SRC thereby introducing the need for additional logic
to aborb this back pressure. For this reason, the interface was anyway
disabled for Darjeeling which uses a high-rate noise source.

This commit removes the interface completely from the top levels and the
two involved hardware block IPs CSRNG and ENTROPY_SRC in order to reduce
complexity.

subject: [aes] Add GHASH module for AES-GCM
body:
This commit adds a first implementation of the GHASH module required for
AES-GCM support. This first version uses a single, pipelined GF(2^128)

and the encrypted initial counter block J_0 (= S). The latency of the
GF multiplier is matched to the latency of the cipher core.

subject: [aes] Align interface of clearing PRNG with masking PRNG
body:
For historical reasons, the clearing PRNG had a req/ack interface for
both the pseudo-random data and the reseed interface. The former is
actually not required as the PRNG can always provide suitable pseudo-
random data, even in case of an outstanding reseed request. This commit
thus simplifies the req/ack interface to a single update signal, similar
to what is used for the masking PRNG.

In addition to simplifying the code, this enables re-using the main
control FSM state previously used for performing the handshake with the
clearing PRNG, to perform an actually required handshake with another
functional block such as the GHASH block used for AES-GCM.

body:
This commit optimizes the clearing logic of the GHASH block to clear
internal registers by loading the cipher core output after the cipher
output has cleared its internal state. This allows reducing the
internal muxing logic by 2x 128-bit wide 2-to-1 muxes and the big
128-bit wide 5-to-1 state mux looses one input, too. When using the
open source synthesis flow, this helps reducing the area by roughly
1 kGE.

subject: [test] Replace AES alert with status read
body:
This test needs to read a CSR from the AES block. `dif_aes_alert_force`
was chosen as the instruction that writes to the `ALERT_TEST` CSR comes
close to the beginning of the function and makes the crash dump accurate

> The address of the function causing the error.  The functions
> that cause the error are chosen so they perform a CSR read
> shortly after the function entry, so crash_dump's mcpc is
> expected to be past the possible error pc by no more than about 8
> instructions, meaning 8 * 4 bytes.

However triggering an alert will be problematic once OTTF starts
catching alerts triggered by tests.

Switch to `dif_aes_get_status` instead which I have confirmed does the
CSR access within two instructions from `aes_csr_access`.

```
200107a0 <aes_csr_access>:
200107a0: 41100537 lui a0,0x41100
200107a4: 08452503 lw  a0,132(a0) # 41100084
200107a8: 8082     ret
```

of OpenTitan changed to use the `master` workflow for the target branch
protection. While this was fine for calculating the PR diff (using the
GH CLI), it also meant that the BLOCKFILE being used by the check script
was the BLOCKFILE on master.

This is not ideal, as we want each non-default branch to be able to
specify a BLOCKFILE for files that should be blocked specifically on
that branch. For example, on `earlgrey_1.0.0`, we do not want to permit
any further RTL changes.

provide appropriate protections.

subject: [rom_ext, ownership] Fix the flash region configuration
body:
I did not write correct test cases that would check a flash
configuration similar to the owner config already deployed in some skus.
This oversight could cause ownership initialization to fail on devies
with such a configuration.

1. Permit a maximum of 3 regions per side in the flash configuration.
   The regions must be fully within the bounds of SlotA or SlotB and
   may not overlap the ROM_EXT region.
2. Apply the region configuration in order.  Previously, there was a
   correspondence between the index of the region in the owner config
   and the MP_REGION register that it would land in, but this makes
   ownership transfers prone to configuration clashes.
3. Flash configuration is done in two passes to configure each side
   independently (the reason for this is to allow next_owner's flash
   config to apply to the non-primary side during ownership transfer).
   The flash_apply function now takex an index parameter to manage
   the desination MP_REGION register between passes.
4. Create a unittest case with a flash configuration similar to the
   already-deployed configuration. Include the ROM_EXT, application,
   filesystem and reserved segments.
5. Update the existing test cases to accomodate the new configuration
   scheme (e.g. applying in order rather than by index).

overwriting the initialized state with the masked cipher core input and
second subtracting Share 1 of S to the GHASH state afterwards.

This commit changes the design to overwrite only Share 0 of the
initialized state with the unmasked saved state and leave Share 1
untouched. As Share 1 of the state is already initialized to Share 1 of
S, no further operations have to be done. This allows saving one 128-bit
multiplexer input (or 300 GE).

subject: [otbn,dv] Isolate HW loop stack countermeasure testing from integrity checks
body:
When testing the countermeasures for the OTBN hardware loop stack, the current_loop_valid
will be high when the loop stack counter is forced to zero. This fault should be detected
and assert the `hw_err_o` of the loop controller. As in this test no SW is run the loop
stack has undefined values (x). When the `current_loop_valid` is high, the integrity
check of the loop address (current_loop_intg_err) is OR factored into the `hw_err_o` as well
leading to undefined error bits.

We prevent this x propagation by defining the loop stack data. The loop info data bits are
set to random data which pass ECC checks. This ensures that always the `hw_err_o` error
triggers and not the ECC check. Using random values which pass ECC checks but make no sense
when interpreted as loop info is also ok. What can happen is that a loop jump (loop_jump_o)
is requested which could result in a SW error due to a misaligned instruction address (from
`current_loop.loop_addr_info.loop_start` via `insn_fetch_req_addr_o`). But OTBN will
escalate anyway so raising a SW error does not affect the test.

See also #28888

subject: [otbn,rtl] Register local escalation signals for timing optimization
body:
Signals contributing to the local controller escalation signal directly factor into the
insn_executing signal inside the otbn_controller.sv. This then drives various commit signals
as well as the DMEM request signal (lsu_load_req_o). By registering these escalation signals,
these paths are shortened which results in better timing/area results. Signals contributing to
the start/stop escalation are also flopped to synchronize the escalation such that
transitioning into LOCKED and the start of wiping activities happen at the same time.

Registered signals:
- urnd_all_zero:    Is high when the local PRNG is all zero and locks up.
                    Potentially timing critical.
- predec_error:     Generated by checking all the registered, predecoded signals with decoded
                    signals and combining these.
                    Potentially timing critical.
- lsu_rdata_err:    DMEM ECC errors of data read from DMEM.
                    Timing critical because source is in memory.
- insn_addr_err:    Is asserted when the prefetched address does not match the requested
                    address. Depends on insn_fetch_req_addr_o and prefetch_ignore_errs_o from
                    the controller which factor in lots of combinatorial signals. Especially
                    the prefetch_ignore_errs_o depends on the internal error which depends on
                    many internal error signals.
                    Very likely timing critical.
- rf_base_intg_err: ECC errors triggered with in the base register file. The control signals
                    for the base register file are not predecoded.
                    So this is likely timing critical.
- non_controller_reg_intg_violation: Based on alu_bignum_reg_intg_violation_err,
                                     mac_bignum_reg_intg_violation_err and rf_base_intg_err.
                                     The former two are generated by checking the ECC of the
                                     MOD / ACC values. The checks depends on the actual
                                     ALU / MAC datapath outputs.
                                     **Highly** timing critical.

Not registered signals:
- escalate_en_i:           This must NOT be not cut. It stems from the system wide escalation
                           control mechanism and such a global escalation must be as fast as
                           possible.
- start_stop_fatal_error:  The error signal of the start stop FSM. Based on EDN urnd ack
                           signal and internal state checking. This error is not cut to
                           synchronize the escalation of the controller and start/stop
                           control.
- controller_fatal_err:    The error signal of the controller towards the start/stop logic.
                           This error is not cut to synchronize the escalation of the
                           controller and start/stop control.
- rf_base_spurious_we_err: This error is already registered at the source.
- insn_fetch_err:          IMEM ECC errors, not computed on the IMEM output but on a flopped
                           signal.

See #28345 for discussion about the impact on security.

Signed-off-by: Pascal Etterli <pascal.etterli@lowrisc.org>

subject: [otbn,sim] Extend DMEM model with valid flag for each entry
body:
Previously the DMEM integrity validity was modelled with an Optional[Int] type
where an int value represented valid and None an invalid state.
The DMEM integrity test then did simply invalidate the whole DMEM by setting
all parts to None.

This is incompatible with a delayed escalation as a failing instruction (e.g.,
a LW) will trigger the escalation but will still retire. As of this it actually
must load a value and a None value cannot be written to a register. To solve
this, we model the integrity with a dedicated valid flag and return the current
value as well. The test now only has to specify that a comparison mismatch is
tolerated.

It would also be possible to modify the insn implementation that if None is
returned a fixed value is written to the register. However, in this case the
insn code would not exactly represent the HW behaviour. As this insn code is
converted to pseudo code for this the ISA description, this approach is less
favourable. Keeping the value field also allows to extend the DMEM model in future
to fully model the injected error (i.e., extending the otbnsim with a command
which lets set DMEM content to the faulted values). With this the "tolerate
mismatch" workaround could be fixed properly.

Signed-off-by: Pascal Etterli <pascal.etterli@lowrisc.org>

This is a workaround to model the ld_insn injection error from the otbn_ctrl_redun_vseq.sv

When a load instruction is injected in parallel to the actual instruction, the OTBN will
not execute the current instruction and will stall (due to how the ld_insn signal factors
into the stall logic). Modeling this behaviour is complicated and would require to duplicate RTL
implementation details in the model. Thus, we add this command/flag which UVM can use to
signal that we should enter the stall state.

subject: [sw,cov] Add on-device OTTF coverage runtime
body:
This change adds a new on-device coverage runtime with OTTF transport.

When coverage is enabled, the runtime can collect profile counter data from the device and send it over the console.
On the host, these raw counter values can be combined with static profile data to recreate the full LLVM profile.

The coverage runtime consists of the following components:
* `api.h`: Provides a set of shared C APIs implemented by transport runtimes.
* `api_asm.h`: Provides APIs for assembly code.
* `printer.h`/`printer.c`: Implements the shared logic for different runtimes.
* Linker scripts (`bss.ld`, `info.ld`, `rodata.ld`): Define special sections for LLVM profile data, counters, and build ID.

OTTF transport implementation is also included:
* `ottf_runtime.c`: Integrates the coverage printer with the OTTF console for data output.
* `ottf_runtime_skip.c`: A no-op version of the runtime for builds where coverage is enabled but not instrumented.

Change-Id: I2e4b135a58b93a257fc37880700e23f4b99defc4
Signed-off-by: Yi-Hsuan Deng <yhdeng@google.com>
(cherry picked from commit 7d450f82cc4519e2de169431b07ce94a1e62351e)

subject: [sw,cov] Disable segment allocation for coverage bss sections

to save firmware size, as it's always filled with `0xff`.

However, unlike standard BSS, this section contains non-zero initial contents,
leading the compiler to mark it as `PROGBITS` and loadable. This PR modifies
the linker script to explicitly allocate this section to `NONE` segment,
preventing the `qemu flashgen` tool from loading it.

The special `NONE` segment tells the linker to not put the section in any
segment at all.

subject: [bazel,cov] Add bazel coverage integration to opentitan_test
body:
This change implements the `collect_cc_coverage` tool for `opentitan_test`.

The coverage collection process now works as follows:

1. A new `collect_cc_coverage` tool (written in Rust) is invoked for
   each test that produces coverage data. This tool is responsible for
   converting the compressed coverage counters (`.xprofraw`) saved by
   opentitantool's UartConsole into the standard LLVM profraw format.
   It achieves this by correlating the `.xprofraw` data with the metadata
   extracted from the ELF files of the device's firmware.

2. The `collect_cc_coverage` tool then uses llvm tools to export an LCOV
   (`.dat`) file, which is the format expected by Bazel's coverage
   reporting.

This integration allows OpenTitan's C++ code coverage to be collected
and reported consistently within the Bazel build system, making it
possible to combined with other test coverage (unit test / OTBN test).

binaries where the FT device ID is compiled into the binary. However,
these are no used with the orchestrator, which provides the ability to
override the fields mentioned above at runtime.

subject: Revert "[rom] Always initialize main SRAM with pseudo random data"
body:
This reverts commit 151a42a741704eeafa84c740cb9fedd12559cbe9.

As discussed in the Security WG meeting on 2025-06-24 and documented in
the related issue lowRISC/OpenTitan#27381, initializing the SRAM with
deterministic pseudo-random data is undesirable. The initialization
should only be performed after having refreshed the scrambling key,
which is why there is a single fuse to control both these features
together.

In the working group meeting, it has been agreed to:
1. Leave the default setting disabled and enable it during provisioning
   to prevent later disabling in the field.
2. To rename the fuse to clarify that this controls both the scrambling
   key renewal and the initialization with pseudo-random data. This will
   be done in a follow-up commit.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

subject: [otp] Change SRAM_KEY_RENEW_EN fuse to SRAM_KEY_RENEW_AND_INIT_EN
body:
This change is done to clarify that the fuse not only controls the
renewal of the scrambling key, but also the initialization of the SRAM
with pseudo-random data. We use a single fuse to control both features
as it would be undesirable to initialize the SRAM with deterministic
pseudo-random data produced by using the default scrambling key.

This is related to lowRISC/OpenTitan#27381.

- The fixed AAD and PTX blocks

subject: [aes/rtl] Improve GHASH masking to reduce SCA leakage
body:
This commit implements a series of improvements for the GHASH masking
scheme to reduce the SCA leakage. With these changes, the implementation
successfully passes formal masking verification using Alma in transient
mode, i.e., when glitches are considered. Prior to this commit, the
implementation would pass masking verification in stable mode only.

The following improvements have been made:

- The result of the final addition of Share 1 of S and the unmasked
  GHASH state is no longer stored into the GHASH state register but
  directly forwarded to the output, and the state input to this addition
  is blanked. The input multiplexer (ghash_in_mux) looses one input.
  (The ghash_state_mux for the unmasked implementation gains one input.)

- The two 3-input multiplexers selecting the operands for the addition
  with the GHASH state (add_in_mux) are replaced by one-hot multiplexers
  with registered control signals.

- The Operand B inputs of both GF multipliers are now blanked.
  The 3-input multiplexer selecting Operand B of the second GF
  multiplier is replaced by a one-hot multiplexer with registered
  control signal. In addition, the last input slice of Operand B for
  this multiplier is registered. This allows the switching the
  multiplexer during the last clock cycle of the multiplication to avoid
  some undesirable transient leakage occurring upon saving the result of
  the multiplication into the GHASH state register (and this new value
  propagating through the multiplexer into the multiplier again).

- The GF multipliers are configured to output zero instead of Operand A
  (the hash subkey) while busy.

- The state input for the addition required for the generation of the
  correction term for Share 0 is blanked.

- Between adding the correction terms to the GHASH state for the last
  time and between unmasking the GHASH state, a bubble cycle is added
  to allow signals to fully settle thereby avoiding undesirable
  transient effects unmasking the uncorrected state shares.

The overall area impact of these changes is low (+0.16 kGE in Yosys +
nangate45).

with:
```

  (0 [0x0] vs 1 [0x1]) Major alert did not match expectation.
```
which could be quite a serious issue if the lockstep comparison
would not detect mismatches.

`alert_major_internal` signal too late. As this signal is
generated purely combinational, the logic asserts this signal as
soon as we are flipping a bit. In the testbench, we though first
wait a couple of cycles before reading this signal, which is often
already too late.

subject: [opentitanlib] add option to ignore SPI console frame numbers
body:
When opentitanlib is invoked via an external C/C++ wrapper library, the
SpiConsoleDevice object is reinstantiated repeatedly to comply with
Rust's ownership rules (and satisfy the borrow checker). On each
reinstantiation of the SpiConsoleDevice struct, the next expected frame
number is reset to 0. This causes the SpiConsoleDevice to ignore a valid
frame when used through an external wrapper library, as is the case with
the OtlibWrapper used in the opentitan-provisioning repo. This was
causing CI issues in
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan-provisioning/pull/165.

As such, this provides a mechanism for users of the SpiConsoleDevice to
ignore the frame number, which frankly  is not necessary when the
SpiConsoleDevice is used alongside the TX-indicator GPIO feature.
This feature does not make use of a circular transmit buffer, but rather
transmits only a single frame in the buffer at a time.

the base sequence splits up messages.

data_in of the TAG block, does not match anymore. Hence, the
tag comparison fails.

subject: [fpv] Make sequence chains compile much faster
body:
If you have a sequence that looks like "A ##1 B ##1 C ##1 D", Jasper
turns out to take quite a long time to compile it. This is rather
annoying, and you can actually hit a timeout.

It seems that the Cadence engineers realised that they could do things
more efficiently and put it behind a flag (presumably because the
change pessimizes some other example).

Ask for the new behaviour, provided we are on a version of Jasper that
supports it.

The magic regex should hopefully match properly. I tested it with the
following shell script:

  pattern="^\(20[3-9][0-9]\)\|\(202[4-9]\)\|\(2023\.\(0[69]\)\|12\)"
  echo -e '2023.05\n2023.06\n2023.12\n2024\n2031' | grep $pattern

This is like the regex in the TCL file, except that a TCL regex needs
"\" before the square brackets (not what we want for grep, because
"\[" would match a literal "[")

And this gives the results you'd hope for:

  2023.06
  2023.12
  2024
  2031

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>
