subject: [alert,fpv] Rephrase the handshake assertion in async rxtx alert fpv
body:
The old version of this assertion had a bit of a hole in it. Digging
into the SVA, we see:

    $rose(prim_alert_rxtx_async_tb.alert_pd)   ##[3:6]
    $rose(prim_alert_rxtx_async_tb.ack_pd)     &&
    $stable(prim_alert_rxtx_async_tb.alert_pd) ##[3:6] ....

This says "alert_p rises and then in between 3 and 6 cycles ack_p
rises and alert_p is stable at that point". That's not quite what we
want!

We really want to say "alert_p rises and then stays stable for up to 6
cycles at which point ack_p rises."

I've rephrased it slightly and also been a bit more careful about
differential signals and who is seeing what. Now, the FullHandshake_S
sequence is explicitly from the alert sender's point of view.

subject: [rom_ext] Integrate ISFB into the boot flow
body:
The Integrator Specific Firmware Binding (ISFB) feature allows an owner to
configure an INFO page to hold application firmware binding information.
The binding information allows owners to implement an anti-rollback
policy with a strike-out mask mechanism and per-product binding based
on product identifier words stored in the INFO page.

The owner can then apply an extension to the application firmware manifest
to specify the strikeout binding (ie: number of unstruck words) and a
series of product expressions which match against the product words.

This feature is currently documented in this
[mini-spec](https://docs.google.com/document/d/19oQtqgDdFU6qunbwgkwNaizYUNCzdLVqmnBpLaDvX5I/edit?pli=1&tab=t.0#heading=h.bw1472fp996n).

configure an INFO page to hold application firmware binding information.

policy with a strike-out mask mechanism and per-product binding based on

1. Check the ISFB page configuration.  Ensure that it is not erasable

2. Check that an unconstrained firmware image can execute.
3. Check that an image with an ISFB extension that meets the

body:
This commit enables testing the GCM.CONFIG.SPARSE in the following ways:

1. The aes_core_fi test is extended to inject invalid values into the
   GCM phase value presented to the internal hardware and ensures that
   with such an invalid value present, the DUT doesn't progress and
   remains idle.

2. The base sequence is extended to randomly write values greater than
   16 or values equal to 0 to the num_valid_bytes field of the GCM
   control register. The hardware resolves such values to 16 and
   continues. Failures for doing so are detected by mismatching tag
   comparisons.

3. The base sequence is extended to all randomly injecting GCM phase
   transitions which are not allowed. Most of these transitions are now
   verified in the aes_config_error test.

4. The aes_gcm_save_restore sequence is extended to randomly inject
   phase transitions which not allowed but which are hard to handle
   in the scoreboard. Also this sequence now performs writes with
   illegal phase values and verifies that the DUT moves back to the

subject: [otbn,sim] Fix flag update trace
body:
The generalization of the CSRs and WSRs in
3d18194e525998fa3ec6398bd66b3aa1ae01bd80 changed the tracing behavior
for instructions which write to the flag groups. With this change a
write to one flag group does not anymore generate also a write trace to
the other flag group.

This commit reverts these changes to the flag tracing. The reason is
that when writing to one flag group, both traces are required because
the RTL actually implements these flag groups as one register. As this
means that in the actual hardware both flag groups are updated it is
sensible to also generate two traces. This ensures we model all register
updates properly.

subject: [otbn,rtl] Properly extend DMEM address of TL-UL request
body:
This commit dynamically extends the width of dmem_index_bus to the correct bitwidth for dmem_index
based upon the configured DMEM size. This cast is only required in case the address range of the
TL-UL visible DMEM does not have the same bitwidth as the total DMEM address range.

This cast was previously removed in 80b99560bd8cac62c3b358fe5cae3e1d94be3b04 because having a DMEM
of 4KiB split into 3KiB visible and 1KiB scratchpad resulted in the same bitwidth for the index
signals. The new dynamic extension makes this part independent of the chosen DMEM size and split
ratio. This is particularly useful for a DMEM extension to 32KiB with a 16/16KiB.

In addition, it also cleans up the unused_dmem_addr_bus assignment. Since
96350848f48e20ef95bf1db182842990195d352d all bits of dmem_addr_bus except [1:0] are used.

Signed-off-by: Pascal Etterli <pascal.etterli@lowrisc.org>

subject: [otbn,rtl] Make load CRC computation independend of DMEM scratchpad size
body:
The DMEM of OTBN is not fully exposed to the TL-UL interface. There is a hidden scratchpad section
above the TL-UL visible address range and the load CRC computation is defined to operate only
on TL-UL writes.

Previously, the CRC computation considered the full DMEM address which can include additional bits
in case the total DMEM requires more address bits as the exposed range. This led to wrong CRC
computations for large DMEM sizes (as well as large offsets). With this change only the TL-UL
address relevant bits are fed into the CRC.

Signed-off-by: Pascal Etterli <pascal.etterli@lowrisc.org>

subject: [otbn,dv] Fix memory bound check in elf.py

subject: [otbn] Increase DMEM to 32KiB
body:
This increases the DMEM to a total size of 32KiB. Only the first 16KiB are exposed to the TL-UL
interface. There is no headroom for the IMEM added to avoid moving the start address of the DMEM
which would require a major OTBN version bump.

A note in case the IMEM should be increased in future:
Setting the DMEM address offset to 0xc000 (giving IMEM additional 16KiB) will not work with the
current RLT/DV state. In theory, using a 32KiB DMEM where the first 16KiB are exposed to the
TL-UL interface should work as the top address of the exposed 16KiB exactly fits inside the address
space given to OTBN. However, a lot of tests fail if doing so. The exact reasons are not clear as
of today but a good starting point is to look into why there is one extra bit set in the
dmem_index_bus signal (or rather dmem_index_bus) when DV writes the ELF to the DMEM via the TL-UL
bus. See around otbn.sv:679. It probably requires having two separate DMEM address width
definitions. Placing a 16KiB DMEM with a 8/8KiB split at 0xc000 does work.

subject: [rescue,test] Add disability test
body:

uses the owner block binary if provided; otherwise, it captures the
owner page 0 Base64 data from the UART console.

The test analyzes the owner block to identify disallowed rescue commands
and then attempts to execute each of them. This ensures that the device
correctly enforces the configured restrictions.

The testing approach differs slightly between rescue protocols:

- XMODEM: The test directly examines the result of the rescue operation
 to confirm if a command was disallowed by the device.
- DFU: Due to the potential for the rescue operation result to be
 inconclusive, the test primarily relies on analyzing device logs to
 determine if a command was rejected. Only when informative device logs
 are absent will the test fall back to checking the rescue operation
 result.

subject: [sysrst_ctrl,rtl] Avoid "inside" in constant expressions
body:
The code that was there wasn't technically syntactically correct. For
details (based on IEEE 1800-2017):

- We're in the middle of a module, and want a
  module_or_generate_item (one option for a non_port_module_item on
  p1138).

- For that, we use a module_common_item (p 1139)

- The relevant type of module_common_item for an
  "if (...) begin ... end" block is is
  conditional_generate_construct (p1139)

- A way to make one of these is a case_generate_construct (p1158)

- The test in a case_generate_construct is a
  constant_expression (p1159)

- But a constant_expression is defined with a production on p1172 that
  doesn't allow the "inside" operator. Indeed, the expression
  production on p1173 is a constant_expression or a few other options,
  one of which is inside_expression.

subject: [dv,cip] Rewrite `_DV_MUBI_DIST to avoid warnings
body:
It turns out that randomising with a distribution like this

  if (0) {
    XYZ dist { [1:0] := 1; };
  }

generates a runtime warning from Xcelium (even though the distribution
expression isn't actually used).

Fortunately, range endpoints can be general expressions, so we can do
everything with ternary operators instead. We can also avoid repeating
stuff if we define `MIN / `MAX macros.

This commit also fixes the weighting for true/false. Suppose we want
to distribute with weights ZeroW, OneW, OtherW for 0, 1, other in a
way that e.g. the fraction of ones is OneW / (ZeroW + OneW + OtherW).

The following would definitely be wrong:

 value dist { 0     := ZeroW,
              1     := OneW,
              [2:9] := OtherW };

Because there are eight "other" values, the fractions end up looking
like OneW / (ZeroW + OneW + 8 * OtherW). Oops!

To make everything line up properly, we multiply by 8:

 value dist { 0     := 8 * ZeroW,
              1     := 8 * OneW,
              [2:9] := OtherW };

and will now have fractions like

 8 * OneW / (8 * ZeroW + 8 * OneW + 8 * OtherW
  =
 OneW / (ZeroW + OneW + OtherW)

Generalising to the macro, there are (MAX_ + 1) possible
values (0..MAX_), rather than the 10 values from 0..9), so we need to
scale up by ((MAX_ + 1) - 2) = (MAX_ - 1).

subject: [otbn] Redefine ACC WSR usage and clearing behavior for SIMD multiplication instructions
body:
This commit changes the behaviour of vectorized (modulo) multiplication instructions regarding the
use of the ACC WSR. These instructions use the ACC WSR to assemble the final result over multiple
cycles. Previously these instructions cleared the ACC WSR to zero in the first cycle and the ACC WSR
contained the final result after the instruction.

Now these instructions do not clear ACC at the start to reduce the amout of data which is
overwritten (reduces toggle rates). They also do now clear the ACC WSR at the end with randomness
from URND. This allows to chain these instructions without having to clear ACC first with a
dedicated instruction if overwriting results would be a security concern.

It is now also defined that the BN MAC internal registers for temporary Montgomery computation
results are cleared with randomness after each Montgomery computation. This also solves the
problematic of overwriting results (it now does not required an explicit "clearing" instruction).

This commit also adapts the simulator implementation of these instructions accordingly.

Signed-off-by: Pascal Etterli <pascal.etterli@lowrisc.org>

subject: [otbn,rtl] Integrate vectorized multiplication instructions
body:
This commit adds the RTL implementation of the vectorized multiplication instructions implemented in
the BN MAC module. The integration requires fundamental changes to the existing BN MAC module as it
now supports multi-cycle instructions which will stall the OTBN during the execution.

The multi-cycle signals are generated by a state machine inside BN MAC. To predecode certain signals
a duplicate state machine runs inside the instruction fetch stage. This duplicate then generates the
signals one cycle earlier such that these can be flopped. Having the FSM duplicated results in a
setup similar to a lockstep core (at least for this part).

For the vectorized multipliations and for the Montgomery implementation the ACC WSR is used to
construct the final result. In addtion, there are two new hidden registers added to BN MAC to store
temporary results. All three registers are cleared using randomness after each instruction / step.
The randomness for the hidden register is based upon a permutation of URND such that each register
is cleared with different randomness. This permutation is based upon a netlist secret which requires
to expose a new parameter. As of this all tops are adapted accordingly.

This change also touches the secure wipe signal names for the BN MAC as the secure wipe now not only
clears the ACC WSR but also the two internal registers used for the Montgomery computation and the
FSM cycle counter (it clears both FSMs).

Finally, we remove a now obsolete waive rule for the clk_i and rst_ni signals because these are now
actually used whereas previously these were only used for assertions. There are new waive rules for
the "static" signal lookup array generation used by the BN MAC FSM.

Signed-off-by: Pascal Etterli <pascal.etterli@lowrisc.org>

subject: [gpio,dv] Fix race condition in gpio_scoreboard
body:
This code was way more complicated than necessary (and also contained
checks on the behaviour of the input ports, which seems a bit
bizarre).

What's worse, there was a race condition at the start of
time (assuming we started in reset). If
gpio_scoreboard::monitor_gpio_straps happens to run before
dv_base_scoreboard::monitor_reset, then it would loop forever without
consuming any time and without seeing cfg.under_reset go high, but
without allowing anything else to run (no #0 or blocking action).

Rewrite the code in a less silly way.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [jtag,dv] Make jtag_if.wait_tck more robust
body:
This was failing a bit mysteriously and it turns out to be that tck_en
was being cleared just after wait_tck had decided to wait for the next
posedge.

The slightly fiddly structure in wait_one_tck is to deal with the case
where the timer finishes at the same time as the clock edge. Without
this, you might see the timer expire and then start waiting for the
next cycle... which happens immediately because we immediately see the
posedge that happened at the same time.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

body:

for the imm_section rom_ext. By default, `tarfile.open()` does not
dereference symbolic links, which means the tarball would contain broken
symlinks if the imm_section rom_ext are symlinks.

This change adds `dereference=True` to `tarfile.open()` to ensure that
symbolic links are followed and their target files are added to the
tarball instead of the symlinks themselves.

subject: [otbn,rtl] Use predecoded mac_en signal in bignum MAC
body:
There was a naming mismatch between the decoded `mac_en_i` and its predecoded counterpart `predec_i.op_en`.
Furthermore, the redundancy check between these two signals was indirect as
`predec_i.op_en` is compared against `expected_predec.op_en` (which is just `mac_en_i` fed through the
control FSM). This indirect routing obscures the redundancy check on `mac_en_i` and an accidental
change chould break this redundancy easily. The redundancy is important becaused `mac_en_i` factors
into critical signals like `operation_valid_o`.

To improve clarity and potentially timing, this commit cleans this up by replacing almost all uses
of `mac_en_i` with its predecoded variant.

The only exception is the FSM control signal. The FSM must continue to use the decoded `mac_en_i` to
advance its state, because its counterpart inside the instruction fetch stage operates on the
predecoded signal.

See also lowRISC/opentitan#29496

subject: [crypto] Remove `busy_spin` in keymgr
body:
As `busy_spin` reads the `mcycle` register, which is only accessible
in machine mode, cryptolib using the keymanager could not be run in
user mode.

This commit removes the `busy_spin` as it is actually not needed.
The flow is as following:
- SW writes the `SIDELOAD_CLEAR.VAL` register
- This register is forwarded to the `keymgr_sideload_key_ctrl` and
  `keymgr_sideload_key` module.
- In the first module, the signal is used to set `prng_en_o`, which
  triggers the LFSR instantiated in the `keymgr` module.
- This LFSR generates random data that is used by the
  `keymgr_sideload_key` module to overwrite they key to clear with
  the random data.

Hence, writing for two cycles to the `SIDELOAD_CLEAR.VAL` register
is enough. As the keymgr cryptolib driver anyways reads back the
`SIDELOAD_CLEAR.VAL` register after asserting and before clearing
it again, we have already more than enough cycles in between.

Signed-off-by: Pascal Nasahl <nasahlpa@lowrisc.org>
(cherry picked from commit b95e722c08cd786a3394e4638c488efebe130e54)

subject: [ottf,spi_console] Use read addr instead of CS for sync with TX ready pin
body:
The current OTTF SPI console implementation, when using a TX ready GPIO
indicator pin, watches to see the chip select signal (the SPI Device's
`STATUS.csb`) toggle 4 times corresponding to asserting/deasserting for
the header read and then the payload read. Using this, the device can
determine when the host has started/finished reading and synchronize
accordingly.

This is not ideal because it depends on a direct signal (CSb) which (a)
could be problematic for different clock speeds if the CS is asserted
for a short time and Ibex does not poll fast enough, since there is no
interrupt here, and (b) is very difficult for emulation flows to manage,
such as QEMU.

Instead, since the SPI device exposes the last read address (and the
exact amount of data to be read is known ahead of time), we can just
check the last read address to determine when the host is finished
reading. We still deassert the TX ready pin after either seeing CS go
low or a read address change, but we now know the transaction is
finished when CS is high and we see a match on our target address.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>
(cherry picked from commit 382e702d865079e84803fe39bf1a48fd9af47c40)

subject: [otbn,rtl] Harden acc_qw_sel in bignum MAC against FI attack
body:
This commits predecodes the acc_qw_sel signal to avoid a tricky SW mitigation against FI attacks,
see detailed problem description below. It is predecoded by refactoring it into a 4 bit signal which
controls the MUXing of the ACC merging for each quad word (64 bits) separately.

The problem when acc_qw_sel is not predecoded:
The acc_qw_sel signal controls which quarter word of the ACC is overwritten with multiplication
results during a vectorized multiplication. These instructions process 64 bits at a time and thus
have 4 updates to the ACC WSR.

This signal did not have a redundand signal. Therefore, an attack on this signal is an issue for the
bn.mulv(m) instructions because:

1) A stuck at fault is induced into the bits such that acc_qw_sel = '0.

Yes this requires in theory two attacks as acc_qw_sel is 2 bit wide. But I think it is reasonable that both gates can be FIed
with only one attack as the signals are quite related. A multiplication thus will write all 4
results into the same QW of ACC. The other 3 QW keep the original value.
This allows that QW0 has the wrong result and the other 3 QW have a deterministic value (the value
before the instruction). This could be bad, especially if we perform a multiplication where not all
vector elements contain actual data. If only, e.g., 7 out of 8 elements contain data and element 8
is all-zero, this would allow to set a QW to zero (a deterministic value).

A SW solution solving this would be to ensure that the ACC register is cleared with a random value before
executing a instruction. This is actually supported as the bn.mulv(m) instructions clear ACC in
their last cycle and the ACC could also be cleared by using a bn.wsrw instruction.
However, with this mitigation we would still not directly detect the attack (we would only have a
wrong result). The same randomization would also be needed for unused input vector elements. This
adds considerable burdens to the programmer and is also a great source of vulnerabilities.

2) The acc_qw_sel signal is faulted transiently.

In this case only one result is written to the wrong QW and therefore one QW would keep its value.
Otherwise there are the same problems and the same SW solution could be used.

As the SW solution is cumbersome and easy to do wrong, this commit predecodes the acc_qw_sel signal
by refactoring it to a single bit MUX per QW.

Signed-off-by: Pascal Etterli <pascal.etterli@lowrisc.org>

subject: [otp, rom, sw] Align with unified bypass and FIPS threshold registeres
body:
This commit re-aligns the ROM and software implementations with the
latest implementation of the entropy_src RTL which has unified
threshold registers for FIPS / CC compliant and boot-time / bypass mode.

Because the hardware now only contains a single configuration at any
point in time:
1. ROM/software needs to select the proper configuration from OTP.
2. OTP needs to maintain separate configuration digest values for each
   mode.

In addition, this commit also introduces a separate alert threshold
configuration for both modes in OTP. Because the modes behave quite
differently, it may be desirable to configure different alert
thresholds.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

subject: [entropy_src] Add CSR to control one-way behavior of threshold registers
body:
The threshold registers themselves have a one-way function built it such
that it's not possible to configure more relaxed values. However, due to
the short window size of the bypass mode (384 bits), the absolute
threshold values used for FIPS mode using larger window sizes will
always be more relaxed despite the distribution of noise samples
becoming more tight (central limit theorem) and thresholds becoming
more tight.

For this reason, this commit adds a lockable THRESHOLD_ONEWAY CSR. After
reset, this CSR reads as Mubi4False and the threshold registers can be
re-configured without restrictions. Once the CSR has been configured
to Mubi4True, it's value can no longer be changed and the one-way
behavior of the threshold registers is enforced.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

the `mask_rom` and `test_rom`. In `mask_rom`, it resides in the last

subject: [util] add script to compute committer stats
body:
This adds a script to compute committer stats for the OpenTitan
repository using the GitHub GraphQL API. Currently this script can only
compute stats for the last 100 pages of commits, but it is a good
starting point to iterate on to create a final product that can compute
stats across the whole history of the repo.

In the future, it may be convenient to additionally filter the results
to only aggregate stats for contributors that are no officially
committers yet, as this script will be used to automate committer
proposals.

Signed-off-by: Tim Trippel <ttrippel@google.com>

subject: [util] Paginate & refactor comitter stats script
body:
Add pagination functionality to the script to compute contributor
statistics for the OpenTitan repository. This allows us to use the
GitHub GraphQL API to query the entire repository history, rather than
just the first/last X commits and PRs.

This pagination requires separating the original query into two queries;
while doing this, also refactor and tidy up the code so that it is more
modular, better documented, and structured in an object-oriented way
that will more easily allow extensions and limit future complexities.

Also adds additional functionality for correctness such as excluding CI
accounts (e.g. "github-actions"), and logic changes to only include PRs
made to the `master` branch (for both PRs and reviews).

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [util] Add optional args to the contributor stats script
body:
Adds two optional arguments to the contributor stats script.
 - A `-l`/`--log-progress` flag which enables debug logging
   per-paginated query, since queries over a large repo can take a fair
   while to complete. Provides more visibile progress.
 - A `-p`/`--pages` option that can be used to limit the number of pages
   per query. This can be used for testing purposes & prototyping.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [util] Add error handling & rate limits to contributor stats script
body:
Make requests in the contributor stats script much more reliable.

Check for HTTP Errors and connection timeouts in the the `requests`
library, and add conditional waits between posting the request and
raising the response status following a simple exponential-backoff
scheme.

Also check response status codes to identify rate limits, and wait for
the amount of time suggested by the GraphQL API in this case. Also check
for other HTTP error codes due to e.g. GitHub server issues.

Finally handle the case of GraphQL errors due to e.g. malformed queries
or GitHub API changes.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [util] Add filter for existing committers to contributor stats
body:
Add a command-line option to filter out those who are already in the
COMMITTERS file from the generated list of contributor stats, so that it
can be used to identify potential candidates to become committers.

This is limited however in that it only looks for current contributors -
anybody who was previously a committer but is not any more will still
be suggested for now.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [util] Find historical committers for committer stats
body:
Extends existing contributor stats script logic to find and filter
committers in the COMMITTERS file from the results, to now find a
complete list of all committers in the (tracked) history of the repo, by
searching the local git revisions of changes and parsing the file
contents at each point.

This is more useful, as it means that using the `--filter` option will
no longer return several historic committers.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [util] Make review statistics more accurate.
body:
(i) Based on experimental testing, the GitHub GraphQL API seems to
(at-least) double-count reviews on PRs, perhaps because it counts the
review and comments? Ensure that we only count each unique reviewer once
per pull request to give more accurate numbers.

(ii) Currently, a PR author is counted as having reviewed their own PR,
because they have left a comment. Enforce in the contribution logic that
reviewers must not have authored the PR they are reviewing.

subject: [dv] add test to bootstrap a multislot flash image
body:
This adds a test that bootstraps a multislot flash image, skipping page
programs of all 0xFF bytes to mimic how opentitantool implements bootsrap.

This fixes #27151.

This commit is a cherry-pick of 7df372f, which was committed to the
earlgrey_1.0.0 branch in May 2025. While rebasing, I've done a bit of
tidy-up to the code, making use of some almost identical code in
chip_sw_base_vseq.

One big change from the original version of the test is that the code
that checks correctness of the written pages is now a loop calling
check_flash_word_32. The original code didn't support checking bank 1
of flash (causing failures when it tried to check nonexistant words
through the memory backdoor of bank 0).

subject: [sram_ctrl,dv] Teach scoreboard about some injected faults
body:
The existing testbench fails in mysterious ways if you allow a TL
transaction after injecting a fault: a strong indication that the
scoreboard has never been used for anything very randomised.

This commit adds another interface to make it a bit easier for the
scoreboard to see when faults are injected (we cheat, and define an
injected fault as "the signal changes just before the clock is low").

The scoreboard can then use this interface to see the injected faults.
In order not to model (copy!) the precise timing for when the local
escalation causes the LC gate to close, the scoreboard has a counter
and allows a "might or might not be closed" state in the middle.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [rom_ext] Disable compiler jump guards
body:
Similar to https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/pull/26636, remove the
guards feature from enabled in the toolchain.

The compiler guards feature is meant as a control flow integrity feature that inserts unimp sequences around branches to protect against instruction skips.

Disabling this saves ~4% ROM size, ~12% ROM_EXT size, and ~1% size of
the crypto library.

From instruction skip simulations in
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/pull/28850 and
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/pull/28549, there is no noticable
security difference between the option enabled or disabled.

subject: [sram_ctrl,dv] Switch signoff tool to Xcelium
body:
This is the main tool used for functional simulation in lowRISC at the
moment, and we're going to be doing the next signoff for sram_ctrl.
Switch to officially use the tool that we are using.

This commit also includes a generated UNR vRefine file for the main
configuration. This was made from a run (that had used Xcelium) with

  dvsim hw/ip/sram_ctrl/dv/sram_ctrl_main_sim_cfg.hjson -i all --cov-unr

I then manually went through the coverage exclusions that had been in
the manual file. Most were auto-generated UNR exclusions (which were
hand-written in this file for some reason). There were two entries
that were worth reading through carefully:

1. There was an explicit exclusion of the StFlush state and its arcs in
   tb.dut.u_tlul_lc_gate.

   This has actually been excluded by UNR! I was slightly concerned
   that this might mean a problem with the UNR flow, so spent a bit of
   time thinking about it.

   The only way to get to StFlush is from StOutstanding, if lc_en_i is
   lc_ctrl_pkg::On when the last outstanding TL transaction clears.

   Because the flush_req_i port of u_tlul_lc_gate is constant zero,
   the only way to get to StOutstanding is if lc_en_i becomes
   something other than lc_ctrL_pkg::On. That means that
   lc_tlul_gate_en stops being On, meaning that either escalate_en[1]
   is a value other than Off or local_esc_reg is true.

   The local escalation mechanism means that either event gets
   registered in local_esc_reg, so the gate will always move from
   StOutstanding to StError.

   (Whew, that was hard! I'm glad that I get some extra reassurance
   from the formal tool.)

2. There was an explicit exclusion of branch coverage for the branch
   that stayed in StErrorOutstanding in the same FSM if
   outstanding_txn was not zero.

   Bizarrely, it was listed twice in the UNR file, where the earlier
   version said it was low risk and should be waived, and the later
   version wrongly said that it was impossible.

   I've written up a careful description (going for the first version:
   I think it *is* possible!), which is now in manual.vRefine.

body:
`RescueParams` derives `Args` from `clap`. The `Args` derive macro
interacts poorly with `Default` when arguments have `default_value`
attributes.

not when initializing the struct via `Default::default()`.

This commit removes `Default` from `RescueParams` to prevent potential
misconfigurations.

A search of the codebase (`grep -r 'Default' | grep -E 'Args|Parser'`)
confirms that `RescueParams` was the only struct deriving both

subject: [I2C, DV, RTL] Remove a non-existent assertion from DV / RTL
body:
Everything started with a failing `i2c_host_smoke` test in Xcelium as:
"Hierarchical name component lookup failed for
`tb.dut.i2c_core.u_i2c_fsm.SclInputGlitch_A`". This was added by
PR #16889 in `i2c_host_error_intr_vseq` as part of $assertoff()
switching the assertion off for SCL/SDA interference tests (
that's the justification given by the author in #16889). Firstly, the
problem is that `i2c_fsm` module was renamed to `i2c_target_fsm` in
PR #22345 which will break the path in $asseroff() hierarchy cause it
to fail. Second, the PR #22345 also removes `SclInputGlitch_A` from
`i2c_target_fsm` but adds a different version of `SclInputGlitch_A` in
`i2c_core`. That version state "the 2 flop synchronized output of scl_i
can't be glitchy" along with a comment saying "To decide whether to
keep this assertion as it is only required for the TB".

The author of #16889 switching the version of `SclInputGlitch_A` which
was checking if the SCL input is glitchy (and not the 2FF synchronized
one). I think it is never checked by DV and if the previous version of
`SclInputGlitch_A` worked then assuming that the synchronized version
could possibly work as well.

I think the best way to define assertion that will support TB / DV
should go inside an SVA interface binded with the RTL and shouldn't
exist in the RTL itself.

Given that. the solution is to remove the assertion from both RTL and DV.

subject: [entropy_src,dv] Clean up the init code in entropy_src_base_vseq
body:
The main change is to try_apply_base_configuration. Before this
commit, the task was run in a spinwait loop that watched for an alert.
If one was asserted, it would then wait until there were no register
accesses for a while and then kill the process.

After this commit, the task takes a reference to a "stop now" bit. If
this bit gets asserted, the task will exit as soon as a register
access happens. This should be considerably quicker. And we no longer
kill processes that have a risk of touching a register, which is
probably rather safer.

For the tasks that I was touching anyway, I've also converted things
to use uvm_reg's read / write / mirror / update tasks (because they
are a slightly more conventional UVM style) and have added early exits
if a reset is asserted.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [flash_ctrl,dv] Make some structures unpacked
body:
For example, consider flash_mp_region_cfg_t. Structs of this type are
randomised in several places (see flash_ctrl_error_mp_vseq, for
example). This isn't going to do what we need if the struct is packed.
For example (without further constraints), each of those seven mubi4_t
elements is going to be have an invalid encoding with probability
14/16.

This might be worked around. Indeed, I see that
flash_ctrl_error_mp_vseq has explicit constraints for the regions,
that will force the fields to take named enum values. But it's
probably more sensible to default to more guessable behaviour.

As well as flash_ctrl_error_mp_vseq, this commit makes the same change
to:

  - flash_bank_mp_info_page_cfg_t (another 7 mubi values, with the
    same analysis).

  - flash_op_t (contains several enums and gets confusingly randomised
    in several places, which is why I noticed this in the first place)

  - rd_cache_t (contains an enum variable)

It turns out that removing "packed" isn't quite enough. The biggest
reason is that there were quite a few "solve before" lines that aren't
actually allowed if you have something more interesting than a bit
vector.

Changes needed:

  - Make the fields of flash_op_t themselves be rand. This is needed
    because calling my_class.randomise(some_class_variable) doesn't
    work if some_class_variable is an unpacked struct whose fields
    aren't explicitly marked rand.

  - This is also needed in flash_mp_region_cfg_t and
    flash_bank_mp_info_page_cfg_t. For some reason, *that* isn't
    visible at compile time, but you end up with a runtime error where
    something is randomised with X values (not allowed by the spec!)
    and the root cause is that we're not actually randomising e.g. a
    region config struct, so it gets its initial value (of X).

  - Rephrase lots of rules of the form "solve xyz before
    flash_op" to things like "solve xyz before flash_op.addr". This is
    because the SystemVerilog spec doesn't allow anything except an
    integer in as a thing to be solved before/after. I think the DV
    engineer just has to pretend to be a compiler. Sigh...

  - Remove some ordering constraints of the form "solve en_mp_regions
    before mp_regions". This is definitely not allowed (because
    mp_regions is an array of unpacked structs, so not a bit vector).
    I'm not completely convinced we care but, if we do, my proposal
    would be to randomise the items of the vector explicitly as we get
    to them ("late randomisation"). The code ends up simpler, I think.

  - Fix flat-out bogus syntax in flash_ctrl_invalid_op_vseq.sv.
    Antonio and I have fixed the same error in quite a few places in
    the past. In this case, it came from commit 9b01461 in 2022.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [adc_ctrl,dv] Put adc_ctrl_filter_cfg inside a proper class
body:

that randomising values that aren't in a *static* structure causes
some exciting problems with "solve before" constraints.

In hindsight, I think this change isn't quite needed: I could have
bodged something into the existing code. But I think it's probably an
improvement anyway (and I've got it working!).

One change is to make some of the class variable names a bit clearer.
For example, the "cond" field in adc_chn*_filter_ctl_* controls
whether the filter matches inside the range or outside of it. I
actually guessed wrong at first, but I think this makes a strong
argument for making the code more explicit on the DV side. That is now
reflected with a variable called "match_outside" (instead of my
original guess of "match_inside", which is exactly backwards!)

Indeed, I've just checked again and looked at
`theory_op_operation.md`. That document *does* mention a field called
"cond" and that it controls whether the filter matches inside or
outside of the range. It *doesn't* say which... This clearly needs
tidying up, but I think that sort of work can be folded into the next
proper release.

    what they do, including careful notes about whether the task can
    be killed (on reset).

subject: [dv,alert] Get rid of two under_reset flags
body:
This was all rather confusing! There were the following signals:

  alert_esc_agent_cfg::under_reset
  alert_esc_base_monitor::under_reset
  dv_base_driver::under_reset

And the alert and escalation side of things maintained them
differently(!): on the escalation side, under_reset meant "under
reset". On the alert side, it meant "has not been initialised since
reset", which is the same as !alert_esc_agent_cfg::alert_init_done.

This commit gets rid of all three flags, relying on
dv_base_agent_cfg::in_reset instead (which gets maintained properly by
the monitors).

Note that it's a little odd to ignore dv_base_driver::under_reset. It
won't matter with this commit (because dv_base_driver doesn't use that
flag directly and nothing subclasses the alert/escalation drivers),
but things are still a little strange. A following commit will get rid
of that flag entirely, but the alert agent was tricky, so I've done it
separately.

subject: [ci] Bump all download-artifact actions from v4 to v8
body:
Pick up the change to the node24 runtime, as Node.js 20 actions are
currently deprecated and will mean upload-artifact@v4 is end-of-life on
September 16th 2026.

The main breaking change is for users whose specified an artifact by ID
(`artifact-ids`) for single artifact downloads. We only download
artifacts by pattern, so this does not impact us. The latest version
makes hash mismatches error by default (which seems sensible, so we'll
leave that enabled) and only tries to unzip zipped files (which is our
existing use case, so there should be no noticeable change).

subject: [adc_ctrl,dv] Expand comments a bit and tidy up adc_ctrl_fsm_sva_if
body:
There is no functional change, but dropping the ASSERT macro makes
things a little easier to read.

The hardware reset assertions should now be a little more
efficient. I don't think we really need to bother asserting that the
signals don't magically start changing somewhere in the middle of a
reset(!), so I've restructured them slightly to check the first clock
after the start of a reset.

The first syntax I used for this (which is equivalent to the previous
version, but without noise from the macro) uses two "clocks" and is of
the form

  @(negedge rst_aon_ni) 1 |=> @(posedge clk_aon_i) XYZ

Here, the |=> waits for the event on the right hand side, so it means
"On the first clock edge after reset is asserted, XYZ". Very nice!

Unfortunately, this isn't actually supported by Verible's
SystemVerilog front-end. Grr! I was very annoyed at first, but
realised that there's actually an even cleaner way to do it. Because
this is a bound-in interface, we can easily define a helper signal.

This commit defines a "start_of_reset" flag, which set when reset is
asserted and then cleared on the first clock. Now, the properties can
be very simple, looking like:

  start_of_reset -> XYZ

(checked on the positive edge of clk_aon_i because of the default
clocking statement).

That's even shorter! Yippee!

When I initially wrote this, I worried about the scheduling because we
clear start_of_reset on the clock edge and look at the value at the
same time. Fortunately, this is ok: the value tested in the expression
is its value from the preponed region (see IEEE 1800, 16.5.1), so
we'll get the value that hasn't yet been cleared.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

be post-processed.  Thus the previous implementation is not expected to
have caused any real problem.  Nonetheless, this change improves this

subject: [tl,dv] Clear the stop flag at the end, not the start, of body()
body:
Before this change, there was a race condition in the rv_dm testbench.

That block's base virtual sequence creates a device
sequence (m_tl_sba_device_seq) in a task called
sba_tl_device_seq_start and then uses fork/join_none to start it in
the background. One sequence that derives from rv_dm_base_vseq is
rv_dm_sba_tl_access_vseq, which calls sba_tl_device_seq_stop at the
start of its body. The result is that you can end up with this
course of events:

  - rv_dm_base_vseq::dut_init calls sba_tl_device_seq_start, which
    starts an instance of tl_device_seq (whose body will run shortly).

  - The start of rv_dm_sba_tl_access_vseq::body calls
    sba_tl_device_seq_stop, which sets the stop flag in the device
    sequence and then waits for that sequence to run to completion.

  - The device sequence finally starts! At the start of
    tl_device_seq::body, it clears the stop flag.

  - The device sequence now runs until it sees the stop flag being
    set.

  - Hang.

The change in this commit moves the flag clearing to the end of the
sequence. Honestly, I don't think we ever run an instance of this
sequence multiple times, so we can probably just drop it. But this is
clearly safe too.

Initial debugging made me wonder whether this was caused by commit
c3b9a23, but I think the race is there either way.

This change fixes rv_dm_sba_tl_access, which is currently broken.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

My previous "clean ups" (61d487c) are kind of nice, but I didn't
understand at the time that a failing assertion doesn't actually cause
the simulation to fail.

The `ASSERT macro handles this by including `ASSERT_ERROR. This either
calls $error or uses uvm_report_error. Do the same thing.

I still believe that this is nicer than the `ASSERT macro, because we
get sensible default clocking / default disable behaviour and I think
the net result is probably better.

As an explicit example, the macro-based definition looked like this:

    `ASSERT(legalAOpcode_A,     h2d_pre_S |-> legalAOpcode_S,     !clk_i, !rst_ni || disable_sva)

and it is now:

      legalAOpcode_A:
        assert property (h2d_pre_S |-> legalAOpcode_S)
        else `ASSERT_ERROR(legalAOpcode_A)

`src_req` and `dst_ack` signals are assigned in the comb blocks of the
FSMs. These signals drive the inputs of the handshake synchronisers.
This appears to CDC tools as combinatorial logic before a synchroniser
and flags an error.

This commit adjusts the logic so `src_req` and `dst_ack` are driven
directly by the FSM the flop explicitly. This modification removes the
glitch error flag by the tool.

It is most likely the synthesis tool optimisation will come to this
solution, however in these cases it is better to code the intent
explicitly.

subject: [clkmgr/cdc] Deglitch on shadow register error alerts
body:
In prior commits the 'err_storage' signal from the 'prim_subreg_shadow'
module  was fed directly to a synchroniser. As the generation logic for
this error is combinatorial it can generate glitches as it settles.
There are several instances of these shadow registers in the Clock
Manager the majority of which are in a different clock domain to the
alert logic, therefore requiring synchronisation. The register interface
is generated from the template file reg_top.sv.tpl in the util/reggen
directory.

To prevent the glitches propagating, this commit adds an additional flop
to the error signal path before the synchroniser for each shadow
register instance with a clock domain crossing. These additional flops
were placed in the template, clkmgr_reg_top.sv was then regenerated with
`make -k -C hw top_and_cmdgen` for `top_darjeeling`, `top_earlgrey` and
`top_englishbreakfast`

This commit resolves issue lowRISC/opentitan#24592

subject: [prim/rtl] Improve prim_fifo_async_simple for rv_dm and lc_ctrl
body:
The `prim_fifo_async_simple` module is currently only used in the
`rv_dm` and `lc_ctrl` blocks in the request/response path between clock
domains. In prior commits the data signals crossing the clock domain
boundary were only registered in the transmitting domain. These data
signals are an aggregate of signals required for the JTAG request. This
aggregate is then distributed in the receiving clock domain. The use of
the data is qualified by the valid signal generated by the crossing
logic, however, this traverses many layers of logic and is difficult to
prove. It can also lead to timing issues due to unconstrained long paths
depending on the SDC definition. This also applies to the response path,
but the aggregate vector is narrower.

Therefore, this commit adds registers to the receiving domain ensuring
the data is stable and cutting the long paths. This reduces the design
effort to generate waivers and ensures the module is safe when used in
other contexts.

NOTE: the waiver in file `opentitan_pub/hw/ip/rv_dm/lint/rv_dm.waiver`
regarding the RESET_MUX in dmi_cdc.sv has been extended to cover the
additional flop in the read handshake logic, `rvalid_q`.

subject: [dv,chip] Tidy up load methods for flash images in chip_sw_base_vseq
body:
The code in chip_sw_base_vseq::cpu_init expects to load up the
contents of flash. Historically, it did so through a backdoor.

Near the release of Earlgrey 1.0.0, there several virtual sequences
were added that load flash over SPI instead. You might expect this to
be controlled through chip_env_cfg::use_spi_load_bootstrap, but the
new sequences skip the code in the base class that does the loading
and re-implement this separately.

I hadn't properly understood how this worked when I ported
ate_bootstrap_disjoint in commit 4a305de, so set the plusarg before
porting the code that would look it it. Even more confusingly, the
ported version of ate_bootstrap_flash_erase (commit 46cc365) asks that
any supplied images should be loaded over SPI... then supplies no
images.

In both cases, the code does the right thing. But it's very confusing!

After the tidy-up in this commit, we just have two behaviours:

  - use_spi_load_bootstrap = 0

    This is the default behaviour. Load up any slot A or slot B image
    that exists, using mem_bkdr_util.

  - use_spi_load_bootstrap = 1

    Load the slot A image (which might well contain slot B as well)
    and write it into flash over SPI.

I'm hopeful that the other similar tests can be ported from the
earlgrey_1.0.0 branch without needing to change this further.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [alert,dv] Simplify how we constrain ping_delay
body:
This number has been very confusing! At the start of 2024, functional
simulations weren't sending pings at all. When I made change
a771270fab3 that year, I interpreted ping_delay as "the number of
cycles to wait before sending a ping". So that we could send
back-to-back ping items but have reasonable gaps between pings, I was
configuring this to be large (> 10,000).

What I didn't notice is that some sequences constrained it to be more
like 10! I think the original idea was that a virtual sequence would
decide to send a ping (for some reason), which would then take a
handful of extra cycles before it was sent.

Unfortunately, this was meaning that some virtual sequences were
sending *lots* of ping transactions, with gaps of just 10 cycles. The
change in this commit switches everything across to the new meaning.
We now send back-to-back items, which translate into periodic ping
requests.

There are a couple of extra tidy-ups in the commit

 - Get rid of use_seq_item_ping_delay. I accidentally removed the code
   that was reading this in commit 1eb96b30. The new behaviour is
   probably better, so let's just use it.

 - Tweak a wait in entropy_src_base_vseq. This was added in commit
   a3f91eec28e, which wanted to make sure the sequence waited long
   enough to see alerts that would be triggered by the previous
   register write. With the new meaning of ping_delay, we definitely
   don't need to wait for it.

body:
Before this change, the code would print lots of warnings about not
understanding parameters. There are two situations where we can
silence it:

1. The parameter type is something like "logic" or "bit [31:0]". These
   parameters can be passed through to the C code perfectly happily.
   Do so.

2. The parameter type is something like "int [123][456]". This doesn't
   make sense to add to a #define line, but we understand what's going
   on and don't need to tell the user about it.

This commit handles both of those cases. There are no longer any
parameters that get skipped, but we still have a warning line that
will come out if any get added.

Note that there are some parameters that used the first form above
and had SystemVerilog-style hex literals. For example, edn_reg_pkg
contains:

  parameter logic [31:0] EdnBootGenCmdResval = 32'hfff003;

This patch converts such things to conventional C literals. In this
case, you get:

  // Reset value for the boot_gen_cmd register.
  #define EDN_PARAM_EDN_BOOT_GEN_CMD_RESVAL 0xfff003

subject: [signing] Fix signature_test failure due to manifest serialization changes
body:
The recent change to `opentitantool` (specifically `drop_null_extensions`
behavior in #29097) altered how manifests are serialized. This caused
`signature_test` to fail when comparing pre-existing signed binaries
(generated with the old tool) against binaries re-generated by the test
(using the new tool). Even if the keys were identical, the binary
comparison failed due to differences in manifest extensions fields.

This commit updates `signature_test` to normalize the original binary
by passing it through `opentitantool image manifest update` (without
changes) before comparison. This ensures both the "original" and the
"verified" binaries are serialized using the current tool's logic,
allowing `cmp` to correctly verify that the keys match.

subject: [dv] Fix and document timing in cip_base_vseq::wait_alert_trigger
body:
There was an off-by-one error in the wait, and the explanation of the
numbers was very hard to follow. Fix the error (by adding an extra
cycle to the wait for an ack to clear) and fix a race condition, while
expanding the code out to make it a bit easier to reason about.

In detail:

- Add an extra cycle to the end of wait_alert_trigger when it is
  waiting for the ack to complete. This lines everything up with "the
  clock where a signal change is seen", which avoids an apparent extra
  cycle between alerts when the ack is reported too early.

- Add an extra half cycle to timeout when waiting for the alert to be
  asserted. This avoids a race condition if the alert takes exactly
  the maximum time before it is asserted.

- Add a bit more detail to the comment that explains the default value
  of max_wait_cycle. It's very easy to get confused about the
  difference between "the signal drops" and "there is a clock edge
  where the signal is low". The new version should be slightly
  clearer.

All of this logic should probably live in the appropriate alert agent,
rather than us doing the error checking in the sequence, but that's a
problem for another commit.

centralized library. It includes version detection, bit-packing for
the new 32-bit headers, and unit tests to verify both V0 and V1
encapsulation.

The V1 format is required to support ML-DSA-87 (MLDSA) certificates,
which exceed the 4KB limit of the V0 format. MLDSA attestation keys
are derived from a 32-byte seed (xi) generated by the Key Manager
(keymgr) using stage-specific attestation diversification. This seed
is subsequently processed by the ML-DSA implementation on OTBN to
generate the final keypair.

subject: [chip,dv] Select one SCK frequency in chip_sw_spi_passthrough_vseq
body:
Rather than trying all frequencies, try a random one. This should make
the test rather quicker, and also simplifies the randomisation a bit.

In particular, we can now constrain read_pipeline_mode = 2 when at the
high frequency (the only mode that was tested at that frequency in
GLS)

Also re-enable 30MHz SCK frequency in GLS. This was disabled in commit
411ac26 because the 30 MHz clock didn't work properly with a read
pipeline without 2 stages. Instead of disallowing it across-the-board,
this commit constrains read_pipeline_mode to have the value that is
expected to work.

To make it easier to see what test was run, the vseq now prints the
SCK period, the passthrough filters and the read pipeline mode. Since
the processor needs to configure the latter two, the SW prints them to
the log too (to make it easy to check everything agrees).

subject: [alert,fpv] Strengthen AlertHs_A in prim_alert_rxtx_assert_fpv
body:
Before this commit, the property in the AlertHs_A assertion looked
something like

  alert_req_i && both_idle |=> FullHandshake_S |-> alert_ack_o

Noting that |-> and |=> are right-associative, this means

  "Suppose there's an alert request when both are idle. Then any full
   handshake that starts on the following cycle will end with
   alert_ack_o being high"

That seems rather weak! I think the author intended it to say that
there would be a full handshake and that handshake would end with
alert_ack_o being high.

With the rewording in the commit, this becomes:

  "Suppose there's an alert request when both are idle. Then a full
  handshake will start on the following cycle, finishing with with
  alert_ack_o being high"

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [keymgr,dv] Make assertion failures in keymgr_if more informative
body:
The assertions are checking the same behaviour, but we can make use of
the fact we're in a UVM context and print out a more helpful error
message.

The only change to the assertion properties themselves is that they
CheckKmacKey, CheckAesKey and CheckOtbnKey now use the observed valid
signal instead of the expected one. This is equivalent (because of
CheckKmacKeyValid, CheckAesKeyValid and CheckOtbnKeyValid), but
probably makes a bit more sense.

The expansion of text is because we now print out more information on
a failure (including both halves of masked values). The motivation for
this was that I'd messed up some wiring when integrating a modified
KMAC agent. Improving the error messages here made it rather easier to
see what was going on.

subject: [dv] Add a "chip_level" fusesoc flag
body:
This gets defined in the cores for chip environments. The advantage is
that these cores can now depend on the environments of IPs, which
won't generate their own RAL definitions (because the chip-level
environment has done it already).

Note that this is different from the existing skip_ral_gen flag. As
far as I can tell, there's no way to set a flag for just the cores
that get pulled in as a dependencies. As such, skip_ral_gen will let
you turn everything off, but I don't think you can turn off just the
RAL for the blocks.

To set the "chip_level" flag, it has to be set to true in the core
file that gets invoked by fusesoc (I think). This is chip_sim.core.

body:
- The goal is to reduce the overall runtime of the DV regression by
  optimizing the reseed values for all blocks/tops. The new values are

  for which I took the minimum values. Then I have reduced reseeding

subject: [prim/rtl] Improve prim_fifo_async_simple DFT for rv_dm and lc_ctrl
body:
The `prim_fifo_async_simple` module is currently only used in the
`rv_dm` and `lc_ctrl` blocks in the request/response path between clock
domains. In prior commits the `wready_o` signal was derived from the
`pending_q` and `not_in_reset_q` signals, the later is a flop reset to
'0 and tied to '1. The intent is to prevent data being accepted and lost
when in reset. Whilst this gives the desired function it will result in
a DFT violation as the data input to the flop is not controllable.

This commit adjusts the logic so the register is driven by the inverse
of the `pending_q` signal. This maintains the function and ensures the
`wready_q` flop is controllable.

Signed-off-by: Neil Webb <nsw@lowrisc.org>

independent timing to secure GCM for SCA (we leave icache as perference

We create an interface to the ibex_disable_icache and
ibex_restore_icache drivers functions for the user.

the use of memshred, i.e., drawing randomness which stalls, and also
from otcrypto_eval_exit which reads from the alert manager which crosses
clock domains. The gcm is constant time when the icache is disabled and
the reading of the alert registers is manually removed. We keep the test
as broken (as we would need to mock out the reading of the alert
registers). However, the test is slightly adapted to use the new

subject: [kmac,dv] Fix type of DPI interface
body:
This argument in the C functions is for what the DPI layer calls an
"open array":

  import "DPI-C" context function void c_dpi_cshake128(
    input bit[7:0]          msg[],
    input string            function_name,
    input string            customization_str,
    input longint unsigned  msg_len,
    input longint unsigned  output_len,
    output bit[7:0]         digest[]
  );

(see section H.8.6 of IEEE 1800-2012) and, as such, should be given an
svOpenArrayHandle on the C side.

The typedef is not very informative: it's actually void*! But it makes
more sense to be consistent with the other equivalent arguments.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>
Co-authored-by: Pascal Etterli <pascal.etterli@lowrisc.org>

subject: [pwrmgr,dv] Restore pwrmgr_repeat_wakeup_reset
body:
Commit 7f9bc41b95 deleted pwrmgr_sec_cm_rom_ctrl_intersig_mubi from
pwrmgr_sim_cfg.hjson.tpl, claiming it was subsumed by
pwrmgr_repeat_wakeup_reset. That test never existed: maybe the author
confused the vseq name (pwrmgr_repeat_wakeup_reset_vseq) with a
sim_cfg test entry. As a result, PwrmgrMubiRomCtrl became a dead enum
value and the sec_cm_rom_ctrl_intersig_mubi countermeasure had no test
driving invalid MuBi4 values on rom_ctrl_i.

Restore test by:
- Adding pwrmgr_repeat_wakeup_reset to pwrmgr_sim_cfg.hjson.tpl with
  +pwrmgr_mubi_mode=PwrmgrMubiRomCtrl and a 4 ms timeout (matching
  the original pwrmgr_sec_cm_rom_ctrl_intersig_mubi entry).
- Refactoring pwrmgr_repeat_wakeup_reset_vseq to unify the duplicated
  drv_lc_ctrl/drv_rom_ctrl loops into a single drv_stim loop, with a
  drive_inputs(phase0) task dispatching via case on mubi_mode to
  drive_lc_ctrl_inputs or drive_rom_ctrl_inputs. The rom_ctrl path
  injects random MuBi4 values (including invalid encodings) on all
  NumRomInputs channels of rom_ctrl_i as background stimulus during
  the wakeup/reset sequence.
- Adding a uvm_fatal default in drive_inputs for unknown mubi_mode
  values.

subject: [dv] Split reactive agents from dv_base_agent
body:
Historically, dv_base_agent has had some extra wiring to allow
reactive sequences, driven by the monitor:

  - The monitor has two ports: req_analysis_port and rsp_analysis_port
  - These are attached to corresponding exports in the sequencer.

The idea is that a reactive sequence can subscribe to the appropriate
exports and respond accordingly.

This isn't really the current convention in the UVM world. The main
problem is that you end up with the stimulus (the sequence) depending
on behaviour of an analysis component. The more standard way to do
this is to broadcast the requests from the driver instead, and pass
them to the sequence that responds.

Even when unused, the existing structure can be problematic. If you
want to make an agent that can be active in either direction ("Host"
or "Device") on an interface, you probably want a different driver in
each case, and it makes more sense for these drivers to have different
sequence item types. This, in turn, means you need a different
sequencer type in each direction. You then build two copies of the
agent ("my_host_agent" and "my_device_agent"). Unfortunately, these
can't share a monitor! The monitor type ends up needing to know the
direction ("REQ_ITEM_T" and "RSP_ITEM_T").

This commit splits out the "agent with a sequencer that reacts to a
monitor" into an intermediate class. The agents that used this
structure can now inherit from that type, giving chains like

  alert_esc_agent < dv_reactive_agent < dv_base_agent

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [crypto] Introduce relocatable binary blob build with self-integrity check
body:
This commit allows to build libotcrypto as a position-independent, relocatable
binary blob. This enables FIPS-compliant runtime self-integrity checking while
allowing applications to link to the cryptolib without requiring jump tables or
custom ELF header parsing.

Key additions:

Build: Added a Bazel rule (opentitan_binary_blob) and configuration flags to
easily toggle between standard static builds (crypto_dev) and the standalone
FIPS module (crypto_fips_all), other configurations can be added later.

Linker scripts: Added static and partial linker scripts (otcrypto_blob.ld,
otcrypto_partial.ld) to pack the cryptolib into a contiguous memory block and
expose the start, end, and hash symbols.

Self-integrity check: Implemented runtime self-hashing in self_integrity.c to
verify the module's own code region. Extended otcrypto_hash_test to validate
the new mechanism.

What is not in:

Currently, the new compilation (--config=crypto_fips_all) can not yet be
guaranteed to work for every crypto test and integration will follow up.
However, the regular static rule still applies to all CI tests.

With thanks to elievap@google.com, yhdeng@google.com,
cfrantz@google.com, and amaury.pouly@lowrisc.org

Signed-off-by: Siemen Dhooghe <sdhooghe@google.com>
(cherry picked from commit bb40700a25a487521e5667f9abb25c3103269f1e)

subject: [crypto] Fix position-independent code (PIC) violations
body:
Resolved three distinct issues preventing the generation of a
relocatable cryptolib:

1. OTBN Addressing: Replaced `OTBN_ADDR_T_INIT` with inline
   assembly to force absolute loads.
   - Root Cause: Under `-mcmodel=medany`, C assumes external symbols
     are relocatable and emits PC-relative `auipc` instructions. Because
     OTBN coprocessor addresses are fixed MMIO locations, shifting the
     `.text` origin stretches the distance, forcing the linker to alter
     the instruction bytes. The inline assembly forces an absolute load,
     bypassing PC-relative relocation entirely.

2. Data Pointers: Moved global `static const` configuration strings
   (e.g., in kmac.c) to local block scope.
   - Root Cause: File-scope constant arrays are allocated in the `.rodata`
     section, forcing the compiler to generate pointers (and subsequent
     linker relocations) to pass them to functions like `memcpy`. By
     moving them to block scope as automatic variables, the compiler
     synthesizes the data dynamically on the stack using immediate
     instructions (e.g., `li`), completely eliminating `.rodata` pointer
     dependencies.

3. Jump Tables: Applied `-fno-jump-tables` to cryptolib driver BUILD targets.
   - Root Cause: To optimize execution, GCC heuristically lowers dense
     `switch` statements (e.g., in `kmac.c` and `entropy.c`) into anonymous
     jump tables stored in `.rodata`, populated with absolute `.text`
     function pointers. Because PIC lacks a dynamic linker to
     fix up these pointers at runtime, binary relocation fatally breaks
     them. Injecting `-fno-jump-tables` via shared `PIC_COPTS` forces
     the compiler to emit inherently position-independent relative branches
     (`beq`, `bne`).

Signed-off-by: Siemen Dhooghe <sdhooghe@google.com>
(cherry picked from commit 527620730dd4a364351ed48da0ed42f146a45186)

subject: [conn,earlgrey] Fix invalid names in connection assertions
body:
Fix various connectivity checks that have been broken by development
since the last earlgrey tapeout.

These tests can be run with:

  dvsim hw/top_earlgrey/formal/chip_conn_cfg.hjson

Before this commit, they failed to elaborate because quite a lot of
signal names had changed (from a change that moved the OTP macro and
then two different port changes related to Darjeeling).

This commit gets things building again. The tests don't
actually *pass* (two different counterexamples), but fixing that will
be a separate commit.

The changes involved were:

+ Commit 2b9e4b3 moved the OTP macro out of otp_ctrl, which broke the
  following connections:

  - In analog_sigs.csv, there is a check for the connection of an
    external voltage signal (OTP_EXT_VOLT) to the macro.

  - In ast_infra.csv, there is a check on the path of a power
    sequencing signal from u_ast to the OTP macro.

  - In ast_scanmode.csv, there is a check for the connection of the
    scanmode DFT signal from u_ast to the OTP macro.

  - In ast_otp.csv, there are checks for four signals ebetween the AST
    and the OTP macro.

  - In lc_ctrl_broadcast.csv, there is a check that the DFT enable
    signal from lc_ctrl is passed properly to the OTP macro.

  - In otp_lc_vendor_test.csv, there is also a check for a separate
    connection from lc_ctrl to the OTP macro.

+ Commit 4befb49 changed the way entropy bits are connected from the
  TRNG in the u_ast to the entropy_src. It had a typo (s/bit/bits/).
  This connection was tracked in ast_entropy_src_cfg.csv.

+ Commit aea12b7 (adding memory tiling for Darjeeling) changed the
  path to the memories inside various blocks (OTBN, Ibex, usbdev). The
  cfg connections for these memories are tracked in ast_mem_cfg.csv.

subject: [aes,dv] Allow key_sideload_set_seq to be aborted, not killed
body:
This commit allows a virtual sequence to ask an instance of
key_sideload_set_seq to come to a stop, which we connect up in
aes_base_vseq as an example.

key_sideload_item has been extended with a flag to say a stop has been
requested. This can be set by calling key_sideload_item::request_stop.
When the flag is set, key_sideload_driver will immediately stop
driving the item.

This mechanism allows key_sideload_set_seq to have a request_stop
function, which will cause the sequence to complete immediately.

The change is prompted by a use in the AES block. There, aes_base_vseq
has always run random instances of key_sideload_set_seq in a loop with
the start_sideload_seq task.

This commit adds a stop_sideload_seq function that causes the
start_sideload_seq task to stop if it is running. It then tidies up
the fork/join structure in aes_reseed_vseq (which was kind of wrong
before) in a way that no longer requires us to kill start_sideload_seq
with disable fork.

subject: [aes,dv] Don't add more resets inside aes_stress_all_with_rand_reset
body:
The outer loop in stress_all_with_rand_reset runs the stress all
sequence (aes_stress_all_vseq), together with some other do-nothing
error sequences and then wants to inject a reset in the middle.

This won't work very well if the internal stress all sequence injects
resets as well. To stop that happening:

  - Give aes_stress_all_vseq a flag that allows it to be told it
    should only run sequences that are resettable.

  - Extend cip_base_vseq::run_seq_with_rand_reset_vseq so that it sets
    that flag.

  - Teach aes_stress_all_vseq that aes_alert_reset_vseq is not
    resettable (it wants to inject resets itself).

  - Make the random vseq selection in aes_stress_all_vseq obey the
    flag that might tell it to only run sequences that are resettable.

The commit is marginally longer than you might hope because:

  - Annoyingly, I had to touch cip_base_vseq (because I stupidly
    hadn't made a task virtual).

  - We need to implement aes_stress_all_with_rand_reset::do_copy
    because cip_base_vseq::run_seq_with_rand_reset_vseq clones the
    sequence each time and we need to make sure the configuration gets
    passed across.

subject: [kmac/doc] Correct peak performance numbers of Keccak core
body:
When updating these figures in b968a168c2faf600c0174b5328bfabe8ffca036c,
I erroneously assumed that the padding was added to every block instead
of just the last block of a message.

So it really takes `block size / 64` clock cycles to load the data into
the Keccak core (rather than a flat 25 clock cycles) and then either 24
or 96 clock cycles for the processing of the 24 Keccak rounds.

This results in 144 (SHA3-224) or 72 bytes (SHA3-512) being processed
every 42 or 33 (unmasked), or every 114 or 105 clock cycles (masked).

subject: [otbn] otbn_fi_sim_test and otbn_tvla_sim_test
body:
Add a new otbn_fi_sim_test target which simulates an otbn application
and performs a campaign of instruction skip tests.
The test works as follows:
- It ingests two test cases. Namely, a test with two different inputs.
- It traces the first test in order to know the program counters of the
  performed test. It checks for an output status value, which is given
in the Bazel target as the ok_symbol.
- For each program counter (with a max occurence of 2), skip the
  instruction and test with both inputs. The user picks a collision
symbol, if the test gives back an ok status and the two cases provide
the same output, the test gives back the program counter calling it an
effective fault injection.

We perform instruction skipping as a form of fault injection testing
since this model is easy to apply and provides a manner of testing the
hardening of otbn applications.

Add a simulation test to the OTBN for Test Vector Leakage
Analysis (TVLA) on the provided test assembly for the OTBN using the
Python simulation framework.
The test runs with the following parameters:
- background_secrets: these are parameters in dmem that have to be
  re-shared at every new run but stay at a fixed secret value. The user
can choose to have these fixed or random.
- num_experiments: these are the number of traces to take. Recall that
  these are noiseless, hence a low number of traces is already good to
get data.
- t_threshold: the t-value at which to flag something as leakage. Given
  that we are noiseless, we expect "loud" leakage, hence a value like 7
is better fitted to filter false positives.
- tvla_secrets: the shared secrets that are run fixed vs random
  (multiple possible). The user also has to give the secret sharing
scheme.

The test takes 10 leakage models into account:
- A HW and HD model of the ALU's output
- A HW and HD model of the ALU's inputs
- A HW and HD model of flag groups 0 and 1
The test will get these values for each PC over the test.

In order to speed up the testing (current bottleneck lies in the Python
simulation itself), we create a simple sed rule via the label `SCA_TEST_REPLACE` which would replace an instruction to what the label says (via a simple genrule Bazel call).

Add the fault and side-channel simulation tests for the current public
key algorithms.

(cherry picked from commit 58112953584d5c1a3298c68ff288b31ef797224a)

subject: [alert_handler] Fix computation of id_to_ping_d signal
body:
This commit fixes the computation of the id_to_ping_d signal to support
power-of-2 number of alerts.

For non-power-of-2 number of alerts, drawn alert IDs which are not in
range get now modified by simply forcing the top bit to zero. This
reduces the area compared to subtracting the number of alerts. As a
result of this area optimization, the range of alerts which are pinged
twice as often is shifted from the low IDs to the mid-index IDs. For
example in the case of Darjeeling, IDs 13-63 are now pinged more
frequently compared to IDs 0-50 before. This is okay from a security
perspective.

software, or one of the hardware interfaces).

The write handler counts the number of bus words and forwards the request

is seen, the full transaction is aborted and terminated.

software, or one of the hardware interfaces)

The Read handler counts the number of bus words and forwards the
requests to the memory protection where each transaction is checked.
If an error is seen, the full transaction is aborted and terminated.

The read data is fed back to the arbiter which then distributes the data

It also supports a loopback from the read to the write interface to

words.

subject: [rram_ctrl,rtl] add rram_ctrl memory protection
body:
The rram_ctrl_mp checks each transaction against programmable and fixed
rules. These rules define which master (sw, host, hw-lcmgr, hw-otp) can
access which partition of the RRAM.

The rule selection is done based on the requested address, partition,
and selected hardware interface.

This module also determines if a request requires
scrambling/descrambling, and if it is ECC protected.

Signed-off-by: Michael Gautschi <mgautschi@lowrisc.org>

subject: [rram_ctrl,rtl] add read-buffer for phy_rd
body:
This commit adds the read-buffer for the rram_phy_rd module. The last
NumRdBuf entries are stored in the read-buffer each holding its address,
data, and an attribute field (valid, verified, allocated). In addition,
a bit is indicating if the data in the buffer is scrambled or not.

Upon a miss, a buffer will be allocated with the address and partition.
When the data is read from the RRAM it will be stored in the allocated
entry and the attribute will update from 'alloc' to 'valid'. A second
read to the RRAM will then verify that the content of the buffer is
identical to the result of the second read. If not, an integrity error
is output.

Signed-off-by: Michael Gautschi <mgautschi@lowrisc.org>

subject: [rram_ctrl,rtl] rd-buf-dep

read-buffer currently has a dependency to an outstanding request. If

subject: [rram_ctrl,rtl] add rram_phy_rd
body:
This module is responsible of issuing read requests to the RRAM.
It also contains a small read-buffer of configurable number of entries
(Default 4). If the requested data is already in the read-buffer, no
RRAM request is sent, but the data is returned from the read-buffer
directly.

This module also issues verification read requests for all read-buffer
entries. This makes sure that any tampering during a read-request will
get detected.

subject: [rram_ctrl,rtl] Add rram_phy_wr

issues requests to the RRAM. Up to 32 RRAM words can be written at the
time by storing them in a store buffer. At the end of each page or at
the end of a transaction, the write module makes sure that the store
buffer is written to RRAM by asserting the wr_last_o signal together
with a request.

subject: [crypto/aes] Remove VLA in redundant call
body:
The high security AES performs a redundant inverse call (decrypt instead
of encrypt). However, to do that we needed an additional buffer to store
the redundant input buffer which is a VLA.
To remove the VLA, the AES call needs a different architecture.
Hence, during an encryption or decryption, we allow to calculate a CRC
of the blocks (this CRC is the same for encryption or decryption of the
same key and buffers). Then, we need to allow to call the inner AES
otcrypto_aes_impl call to work with a NULL output buffer.
This allows to then check the checksums instead of the additional
buffer.

This change removes ~250 bytes in size.

(cherry picked from commit 15f07bf39404be9390bbbb465426e8b15c1987bd)

body:

creates both the uncompressed and compressed binary relying on garbage
collection to filter out the unused binary.

Change the otbn.c and otbn.h in the cryptolib to use LZ4 from lib/base
in order to decompress the loaded imem and dmem from an application.

The cryptolib (lib/crypto) uses the compressed binaries, however, the applications from silicon_creator (using
silicon_creator/lib/drivers/otbn.c/h) still use the uncompressed version.

This option saves the cryptolib ~5400bytes while increasing ~400bytes to
load LZ4.c while providing backwards compatability for the boot.

Concerning the CRC: The CRC for the imem/dmem is calculated before
compression. For loading to OTBN, the OTBN is given the CRC of the
uncompressed payload before and checks itself the CRC of what it
receives. I.e., the CRC still provides end-2-end protection.

subject: [crypto] Fix usage of launder32()
body:
launder32() is an optimization barrier. In the cryptolib it is used
such that a redundant check after a guard (e.g. HARDENED_CHECK_EQ)
actually re-reads the live value. If the guard is a bare comparison,
the compiler already knows the value equals the constant, so the
redundant check just compares the constant against itself and always
passes.

This commit applies launder32() to the operand in the guard condition
and not in the check. This hides the value from the compiler, so the
redundant check has to reload it and compare the actual value and not
the immedate placed by the compiler.

subject: [opentitanlib] Generalize VMEM parsing for word sizes & address stride
body:
The existing VMEM implementation assumed that VMEMs would always contain
32 bit words, and that we always want to interpret the VMEM with byte
address strides. This is true for the existing use case of SRAM
programming, but will not be true if we want to load other VMEMs onto
the FPGA such as the scrambled ROM or OTP configurations, which have
39- and 22-bit word sizes respectively and both use word address strides
in their VMEM files.

Update the VMEM model and VMEM parsing logic so that we now store
Vec<Word> instead of Vec<u32>, where a Word is essentially just a
Vec<u8> of bytes stored in Big Endian order. Likewise, make VMEM parsing
and addressing logic consume an address stride argument, so that we know
how we should traverse VMEM addresses when e.g. merging sections or
enumerating the various data-address pairs.

Finally, this changes the existing VMEM consumer (load_sram_program) to
make use of these changes.
