subject: [opentitanlib] Implement optimized batched DMI write ops for OpenOCD
body:
This commit introduces a `batched_dmi_writes` method to the `DMI` trait,
which implementers can override to provide optimized implementations
that batch multiple sequential DMI writes, without caring about reading
out the returned values.

This will be a particular pain point for interaction with the
DMI in the FPGA bkdr_loader, and as such optimizing these writes can
potentially give us a 5x speedup by reducing the number of JTAG
transactions and the amount of idle time spent waiting for results
(i.e. for reducing the overhead of each write).

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [opentitantool] Add FPGA bkdr write & verify commands
body:
Add an `fpga backdoor write` command to OpenTitanTool / OpenTitanLib
which can be used to write to target memories via the backdoor loader
(when it is in its preloading mode, entered via `fpga backdoor enter`).

Options are available for customizing the offset and read and whether
readbacks & status checks are implemented for verifying the write (which
takes much longer, due to the various optimizations that are possible
when writing but not when reading).

3 different input formats are supported - hex (as args to the command),
clear (clear some number of words with a given repeated byte pattern),
and vmem (as a path to some VMEM file). This should be enough to support
a variety of use cases - writing VMEMs of the scrambled ROM and OTP
images, clearing some target's memory, and manually modifying specific
memory values via fine-grained commands.

An `fpga backdoor verify` command is added - this is basically the same
as `fpga backdoor write --verify`, but without doing the actual write
operation. The intention is that you can read and verify that the
contents of some memory matches your input, without needing to perform
any write operation beforehand, or deal with the manual comparison
logic yourself outside of OpenTitanTool after reading.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [opentitantool] Add a command for batched FPGA bkdr_loader writes
body:
Adds an `fpga backdoor batch` command to OpenTitanTool / OpenTitanLib
which can be used to batch multiple write operations to target memories
via the backdoor loader (when it is in its preloading mode, entered via
`fpga backdoor enter`).

This command exists despite the presence of `opentitantool --exec` to
reduce OpenOCD overhead from repeated writes. We may want to load many
images onto the FPGA (e.g. ROM, OTP, flash), and for each opentitantool
command a new instance of OpenOCD will be spawned and connected to the
backdoor TAP. Rather than incur this heavy overhead, we can spawn
OpenOCD once and batch together all of the writes.

Due to the added complexity of dealing with nested/chained sub-commands,
a limited subset of write options are supported here (only VMEM formats
for now). You can still choose to `--verify`, but this will apply to all
writes that are completed. There is also a `--start` option which will
perform `fpga backdoor exit` for you, since that command would also
require an additional OpenOCD instantiation which we would like to
eliminate.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [bkdr_loader,rtl] Register mux signal
body:
The muxing of the jtag was previously dependent on the state. This can
lead to glitches after implementation because the state is a multibit signal.

Vivado uses one-hot encodings for FSM states. Hence, the bkdr_loader mux
signal depends on three registers (despite being declared as a 2b signal).
The state transition from PRELOAD to SWITCHING happens right when we
write to the done signal and can lead to a glitch if the three state
bits don't change at the same time.
If it happens on the JTAG clock, it will upset the JTAG statemachine
and lead to transmission errors.

A simple fix is to register the mux signal.

Ideally the mux-signal would be synchronized to the jtag clock domain.
But this is tricky because we cannot rely on the JTAG clock being active.

The already implemented delayed switching should be sufficient if we can
guarantee that the jtag is inactive when the switch is performed.

Signed-off-by: Michael Gautschi <mgautschi@lowrisc.org>
Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [opentitanlib] Downgrade FPGA bkdr_loader `DONE` write error to warn
body:
This *should* be solved by the RTL fix to the backdoor loader that stops
the JTAG glitch due to the mux that is dependent upon multiple registers
- however this behaviour manifests depending on the state of the RTL and
the build seed. So to be safe and derisk this transition a bit, we
explicitly ignore errors on this write only, and loudly log a warning.

If there is instead some error in another way such that the write is
not completed, the subsequent FPGA test will fail and CI will fail much
more noisily. The intention is to monitor the results for a few
days/weeks across multiple bitstream builds, and revert this change when
we have confidence that this issue is completely fixed.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [opentitanlib] Explicitly shutdown OpenOCD before bkdr_loader transition
body:
There could potentially be some side effects if OpenOCD is still
"talking" to the downstream JTAG TAP at the moment we transition into
mission mode and the JTAG is muxed back to the rv_dm and lc_ctrl. To
eliminate problems here, explicitly drop self (and thus drop the JTAG
connection, and hence shut down OpenOCD), *before* we wait for the
transition to complete. We must still wait for the transition afterwards
to prevent accidental use of the FPGA whilst it is still transitioning,
which could cause unexpected errors.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [ci,bazel] Replace spliced bitstream dependency in SW target selection
body:
Previously, we pruned anything that has a dependency on the spliced
bitstream for the list of software targets to be built. This is because
the CI runner does not have support for bitstream splicing, but also
acts as a bit of a "catch-all" way of filtering out anything that needs
a bitstream, and generally any OpenTitan tests which support FPGA
environments - since those will be built in the relevant FPGA jobs
anyhow.

Since the spliced bitstream will be removed, we should be a bit more
explicit about what we're trying to exclude here. For tests, it makes a
lot more sense to use appropriate Bazel test tag filters and tags on the
test. This will let us catch anything that depends on Verilator, a CW340
bitstream, or QEMU specifically.

However, tests that are aliased (e.g. with `opentitan_alias_test`) will
not inherit all their parent tags, and will appear as valid build & test
targets (to prevent issues with duplicate test appearances when
querying). To stop us building these aliased tests, we filter out any
targets tagged with 'FPGA', and the set of targets which (transitively)
depend on such targets.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

body:

of an execution environment, with the ability to override the file that
is provided using `src`.

This is intended as a partial replacement for the bitstream splicing
flow, which is currently overloaded - it is being used for both
bitstream splicing (as the name suggests), and as a hook for build
options to be able to modify the OTP and ROM that is spliced in and
used for test execution.

Bitstreams will no longer be spliced when using the backdoor loader
flow, which means the OTP and the ROM can be directly overwritten.
However, we still want the option to have build options hook into and
overload the ROM or OTP (e.g. on a Bazel transition) - so replace them
with these two rules, which targets can use accordingly.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [manuf,bazel] Orchestrator changes for FPGA loading flow

the orchestrator source to package the ROM and OTP files separately into
the Orchestrator zip, and to extract and load them when running the CP
stage of FPGA provisioning flows.

The underlying `bitstream_splice` target will likewise no longer exist
after the Bazel transition to the fpga_bkdr loader are merged - as such,
we define new targets and build options to transition on, which are just
local to the orchestrator now. Also update the docs accordingly.

body:

In such cases, the test logic will not work, as the FPGA will also need

to pass these as arguments through to opentitantool commands so that we
can load these memories via the bkdr_loader on the FPGA.

We likewise now package a patched version of OpenOCD in the dev bundle,
since this will be needed to load the FPGA memories over JTAG. OpenOCD
will include the CMSIS-DAP adapter config by default, but we also
include it here for completeness to allow users to make local
modifications to the flow.

subject: [bazel,fpga] Replace bitstream splicing flow with bkdr_loader
body:
Instead of using a bitstream spliced with the ROM and OTP, we always use
the same base CW340 bitstream when running on FPGA. The scrambled ROM
and OTP images are then loaded over the FPGA-unique bkdr_loader IP.

To reduce the difference from the previous behaviour and avoid side
effects being built up in NVM (e.g. flash info pages) across test runs,
we zero other memories at the start of each test. This importantly
encompasses retention SRAM and the flash info pages, but we also clear
the flash data pages for good measure, to be as close to the previous
spliced bitstream flow as possible. The SRAM of a loaded bitstream would
be initialized to some scrambled value, and so we opt not to zero it
instead (it is also unlikely that any tests would be meaningfully
impacted by state carried across in SRAM).

Since the backdoor loader requires JTAG, JTAG is now made a dependency
of every test. All other consumers of the spliced bitstream target have
been converted, so we now simply remove this target and the logic for
splicing the bitstreams, as this will not be supported going forward.

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>

subject: [crypto] Move ptr_checksum integrity define to a generated header
body:
The ABI of cryptolib potentially changes depending on whether the
`OTCRYPTO_DISABLE_BUF_INTEGRITY_CHECKS` macro is defined or not.
When we're exporting cryptolib for external consumption, we need to be
careful to avoid the case where cryptolib is compiled with this feature
undefined (i.e. the integrity checks are enabled at runtime), but where
a user might try to use this define (to reduce code size / footprint),
leading to undefined behaviour.

So, rather than exposing this compile-time gate as a #define through
Bazel targets (based on some config setting), create a generated
`api_config.h` header file which contains the option that cryptolib was
compiled with. This way the option is not exposed to downstream users,
and we correctly capture the configuration that cryptolib was compiled
with (as you might, for example, want to build cryptolib with this
feature disabled, which is not the default option).

Signed-off-by: Alex Jones <alex.jones@lowrisc.org>
(cherry picked from commit 728ac11c55a760cd0d638cbdd1f10126b9c6a094)

  drop its 1em vertical margins. Previously #menu-bar grew to fit the
  logo's outer box (logo + 1em top/bottom), rendering taller than the
  CSS variable and causing content/sidetoc offsets computed from
  --menu-bar-height to sit above the visible bottom of the bar.
- Drop the html.sidebar-visible #menu-bar selector so the menu bar's
  sticky behaviour is governed only by mdbook's scroll-direction toggle

subject: [site] Take over menu-bar scroll handling on the docs site
body:
Replace mdbook's #menu-bar visibility logic (controllPosition in
book.js:633-678) with a capture-phase scroll listener in pagetoc.js
that toggles only the .sticky class. Solves two related issues:

1. Clicking a pagetoc entry or heading anchor caused the menu bar to
   pop in or out depending on the jump direction. The visual noise was
   the result of mdbook treating the instant scroll triggered by hash
   navigation the same as user-initiated scrolling.

2. After such a jump, the menu bar would sometimes render mid-viewport
   for a single scroll tick. mdbook's algorithm writes an inline
   `style.top` computed as `prevScrollTop + minMenuY` on the scroll-up
   branch. That formula is only stable when scroll deltas are small;
   the first real scroll event following a hash jump effectively has a
   huge delta (mdbook's prevScrollTop reflects the pre-click position),
   which deposits the menu bar at an intermediate document Y until the
   next tick snaps it back to the top.

The new handler:

  - Runs in capture phase on window and stopImmediatePropagation's,
    halting mdbook's document-level scroll handlers entirely.
  - Toggles #menu-bar.sticky based on scroll direction. Positioning
    is left to the existing CSS rule
    (#menu-bar.sticky { position: sticky; top: 0 }), so no inline
    `style.top` is ever written and no intermediate state is possible.
  - Clears menu.style.top on init and every scroll, neutralising any
    stale value mdbook's IIFE wrote before we took over.
  - Maintains a 500ms suppression window after same-page hash-link
    clicks during which the .sticky state is left alone, so jumping
    to a heading doesn't flicker the menu.
  - Invokes updateDynamicHighlight inline (the previously separate
    scroll listener for the pagetoc highlight is removed, since
    stopImmediatePropagation would otherwise block it).

Signed-off-by: Harry Callahan <hcallahan@lowrisc.org>

subject: [i3c] Implementations of HCI DAT and DCT
body:
The HCI specifies two data structures (DAT and DCT) to
pass device information between the driver software
and the Controller logic.

The Device Address Table (DAT) is used during regular
I3C traffic and provides the Controller hardware with
device properties and configuration.

The Device Characteristics Table collects properties
of the Targets involved in the Dynamic Address
Assignment (DAA) procedure and conveys them to the
driver software.

Since the two tables have much in common, a submodule
i3c_dxt implements them both.

subject: [kmac,dv] Rewrite kmac_app_agent to be more general
body:
This work adapts the agent to match the newly defined interface with
minimal changes. This should allow OTBN to interact with KMAC through
the interface in a more complicated way than existing users.

The agent that was in place isn't really able to handle the tweaked
protocol, so this commit rewrites it to allow extending things
smoothly.

Upsettingly, the commit is enormous! I couldn't figure out how to
split it up into smaller pieces. :-(

Important changes:

 - The agent gets split in two ("kmac_app_device_agent" and
   "kmac_app_host_agent"). These have different sequencers,
   corresponding to the fact that they fundamentally drive different
   sorts of items.

 - We no longer use push_pull_agent. It was already a slightly awkward
   fit (I think) and can't really support the new protocol.

 - kmac_app_device_driver now watches app requests and creates
   sequence items to represent these requests. They get
   broadcast through m_req_port. That port is connected to the
   sequencer's m_req_fifo, which can be consumed by the sequence that
   sends responses.

 - Sequence items are a bit more structured:

     + A request is sent in multiple beats, which each get a
       kmac_app_req_item where the last has m_last set.

     + The items representing the beats of a request are grouped into
       a "packet", represented by a kmac_app_req_packet_item. This
       contains a queue with the kmac_app_req_item objects for the
       beats.

     + A response is represented by a kmac_app_rsp_item.

     + The monitor sees complete transactions (a request followed by a
       response) and represents this as a kmac_app_mon_item, which
       contains a kmac_app_req_packet_item and a kmac_app_rsp_item.

 - The signals in kmac_app_if are now driven through clocking blocks
   in both directions, depending on an if_mode variable.

 - We don't use phase sequences any more. I think this is not really
   recommended and we can just start the "device responder" sequences
   from the test: probably a bit clearer. For example, see
   keymgr_base_test.sv (three lines of code).

Minor ("while we're at it") changes:

 - It also exposes the request and response as inout ports, which
   makes it a bit easier to use. See hw/ip/keymgr/dv/tb.sv for an
   example of the change.

 - Any new or dramatically-altered classes use out-of-block
   definitions and I've added meaningful documentation comments to
   functions, tasks and class variables.

 - The imports in kmac_app_agent_pkg are a bit more precise (mainly
   because I was concentrating to make sure I got the right thing
   from the right place).

 - The StrbAlignLSB_A assertions in kmac_app_intf were more
   complicated than needed. Group them into a single assertion. Also,
   express the assertions with default clocking/disable to make them
   easier to understand.

 - Rather than using field macros for the new classes, I've defined
   do_print/do_copy manually. This is probably a bit more efficient at
   runtime and (more importantly) lets us be explicit about things
   like radixes. For example, kmac_app_req_item always uses
   hexadecimal for its m_data field.

 - Since the strobe line is always required to be contiguous and
   aligned to the lsb, kmac_app_req_item represents it as just the
   number of valid bytes (m_num_bytes). This makes some of the code
   deailing with the item a bit simpler.

   For example, see kmac_app_host_seq: handling partial words when
   cfg.inject_zero_in_host_strb is now rather less mysterious.

 - When porting the function from kmac_app_item, I renamed
   get_is_kmac_rsp_data_invalid to just is_kmac_rsp_data_invalid.
   There's no need for the "double accessor name".

 - Since I was having to touch the code anyway, I've made the way
   scoreboards consume items from the agent a bit simpler. For
   example, keymgr_scoreboard now has two imp imports (for requests
   and transactions) and doesn't have to manually maintain fifos in
   the same way.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [rom_ctrl,dv] Add a mechanism for forcing the address counter
body:
This was surprisingly tricky to wire up, but works as follows:

  - There's a new boolean plusarg ("+skip_middle_of_rom"), which is
    treated as 0 if not supplied.

  - The rom_ctrl_fsm_if interface gains two new tasks (wait_for_addr
    and force_addr), which can be used to wait until the ROM counter
    gets to a particular count or to force it to be a particular
    value.

  - We define a driver for that interface, rom_ctrl_addr_force_driver,
    which consumes rom_ctrl_addr_force_item items that tell it to jump
    from one count to another.

  - That driver gets a sequencer and is created in the environment (if
    the plusarg was set)

  - There is also a tiny sequence (rom_ctrl_skip_middle_seq) which can
    be used to run a single item to jump from "near the start" to
    "near the end".

  - The rom_ctrl_base_vseq gets a handle to the sequencer (provided by
    rom_ctrl_base_test) and, if the plusarg is set, runs the sequence
    to skip over the middle of ROM.

If you just make those changes, all the block-level tests start to
fail! This is because the scoreboard checks (very sensibly) that
rom_ctrl sends the right data to KMAC, and we're now telling it to
skip some of it.

As such, we also have to change the scoreboard to allow this behaviour
and check that rom_ctrl did indeed send some of the start of ROM
before possibly skipping over a part in the middle, then finally
sending the end of ROM.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [otlib] Try to use susfs to enable/disable USB hub ports if possible
body:
Controlling USB hub power by directly sending control requests to the
hub can sometimes confuse the kernel because it does not necessarily
detect the device connection/disconnection anymore. For this reason,
a sysfs interface was added to kernel 6.0. This commit makes the USB
hub code try to use this interface if possible, and fall back to
direct hub operations otherwise. Note that this requires write access
to /sys which is a potential security risk.

subject: [sw] Increase stability of manufacturing tests by reflashing bitstreams
body:

most tests, this works flawlessly, however there is an increase in failure rate and flakyness
in the manufacturing tests. This commit *temporarily* introduces reflashing calls after certain
individual tests again. The test which used to carry the `changes_otp = True` flag now evoke
a reflash again after execution.

The failure distribution seems to be bitstream-depended and even varies between runs. It could be
a timing-related issue or residual state in non-reset flip-flops which cause a cascading of errors.

  my_var = 123;

subject: [prim,rtl] Use effective_rst_n in SyncReqAck(HoldReq/AckAckNeedsReq)
body:
This commit doesn't change the behaviour of either assertion, and
works by the following steps:

  - Since effective_rst_n is rst_src_ni && rst_dst_ni, its negation is
    !effective_rst_n = !rst_src_ni || !rst_dst_ni. As such, we can use
    it to make the assertion disables a bit simpler.

  - To make sure that SyncReqAckAckNeedsReq can see effective_rst_n,
    the assertion is moved inside the `ifdef INC_ASSERT (which will
    have no effect: the assertion is empty if INC_ASSERT is false).

  - I find the long chains of macro arguments rather confusing, so
    I've expanded things out. Among other things, this avoids breaking
    the property in what was previously a slightly odd place.

  - At this point, it becomes noticeable that SyncReqAckHoldReq has
    (req_chk_i && chk_flag) as part of its antecedant. Since the
    property runs in zero time, there's no need to have the negation
    of that expression in the disable iff line as well.

This change is motivated by a follow-up DV change that I intend to
make, where we disable these two assertions by forcing a signal.
Conveniently, the (assert-only) effective_rst_n signal isn't used by
anything else, so we'll be able to safely force its value to disable
the assertions if we need to.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [kmac,dv] Control some reqack assertions from a bound-in interface
body:
The existing code in kmac_common_vseq and kmac_lc_escalation_vseq
doesn't actually elaborate with Xcelium when masking is disabled
because it tries to access bits of the design that don't exist.

Details of this change:

  - Define a reqack_data_if interface that can be bound into an
    instance of u_prim_sync_reqack_data.

  - The interface uses upwards hierarchical references to force the
    value of an (already dv-only) effective_rst_n signal, disabling
    the SyncReqAckHoldReq and SyncReqAckAckNeedsReq assertions.

  - That interface *can't* be passed to the environment because its
    type would cause elaboration errors when masking is disabled (so
    there is no bound version).

  - Instead, we control the way that assertions are disabled with a
    single-bit pins_if. This type *can* safely be passed to the
    environment.

  - When something in the environment (a virtual sequence) wants to
    disable the assertions, it sets the pin of that interface to 1.
    The variable name should make it reasonably clear what's going on:

      if (cfg.disable_reqack_assertions_vif != null) begin
        cfg.disable_reqack_assertions_vif.drive(1);
      end

  - That causes the reqack_data_if.assertions_disabled signal to go
    high, which causes the force statement to set effective_rst_n to
    zero, which disables the assertions.

(Whew, this was complicated!)

As an extra tweak (since I'm touching the code), this also changes
kmac_lc_escalation_vseq to re-enable assertions when the sequence
finishes, in case we ever want to run it before another sequence.

subject: [topgen,dv] Generate better names in the chip RAL
body:
This is motivated by trying to get vertical reuse, where we use the
block-level environment for an IP in the chip level as well.

Unfortunately, some of the names in the chip ral don't actually match
the block-level RAL before this commit. For example, a block-level
test for rom_ctrl gets the following autogenerated code:

    package rom_ctrl_regs_ral_pkg;

... (snip) ...

      class rom_ctrl_regs_reg_alert_test extends dv_base_reg;

The chip-level version contained this instead:

    package rom_ctrl_rom_ctrl_regs_ral_pkg;

... (snip) ...

      class rom_ctrl_rom_ctrl_regs_reg_alert_test extends dv_base_reg;

This doesn't really work if the block-level environment wants to
reason about the register model.

The root for the change in name is in top_uvm_reg.sv.tpl. That wants
to represent registers and memories in the chip, which are the values
from the block-level environment *except* with extra customisation
that was provided by the hjson describing the chip layout.

The code in topgen.py noticed this and defined a new block description
for each instance with that sort of customisation. This is a good
idea: you might have two differently customised instances of a block
and they will want different uvm_reg_block descriptions.

For example, top_earlgrey currently has this situation with the
sram_ctrl, where we want to distinguish between
sram_ctrl_main_sram_ctrl_regs_ral_pkg and
sram_ctrl_ret_aon_sram_ctrl_regs_ral_pkg.

But *don't* need to make such distinctions if there is only one
customisation: we can just modify the generated type and leave its
name unchanged.

That's what the code in this commit does (complete with careful
comments explaining what's going on because I found it really hard to
understand!)

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [sram_ctrl,dv] Correct expected timing in sram_ctrl_throughput_vseq
body:
I changed the timing of tl_agent with commit 46f5ef0. Before that
commit, the driver busy-waited for items, which meant that it would
always see an item on the posedge of the clock. That change avoids the
busy-wait (which is probably a good idea), but the cost is that it has
to wait for the next clock edge when an item appears. Doing so makes
sure it starts sending the item just after the clock edge: much
clearer in the waves and avoids weird "zero-time items" if the item
appears at the driver early in a time slice that also includes a clock
edge.

The downside is that this might mean this transaction takes an extra
cycle, which broke this sequence. This commit fixes things by ensuring
we're in this situation and then adding an extra cycle to the expected
count.

subject: [cip,dv] Look up memories through root map in scoreboard
body:
This is worth doing if you are doing vertical integration. The problem
is that uvm_reg_map associated with a uvm_reg_block won't
have the memories mapped to offsets (because this only seems to get
applied to the root map). If the cip_base_scoreboard is pointing at a
dv_base_reg_block that corresponds to an IP, we need to go up to the
root map before search for a memory at a given address.

This commit updates code in process_mem_read, is_tl_mem_access_allowed
and is_data_intg_passthru_mem.

For the first two examples, we factor out a new get_mem_at_addr
function, which returns a dv_base_mem (or generates a uvm_error on
failure).

The new function avoids using csr_utils_pkg::get_mem_access_by_addr.
That function is really designed for sequences. Rather than changing
the that, let's do the (simple) look-up in the scoreboard itself. One
plus of doing this is that any failures now come from a component, so
they can print out a helpful hierarchical path into the testbench.

The is_data_intg_passthru_mem example is different because there might
not be a memory at the address (and we don't want an error in that
case). There, we just add the call of get_root_map manually.

subject: [ci,fpga] Ensure FPGA priming test for CI runs is not cached
body:
Without disabling caching on the FPGA priming test in CI, we can get the
following failure mode:

1. A PR runs with some bitstream A. This is based on some earlier
  common ancestor and is not up-to-date with the latest `master`.
2. A 2nd PR that makes only SW changes runs with some bitstream B. The
   test results for that bitstream were cached by Bazel on the run that
   merged the bitstream, so Bazel identifies it can just cache the
   priming test.
3. Some genuine SW change from that 2nd PR (e.g. changing a test) causes
   a cache miss, so Bazel re-executes the test. But it notices that the
   bitstream does not match and so loads the bitstream and then the ROM
   & OTP. If the test is already one that takes some time, this could
   push the test over its timeout and cause intermittent failures in CI
   runs.

make all that much sense.

  alert receiver gets asked to send a new ping then the receiver's
  ping_ok_o output will be false until (and including) the first time
  that the receiver is being asked to send a ping"

That's a rather convoluted way of saying:

  "If the alert sender is in the middle of replying to a ping and the
  alert receiver gets asked to send a new ping then the receiver's
  ping_ok_o output will be false".

Since requests to the alert receiver are under the control of the
environment in the formal testbench, *this* can be simplified to:

  "If the alert sender is in the middle of replying to a ping then the
  receiver's ping_ok_o output will be false".

That is true, and it means that the receiver won't ever manufacture
extra ping_ok_o signals. Doing so isn't really a concern: they would
cause the spurious_alert_ping signal in alert_handler_ping_timer to go
high, which is treated as a ping failure. But it's probably not a bad
idea to assert that this doesn't happen.

This commit replaces the complicated assertion that was there before
with something much simpler, less intrusive, and slightly stronger.

    register and debug memory interfaces.

subject: [rom_ctrl,dv] Use up-references instead of abs. paths in rom_ctrl_if
body:
This is necessary if you want to access signals inside the rom_ctrl
instance into which we are bound, but don't want to encode the
block-level testbench structure into the interface.

Getting this right is a little tricky:

  - The interface (rom_ctrl_if) that gets registered with the
    environment has no parameters and no hierarchical up-references.

    This avoids needing to pass any parameter into the environment
    type, and (a nice side effect) will also avoid elaboration errors
    if we don't happen to bind in that interface in a testbench.

  - The interface (rom_ctrl_bound_if) that actually communicates with
    the design does so through hierarchical references and consumes
    the SecDisableScrambling parameter from the design so that it
    knows whether the scrambling-dependent code actually exists.

  - It instantiates rom_ctrl_if inside it, and has a very simple
    "communication protocol" that allows the inner interface to
    request the outer one to do things (override a bus ROM index, the
    sel_bus_qq signal, or the kmac_done_i signal to the FSM).

  - To avoid elaboration errors if rom_ctrl_bound_if doesn't happen to
    have any bound instance, the hierarchical references are all
    hidden inside a gen_bound block that is dependent on a Bound
    parameter being 1 (not the default value).

subject: [dv] Fix the broken "memoization" for dv_base_reg_block::mem_ranges
body:
The existing approach only worked if the user remembered to call
compute_mem_addr_ranges() before looking at the memory ranges.

In the block-level environments, this worked because they called
set_base_addr() (which calls compute_mem_addr_ranges) just after
creating the register model in dv_base_env_cfg::make_ral_model.

At chip level, the environment creates a chip-wide register model,
which called compute_mem_addr_ranges for the chip-wide reg block, but
this didn't recurse to sub-blocks.

One option would be to fix the recursion, but that seems more
complicated than just doing the software engineering correctly.
Make the field local and have a memoized getter function. Now it's
impossible to use wrongly.

Since this touches adjacent code, this also improves the UVM_HIGH

read in the logs.

subject: [i3c] DWORD construction and splitting
body:
On the Target side, in order to reduce the amount of
logic operating on the I3C clock signal (SCL),
received data is transferred as bytes (SDR) or 16-bit
words (HDR-DDR) to the core logic, where it must be
assembled into 32-bit DWORDs before writing into
the message buffer.

Similarly, on the transmission path, DWORDs from the
message buffer must be decomposed into SDR bytes or
HDR-DDR words of 16 bits.

These sizes, 32 bits for DWORDs and 8/16 bits for
units, are fixed by the HCI and I3C specifications,
respectively.

The conversion is performed by these two simple
modules, which are used only on the Target side
because the Controller logic is more readily able
to work with larger units directly.

subject: [sram_ctrl] Support non-power-of-2 memory sizes
body:
This commit extends the RTL and the DV of SRAM_CTRL to support
non-power-of-2 memory sizes. The RTL changes are minimal, most of the
changes have already been done as part of prim_ram_1p_scr, see commit
071e0be342fa7417c004afb8718d1b72c79299de.

Most of the DV changes are related to:
1. Specifying the memory size as number of bytes rather than by
   defining the number of address bits,
2. correcting the prediction for accesses to unimplemented addresses in
   in the range [MemDepth * 4 : 2 ** AddrWidth - 1),
3. not triggering accesses to unimplemented addresses for throughput
   tests as they have a different timing which is harder to predict,
4. extending the minimal a_valid length before retracting a request for
   the access_during_key_req sequence to avoid signaling delayed
   out-of-range-access errors.

subject: [rom_ctrl,dv] Allow aborting a sequence forcing the address counter
body:
This is motivated by the chip-level use case. The problem is that you
want to run some virtual sequence "in the background" that will force
values in the ROM address to skip over the middle of ROM when
computing the digest. But what should you do when the main virtual
sequence (chip_vseq) completes? It's not a good idea to leave
rom_ctrl_skip_middle_seq running because it will cause all sorts of
confusion if we run another top-level virtual sequence.

As such, it's nice to be able to ask the sequence to abort what it's
doing. This commit does so in the following steps:

  - rom_ctrl_skip_middle_seq::abort() works by calling m_item.abort():
    the abort method on the item that it is driving.

  - The item also provides get_aborted and wait_until_aborted methods
    to allow a sequence / driver to see what's going on.

  - The driver uses rom_ctrl_addr_force_item::wait_until_aborted to
    drop out early if abort() is called when the driver is waiting for
    the hardware to read a particular address.

  - To make sure that abortion is instant, there's also a slightly
    complicated dance needed so that the driver will respond
    immediately, but won't kill a process that's driving things (or
    leave it lying around).

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [rom_ctrl,dv] Fix rom_ctrl_corrupt_sig_fatal_chk
body:
Recent changes had broken this test for two different reasons.

 1. Skipping the middle of ROM doesn't really work for this sequence
    because it's unlikely we'll get the chance to inject a fault
    before the end of ROM has been read.

    Fixing this is simple: set the +skip_middle_of_rom plusarg to zero
    for this test.

 2. Commit 4552fb1 added a nice mechanism for forcing the address
    counter. Because we needed to make sure everything saw the address
    in the right way, this forces addr_d and then waits until the "go"
    signal is asserted (which will copy the address to addr_q).

    That commit also changed rom_ctrl_corrupt_sig_fatal_chk_vseq to
    use the mechanism. But that doesn't work! The problem is that we
    want to change the address after ROM has been completely read (so
    go will never be asserted again). Forcing addr_d doesn't do
    anything.

    This commit teaches the machinery in rom_ctrl_fsm_bound_if to cope
    with both situations.

subject: [dv] Look up more registers through root map in scoreboard
body:
The is_tl_access_mapped_addr function is designed to tell the
scoreboard whether an address is actually mapped to something in the
block.

This works by asking a uvm_reg_map to look up the address. *This* only
works with the root map, because UVM doesn't pass the addresses to
child maps when setting everything up.

It matters for a chip-level simulation with a block-level scoreboard
sitting inside it. In this case, "block" might be the block's
uvm_reg_block, and block.get_default_map() will return that block's
local map, rather than the chip-level one.

One example of this going wrong the is is_tl_access_mapped_addr
function. Without using the root map, the scoreboard will conclude
that the address is unmapped, and will expect a TileLink error in the
response.

subject: [dv] Wait for the slower clock in scoreboard's check_alert_triggered
body:
The cip_base_scoreboard::check_alert_triggered task worked by counting
cycles an cfg.clk_rst_vif. This is ok... as long as the alert
interface is running that fast.

In the chip-level testbench (hw/top_earlgrey/dv/tb/tb.sv), there are
multiple alert_esc_if instances, but these all run with the clock
signal from the alert handler. This is reasonable: it's at one end of
each link. The alert handler runs on the io_div4 clock. As such, some
of the ten cycles in an alert handshake are counted on that clock.

This was a problem when setting up vertical reuse. The specific block
was rom_ctrl, which is on a faster clock. The logic in one check in
the scoreboard is "if you think there should be an alert, wait ten
cycles and fail if one hasn't come out in that time". The existing
code was counting cycles of rom_ctrl's clk_i signal, which is running
much faster than the other end of the interface.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [crypto] Prepare for version increment
body:
Cryptolib uses kOtcryptoLibVersion1 as version of the library and in key
configs.
This commit adds a kOtcryptoLibVersion2 magic number.

We create a new API call otcrypto_lib_version() which returns the
version of the library. We then switch all tests and internal cryptolib
functions to use this call to automatically reference the current
version.

Integrity was also rejecting keys which did not set the current version
number, however, the library has to be backward compatible, so we
removed the check. Later on, we can decide what to do on certain version
numbers.

The documentation was also updated in this regard.

Signed-off-by: Siemen Dhooghe <sdhooghe@google.com>
(cherry picked from commit 5a71eb844c52c1f8205668d05aeb6f733135974a)

subject: [crypto] Add key migration options
body:
As we would move to higher version numbers for the library, we allow for
migration options to increment older key version numbers. As such, we
add to the documentation, add the api function (which is just a simple
function from now checking it is the current version), and the integrity
check checks whether we are on the current version and would reject if
it is not the case.

For clarity, only blinded keys have a version, unblinded keys do not.
The version is mainly there for masking.

Due to hardware keys using their version numbers as part of the
diversifier, we can not migrate those.

subject: [rom_ctrl,dv] Teach chip test to understand +skip_middle_of_rom
body:
This works by running a copy of rom_ctrl_skip_middle_with_digest_vseq
to force the address and also the digest responses in rom_ctrl,
causing it to skip over reading the ROM at the start of the test.

The only other tricky thing that needs doing is to disable some of the
checks in the bound-in rom_ctrl_scoreboard. The problem is that we
force the signals when they arrive at the FSM. This is much easier,
because it's rather messy to get a hierarchical up-reference to a port
of rom_ctrl itself. To do so would mean that rom_ctrl_bound_if would
need all the parameters of rom_ctrl itself and then would have to
refer to it with all of them.

If we just force a signal on a port of the FSM, that works perfectly
well... except that rom_ctrl_scoreboard can't see that we forced it! I
think the right thing to do in this situation is just to disable the
checks that are based on knowing what the KMAC response contained.

subject: [host/tools] Support multi-board workstations
body:
Allows developers to target specific hardware setups
on multi-board workstations by propagating `--usb-serial`
to all phases of Bazel FPGA test scripts.

Previously, running tests on a workstation with multiple
connected debuggers (e.g., HyperDebug) failed because
Bazel FPGA test rules run in a multi-phase script
(Setup, Test, Cleanup), but the global arguments
(like `--usb-serial`) were only forwarded to the middle
Test phase. This caused the Setup and Cleanup phases to
crash due to device ambiguity because `opentitantool` did
not know which debugger to connect to.

This change fixes this issue by updating the Bazel FPGA
test rule wrapper script to capture global arguments and
forward them to all execution phases (Setup, Test, and Cleanup).
Native JTAG serial propagation already handled by the
underlying HyperDebug transport driver will now receive
the serial number correctly in all phases.

Developers can now run FPGA tests targeting a specific
board using:
`bazel test --test_arg=--usb-serial=<serial> //target`

Signed-off-by: Bastien Gillon <bgillon@google.com>

subject: [dv] Check CSR-fetch permission per reg block
body:
Prior to this commit, `dv_base_reg_block::allows_csr_fetch` was only
read from the top-level RAL model.  `tl_instr_type_err` consulted
`get_allows_csr_fetch()` on that model alone, but chose the register to
fetch from with `get_registers(..., UVM_HIER)`.  A hierarchical model
could therefore not exempt an individual sub-block: the flag either
applied to the whole model or was ignored.

This commit adds `dv_base_reg_block::get_nofetch_csrs()`, which walks
the hierarchy and drops every register whose containing block, or one
of that block's ancestors, has `allows_csr_fetch` set.  It also adds
`has_nofetch_csrs()` for the common question of whether that list is
non-empty.  `tl_instr_type_err` now picks from the filtered list, so
`pick_rand_csr_addr()` becomes `pick_rand_nofetch_csr_addr()`.

Behaviour is unchanged for the existing user of the flag: a model that
carries it is an ancestor of all of its own registers, so it filters
out every one of them just as before.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [dv,chip] Mark rv_dm debug mem CSRs as fetchable
body:
Prior to this commit, `chip_tl_errors` and
`chip_csr_mem_rw_with_rand_reset` failed on nearly every seed with a
`d_error` mismatch on `chip_reg_block`, reported as `Fetch from CSR`
(see #31085).  `tl_instr_type_err` picked a register in the `rv_dm_mem`
sub-block and fetched from it, and the scoreboard predicted an error
response.  The design is right to answer without an error: rv_dm drives
its whole debug memory window through one `tlul_adapter_reg` whose
`en_ifetch_i` follows the life-cycle debug-enable, because the debug
ROM in that same window has to be executable, and `dm_top` does not
distinguish a read from a fetch.  `rv_dm_env_cfg` already accounts for
this at block level, but no chip-level environment did.

This commit sets `allows_csr_fetch` on the chip RAL's `rv_dm_mem`
sub-block for both tops, so the sequence no longer fetches from those
registers.

Resolves: #31085

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [dv] Speed up csr_aliasing_seq
body:
Historically, the sequence ran the following pseudocode:

  for (dest in registers) {
    dest <- random_value;
    for (src in registers) {
      read_and_check(src);
    }
  }

This iterates over all registers, writing a value and then reads every
register to check that it has changed in the way we expect. That loop
is obviously quadratic in the number of registers, which is a problem
if you have lots of registers(!)

To try to work around that problem, the initial version of OpenTitan
repository had two tweaks:

  - Instead of writing to each register (in the outer loop), we pick
    some segment of registers to write. This is actually done in
    csr_base_seq::set_csr_test_range and the size of the segment can
    be controlled by plusargs.

    Interestingly, this isn't actually used in the repository: it is
    controlled (in csr_base_seq) by plusargs +num_csr_chunks and
    +test_csr_chunk. They have been possible to supply since the start
    of the repository history, but are never actually used.

  - If there are lots of registers then, instead of reading each
    register (the inner loop), we actually pick up to 100 registers at
    random and read them instead.

After this commit, the code works by writing "chunks" with multiple
registers each time.

To compare the expected run time, consider a testbench with lots of
registers (a chip simulation for example). In this situation, the
all_csrs queue is trimmed down to 100 registers.

Before this change, a run with N registers in test_csrs would have
100*N register operations (for each register, write it and then read
100 randomly selected registers).

After this change, the run works in N/10 chunks: write each register
in the chunk and then read 100 registers. This takes (N/10) * 100 =
10*N operations.

If N is large, which will be the case for chip-level simulations, this
will be about a factor of 10 quicker.

Note that CSR exclusions make this a bit more fiddly to implement. To
make sure that the chunks are evenly sized, the implementation starts
by sampling the registers that are allowed to be
written (regs_to_write) and the registers that are allowed to be
read (regs_to_read). It then splits regs_to_write into chunks of size
10 and picks random samples of 100 registers from regs_to_read.

subject: [prim] Add a virtual core for prim libraries
body:
Prior to this commit, a core that needed a technology library had to
name a specific technology library, e.g. `lowrisc:prim_generic:all`.  A
core that is generic over the technology had no way to state the
dependency, so omitting it left nothing to say the requirement existed.

This commit adds the virtual core `lowrisc:virtual_prim_tech:all`, which
every technology library implements and maps to itself.  A core depends
on it to say that it needs some technology library without naming one,
and selecting a library with `--mapping` then resolves both that
dependency and the individual primitives.

subject: [hw,prim] Drop fileset_partner for mappings
body:
Prior to this commit, the parts of a chip that a partner replaces -- the
technology library, the AST, the pad orientation and scan role packages,
the physical pads and the JTAG ID -- were swapped with the
`fileset_partner` flag.  That is a second selection mechanism, predating
FuseSoC's virtual cores, and it is all-or-nothing: replacing any one of
those cores required supplying all of them.

This commit expresses each of them as a virtual core instead, for both
Earl Grey and Darjeeling.  The open-source cores declare the virtual
VLNV they implement, `chip_earlgrey_asic.core` and
`chip_darjeeling_asic.core` depend on the virtual cores and carry the
`mapping:` block selecting the open-source implementations, and the
chip-level flows apply that mapping.  The mapping lives in the chip core
because which analog top, pads, scan roles and JTAG ID a design is built
with is a chip-level choice.

The virtual VLNVs are named per top, e.g.
`lowrisc:virtual_systems:top_earlgrey_ast`, so that each has exactly one
implementation and a build cannot silently resolve to the other top's.

The flow configs and `hw/ip/prim/README.md` change in the same commit:
once a chip stops depending on a technology library a flow without a
mapping resolves the primitives non-deterministically, and the guide
documented a flag that no longer exists.

subject: [ci] check-vendoring: fail on untracked re-vendored output
body:
check-vendoring.sh re-vendors each dependency and diffs the result against the
tree, but only looked at tracked files. A re-vendor that produces a file which
is not committed therefore passed silently, so the tree could drift from what
the vendoring tool actually generates.

Two such drifts exist today and have to be fixed in the same commit, or the
stricter check lands red:

- Remove the wycheproof and lowrisc_misc-linters vendor configs. Both vendored
  copies went away once each moved to a Bazel dependency: wycheproof test
  vectors to the @wycheproof http_archive (used by cryptotest via
  @wycheproof//testvectors[_v1]), vendored dir removed in dcdae64901; and
  lowrisc_misc-linters to the lowrisc_misc_linters Bazel module, switched over
  in 60b76ae0c3. Their *.vendor.hjson / *.lock.hjson were left behind, so
  util/vendor.py re-materialises the removed directories as untracked trees on
  every sweep. Nothing references the vendored paths anymore.

- Restore sw/vendor/eembc_coremark/docs/html/index/General2.html, deleted as
  collateral damage by 641d7e74f1 ("[doc] Add some documentation on SW top
  creation"). Re-vendoring coremark regenerates it, byte for byte, from the
  revision the lock file pins.

Both are precisely the class of silent drift the check now catches.

Restoring that file also means fixing what deleted it in the first place, or
the two checks fight: check-links.sh has been running

    rm -f sw/vendor/eembc_coremark/docs/html/index/General2.html

on the working tree since it was added in d98e7ad1c5, because the file is not
valid UTF-8 (upstream generated it that way) and lychee errors out on any input
it cannot decode. That is how the file came to be missing for a year: a local
run of the link check deleted it and 641d7e74f1 swept the deletion up. Neither
CI job ever noticed, each getting its own checkout, but a local `nix run .#lint`
ends every run with a dirty tree.

The rm is redundant: `--exclude-path sw/vendor`, passed since that same commit,
already keeps the file out of lychee's input set. Dropping it leaves the check
read-only, as a check should be. Verified by running check-links.sh with the
file present: 13618 links, 0 errors, tree clean afterwards.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: [ci] Categorized lint runner shared by CI and local runs
body:
Replace the duplicated quick-lint/slow-lint scripts and inline CI steps
with a single categorized runner, ci/lint/run.sh, that is the source of
truth for both CI (one category per job) and local runs.

- Add ci/lint/{run.sh,lib.sh}: hygiene/format/gen/hw/bazel categories.
- Run the flow inside an FHS sandbox (flake.nix buildFHSEnv, as the eda
  shell does), exposed as the `nix run .#lint` app so /bin/bash exists for
  the many scripts, dvsim makefiles and generators that hardcode it. As an
  app (not just a devShell) it runs non-interactively: the FHS runScript
  takes the category as arguments. CI invokes `nix run .#lint -- <cat>` so
  CI and local runs are identical. Add the prepare-nix composite action.
- Reduce ci/jobs/{quick,slow}-lint.sh to compatibility shims.
- Give util/get_workspace_status.sh a portable `#!/usr/bin/env bash`
  shebang: Bazel runs it as --workspace_status_command in its own
  server/sandbox, outside the FHS, so it cannot rely on the sandbox's
  /bin/bash.
- Only run check-generated destructively in CI: it does
  `git clean -fxd && git reset --hard` under OT_DESTRUCTIVE=1, which would
  wipe a local working tree; gate it on GITHUB_ACTIONS (matching its own
  warning) and skip locally.
- Scope the ruff check to changed files, and point it at a rule set of its own
  in ci/lint/ruff-ci.toml rather than the one in pyproject.toml. That one is
  aimed at editors: `preview = true` shows contributors the whole backlog of
  suggestions so the tree can be cleaned up over time. It cannot gate, and not
  only because of the several thousand outstanding findings -- since ruff 0.15,
  `preview = true` replaces the default selection with the preview default (59
  -> 407 rules) and `extend-select` adds to that, so the enforced set grows on
  its own with each ruff release and an unrelated dependency bump would fail
  the lint on untouched code. This is live: the devshell resolves ruff 0.15.20
  from uv.lock while python-requirements.txt, which CI installed from before,
  still pins 0.14.12; the same config means 63 rules under the one and 425
  under the other. The CI config lists rules explicitly, starting at what
  master enforced (pycodestyle errors, pyflakes and the two preview rules
  pyproject.toml names) plus five families the tree is already clean against,
  and carries the backlog with per-family counts so it can be ratcheted up as
  those are fixed. Keep the Bazel-backed licence and lock-file checks in the
  bazel category.
- exec-check.sh: skip git-ignored paths so a local .venv etc. does not
  produce false positives.
- Run every category in the merge queue, where master's workflow ran only the
  quick-lint half. The queue is where the merged result gets checked, and most
  of these categories check properties of that merged tree rather than of a
  diff: generated files matching their sources, vendored directories matching
  what util/vendor.py produces, or the hardware linting cleanly. Two PRs can
  each pass on their own and still break one of those once queued together --
  one editing an hjson while the other edits a file generated from it, say.
  Lint is cheap relative to the build and test jobs the queue still skips.
  The diff-scoped checks inside the categories still behave sensibly there:
  the queue branch contains master, so the merge base is the master tip and
  they see the queued changes. The pull-request-only checks (commit metadata,
  licence headers, whitespace, header guards) stay off, as OT_RUN_PR_CHECKS is
  set for pull_request events only.
- Skip Verible for englishbreakfast. Driving `hw` over every top in
  ALL_TOPS newly included it, but master's workflow only ever linted
  earlgrey and darjeeling. Having never been exercised by CI, the
  englishbreakfast lint cfgs have bit-rotted and no longer resolve:
  top_englishbreakfast_lint_cfgs.hjson names cores that do not exist,
  e.g. lowrisc:englishbreakfast_ip:otp_ctrl (englishbreakfast has no
  ip_autogen/otp_ctrl), so fusesoc fails before any linting happens.
  Repairing those cfgs is a hardware-side change of its own, so keep
  exactly the coverage CI has today. The countermeasure check still runs
  for englishbreakfast, matching master, and the matrix leg stays in place
  so the top is easy to re-enable once its cfgs are fixed.

subject: [ci] Replace third-party Verible job with an advisory sweep
body:
The standalone `verible_lint` job used chipsalliance/verible-linter-action,
which downloaded its own Verible (v0.0-3430) rather than taking the pinned
v0.0-4080 from the devshell, applied every *.vbl waiver globally instead of
per-core, and could not be reproduced locally. It also never gated anything:
the action's fail_on_error input defaults to 'false' and the job did not set
it, so reviewdog reported findings without ever failing the build.

Its gating value was already a subset of `lint_hw`, which runs the same rules
file through dvsim with correctly scoped waivers. What it uniquely covered was
the ~2500 .sv/.v files no lint cfg reaches: vendored RTL, DV/FPV sources,
pre_dv/pre_sca testbenches, unintegrated IPs and alternative prim technology
variants.

Replace it with a `sv` lint category that sweeps the whole tree from the
devshell, so the coverage survives and `nix run .#lint -- sv` reproduces it.

per-core for files no core lists, and a few dozen files (UVM class files meant
to be `include`d, ibex formal fragments needing harness macros) cannot parse
standalone, so Verible reports parse errors that are artefacts of linting them
individually. Waivers are enumerated with `git ls-files` rather than `find`,
which also stops copies left in scratch/*/fusesoc-work/ by a local dvsim run
from being concatenated twice.

subject: [ci] Make the lint jobs' use of Nix fast and quiet
body:
Two problems with `nix run .#lint`, both from every lint job realising the
devShell closure itself as its first act.

It buried the tool output. Hundreds of "copying path" lines, plus any build
logs when something misses the binary cache, were interleaved with the lint
output in the same step.

And it was slow. On run 30355084066 the SV sweep step took 6.3 min for 21s of
linting, and the format step 6.4 min for a few seconds of it. The closure is
~7 GiB over ~690 paths, and nothing builds from source -- 35 of 40 sampled
paths are on cache.nixos.org and the rest on the lowRISC cache -- so this is
pure download, paid six times per run at roughly 20 MB/s.

Realise the closure once in prepare-nix, restoring it from the Actions cache
first, and run the categories with --quiet so they print tool output only. Nix
cannot prebuild the environment the usual way: the FHS devShell derivation is
not meant to be built directly and flake apps are not installables, so add a
`--warmup` argument to run.sh that enters the sandbox and exits. All six
categories share one closure, so warming it costs no extra work.

The cache is keyed on flake.lock and flake.nix, which is what determines the
closure; on a miss the key prefix still restores the previous store, leaving
Nix to fetch only the delta. Writes are confined to master, and to a single
dedicated workflow:

- GitHub scopes an entry to the ref that created it, and only default-branch
  entries are readable from every branch, PR and fork. An entry written by a PR
  would be invisible to every other PR and would just consume the quota.
- All six lint jobs build the same closure, so letting each save would upload
  the same multi-gigabyte entry six times per push for one usable result.
- Making it a workflow of its own rather than a side effect of one lint job
  means population is explicit -- on flake changes, weekly, or on demand --
  instead of depending on which master push happened to run the lint jobs.

The repo uses no other actions/cache, so the 10 GB quota is free.

Also raise http-connections and max-substitution-jobs, since the fetch is
IO-bound rather than limited by the defaults' 25 connections, and pass
--no-warn-dirty, which drops the "Git tree is dirty" warning from local runs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: James McCorrie <james.mccorrie@lowrisc.org>

subject: [ci] Find empty test suites with one query instead of one per suite
body:
`tests(<suite>)` answers whether a suite is empty, but asking it per suite
meant one Bazel invocation per test_suite target: 1631 of them, 4m10 of the
12m29 the bazel lint job took on run 30358025990, and 5m11 locally. The
queries themselves are trivial -- the server has the graph loaded -- so
almost all of that is client startup and round trips.

Read the declared contents of every suite in one query instead, and resolve
emptiness here: a suite holds a test if any of its members is a test target,
or is a suite that itself holds one. Members come from the `tests` attribute,
or from `$implicit_tests` when `tests` is omitted, which is how Bazel models
a suite selecting its own package. A member label that resolves to neither a
test nor a suite counts for nothing, which is how nonexistent members and
non-test rules drop out.

That settles all but a handful of suites, and each remaining candidate is
still confirmed with the `tests(<suite>)` query it would have run anyway, so
nothing reported rests on this resolution being faithful to Bazel. Two
queries plus one per candidate, of which the tree currently has three.

Verified against the previous implementation over the whole tree: the same 36
findings, in the same order, in 2.2s rather than 5m11.

The obvious formulation is a single `rdeps` query,

    kind("^test_suite rule$", //...) except rdeps(//..., tests(//...))

but it cannot be used: reverse-dependency queries preload the transitive
closure, and the closure contains a dangling reference,

    no such package 'hw/ip/otp_ctrl/data/earlgrey_skus/sival/keys'

so the query fails without --keep_going and returns partial results with it.
This is also why the per-suite form worked at all: `tests()` expands suite
membership without walking the dependency graph.

One case is resolved by query rather than statically. A suite's `tags`
filter its contents, and how many members survive that filter is not visible
from the graph, so a suite carrying such a tag is always treated as a
candidate. `manual` is exempt: it keeps a suite out of wildcard patterns but
drops no tests, which the whole-tree comparison above confirms across the
1629 suites that carry it. Only two suites in the tree carry any other tag,
so this costs two queries at most.

Signed-off-by: James McCorrie <james.mccorrie@lowrisc.org>

subject: [ci] Split the bazel lint category so its slow checks run in parallel
body:
The bazel lint job took 12m29 on run 30358025990 while every other lint job
finished in 2 to 4 minutes, making it the critical path for the whole lint
stage and so for everything gated on it. Its checks ran back to back in one
job, and two of them accounted for most of the time: the test-suite query
sweep at 4m10, and alert classification at 4m33, of which the first top pays
4m12 to build //sw/host/opentitantool and the second then reuses it. The
remaining checks came to under a minute between them.

The query sweep is no longer slow, so what is left is one expensive build
sitting behind a minute of cheap queries. Give the category a group argument
and run the two groups as separate matrix legs: `graph` for the query-only
checks, `alerts` for the two alert-classification checks. The category now
costs its slowest leg rather than the sum, and the `alerts` leg -- almost
entirely that one build -- is what remains to be improved.

Both alert-classification checks stay in the same group deliberately: split
apart, each leg would pay for its own opentitantool build.

`nix run .#lint -- bazel` with no group still runs everything in sequence, so
local runs are unaffected. The groups are for CI to fan out over, in the same
way the `hw` category already takes a top name. quick_lint aggregates the
matrix under the existing lint_bazel job id, so neither the downstream
`needs:` lists nor the branch ruleset need touching.

subject: [ci] Show Bazel's output in the alert-classification check

the log says nothing about why: the subprocess captured both streams and
printed them only on failure, so Bazel's progress -- and the cache statistics

parses, and let stderr through.

subject: [topgen] Keep --check-cm out of the source tree
body:
--check-cm is a check, but it was handled at the very end of main(), after
topgen had already written the whole top into the tree: generate_top_only(),
generate_full_ipgens() -- which renders each ipgen block with
overwrite_output_dir=True, so hw/top_*/ip_autogen/<ip>/ is wiped and
re-rendered -- generate_xbars() and generate_rust() all run first.

ci/scripts/check-countermeasures.sh therefore rewrote several hundred files on
every run, for earlgrey and englishbreakfast, which `nix run .#lint` now does
locally. Most of them come out byte-identical, but the documentation does not,
because the checked-in files are the output of the *full* `make top_and_cmdgen`
flow and --check-cm exits half way through it:

- The templates emit CMDGEN blocks empty and a later `cmdgen -u` pass fills
  them in, so every block under ip_autogen/*/{README,doc/*}.md was emptied.

- pinmux's doc/pinout_*.md and doc/targets.md are written later still, by
  util/topgen/gen_top_docs.py, so overwrite_output_dir deleted them outright.

Move the check up to just after intermodule elaboration and render only what it
reads -- the ipgen blocks' Hjson and RTL -- into the temporary directory that
name_to_hjson already points at, the way --top-ral does. Nothing else topgen
generates is needed: the generic and top-only blocks it inspects are read from
the source tree either way. The source tree is left untouched, and freshness of
the generated files stays covered by check-generated.sh, which regenerates
everything and is destructive by design.

_get_otp_ctrl_params() now takes cfg_path rather than out_path, as

subject: [i3c] HCI/Controller-side IBI handling
body:
The `IBI_PORT` of the HCI presents an interleaved stream of
IBI Status Descriptors and IBI payload DWORDs.

Since the IBI Status Descriptor cannot be constructed until
the DWORDs have been received and written into a logical FIFO,
the status descriptors must be conveyed via a separate FIFO
and combined at the HCI/Driver side (see `i3c_hci_ibi`).

Additionally, to prevent a deadlock at the HCI/Driver side,
and to accommodate the limited width of the `DATA_LENGTH`
field in the status descriptor, the IBI payload data must be
split into 'segments' of no more than a programmed length.
This is handled by the `i3c_controller_ibi` module.

Remove the clock-gating enable signal from `i3c_hci_ibi` just
to keep all logic state consistent in the event that software
violates the prohibition on reading from IBI_PORT when the
PIO queues are not enabled.

Lastly, this PR corrects the IBI_CONFIG.SIZE_VAL to match the
latest default configuration and clamps the level/count values
reported for the IBI FIFOs/queues.

Correct the reset values of `ALT_QUEUE_SIZE` fields.

subject: [i3c] Controller-side timing and support modules
body:
Assorted support modules for the Controller functionality,
upon which the remaining Controller top-level, FSM and
transceiver logic depend:

i3c_cmd_decode

 - Command decoding decides whether to accept or reject
   a Command Descriptor that has been supplied by the
   software driver via the HCI Command Queue, and then
   extracts appropriate information for use by the FSM.

i3c_timing_pkg

 - Default timimg parameters are calculated from the
   configured ClkFreq parameter (i3c_timing_pkg).
   These parameters may be overridden by software if
   required.

i3c_dat_cache

 - DAT cache retains information about the devices in
   the Device Address Table (DAT) w.r.t. how we should
   respond to In-Band Interrupts and Controller Role
   Requests received from those devices.

i3c_ctrl_req_gen

 - Request generation logic that builds a transceiver
   request based on the current state of the Controller
   FSM.

i3c_stby_ctrl_regs

 - Just implements some Standby Controller registers
   that exhibit special behavior such as conditional
   write accesss; this module is unimportant right now
   since Standby Controller functionality has been

directory. The network namespace stops downloads, but not reads of

subject: [dv,mem_bkdr_util] Support file ops on tiled memories
body:
Prior to this commit, `mem_bkdr_util` could read and write a memory
image file only through the `MEM_BKDR_UTIL_FILE_OP` macro, which the
testbench expands into `$readmemh`/`$writememh` on one hierarchical
path.  Those system tasks take a single unpacked array, so they cannot
serve a memory that is composed of several tiles, even though the
per-word `read()` and `write()` of this class already are tile-aware.

This commit adds `load_mem_from_file_tiled()` and
`write_mem_to_file_tiled()`, which go through `read()`/`write()` word by
word.  `load_mem_from_file()` and `write_mem_to_file()` dispatch to them
when the memory has more than one tile, so a tiled memory no longer
triggers the `readmemh_event`/`writememh_event` that drive the macro.

The load leaves the parsing of the file to `$readmemh`, which fills a
temporary array of the depth of the memory; only the deposit is done
word by word.  The store formats the file itself, because `$writememh`
would write the full width of `row_data_t` rather than the width of the
memory.

This commit also makes `is_tiled()` public, so that a testbench can skip
`MEM_BKDR_UTIL_FILE_OP` for a tiled memory.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [dv,rom_ctrl] Make the ROM memory array path overridable
body:
Prior to this commit, the hierarchical path to the ROM memory array was
hard-coded as `<prim_rom>.mem` in the block-level and chip-level
testbenches, and `rom_ctrl_bkdr_util` did not forward the tiling
arguments of `mem_bkdr_util`.  A technology-specific `prim_rom` that
composes the ROM from several memory macros therefore had no way to make
the ROM backdoor work: there is no single array spanning the ROM, and no
core it could map in to say so.  This is the problem that
`lowrisc:virtual_dv:rram_ctrl_bkdr_util` solves for the RRAM macro.

This commit adds `rom_ctrl_bkdr_util_hier.svh`, an include file that
describes the ROM array layout relative to the `prim_rom` instance: the
path to the array of one tile, the number of tiles, the `path` argument
of `mem_bkdr_util::new`, and its `tiling_path` and
`tiling_suffix_fmt_str` arguments.  It lives in its own core,
`lowrisc:dv:rom_ctrl_bkdr_util_hier`, which provides
`lowrisc:virtual_dv:rom_ctrl_bkdr_util_hier` so that another
implementation can be mapped in without duplicating the
`rom_ctrl_bkdr_util` class.  The open-source `prim_rom` is described as
a single array named `mem`, so behaviour is unchanged.

This commit also makes `rom_ctrl_bkdr_util` forward the tiling arguments
to its base class, and changes the testbenches to derive `depth` and
`n_bits` from one tile scaled by the number of tiles.  In the top-level
TB of Earl Grey, `MEM_BKDR_UTIL_FILE_OP` gets skipped for a tiled ROM,
because `mem_bkdr_util` then handles the file operations itself.  The TB
of Darjeeling, whose ROMs are single arrays, passes the tiling arguments
that say so.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [alert,dv] Response to requests dropped during reset
body:
The alert uncovered when clkmgr_sec_cm test was run is: "Timeout waiting for
end of ack for alert fatal_fault".

alert_receiver_driver discards a request item in drive_req()'s
reset_wait loop. When the cfg.in_reset is asserted the loop ignores
any item that arrives since it won't be driven.

The item had already been pulled off the seq_item_port by get() so the
sequence that sent it had already returned finish_item() and moved onto
get_response(). However, drive_req() didn't call
seq_item_port.put_response on the discarded item, so the get_response()
called blocked forever stopping the sequencer from producing any
subsequent items. The fix calls seq_item_port.put_response() on any item
that gets pulled off m_receiver_requests while this loop is discarding
items during reset.

Signed-off-by: Ed Baker <edward.baker@lowrisc.org>

subject: [dv] Increase sec_cm fatal_fault wait margin to 8 cycles
body:
check_sec_cm_fi_resp waits up to max_wait_cycle peripheral clock cycles
for the fatal_fault alert to fire using the default of 7. This occasionally
failed with "did not fire in 7 cycles" even though the alert was about
to fire just one cycle later.

This was confirmed by tracing the signal chain in the waveform and
correlating with run.log timestamps. wait_alert_trigger begins counting on
each posedge of the peripheral clock with the first posedge after the
fault is injected being counted as 1 clock cycle. The fault being
injected is detected and latched on clk_main but
is_alert_handshaking (wait_alert_trigger watches this) sits on the
peripheral clk. clk_main and peripheral clk are asynchronous and the
frequency of the peripheral clk is randomised by seed. So the number of cycles it takes for
the injected fault to be responded to varies. This was measured
directly with a fixed seed reproducing the failure on u_clk_main_aes_trans:
(111118716803140766782667161843080550331066687643124163397450426690832451081729).
An example of a fault that takes 8 cycles for a response is injected at
580,023,262ps with the response being asserted at 580,326,350ps. With a
peripheral clock period of 41667ps. Dividing the raw time gap by the
period gives 7.27, while counting the number of posedges gives 8. The same test
fails at max_wait_cycle=7 and passes at max_wait_cycle=8

The override was only scoped to check_sec_cm_fi_resp() not the
max_wait_cycle default in cip_base_vseq::wait_alert_trigger(), since the
default is relied on by several other IPs (e.g. flash_ctrl and
otp_ctrl) whose alert paths haven't been investigated. Two other call
sites follow this same pattern of local overrides rather than changing
the shared default (cip_base_vseq.sv's own .max_wait_cycle(4) and
sram_ctrl_readback_err_vseq.sv's .max_wait_cycle(20)).

Signed-off-by: Ed Baker <edward.baker@lowrisc.org>

subject: [alert,dv] Split up alert_esc_seq_item
body:
After this change, the fields of actual sequence items are split
between subclasses (alert_seq_item and esc_seq_item).

Once we've made these changes, we can give more specific types to the
drivers and sequences (which are all specialised to only work for
either alerts or escalations). These checks have to be done at runtime
though because the drivers and sequences communicate through a shared
sequencer, which uses the alert_esc_seq_item base type.

The same "base component" type is needed as alert_esc_base_driver. I
strongly suspect that the code was working by chance before (since
some changes I made a month ago), but we need some fixed (and
non-parameterised) type for a base driver in order for it to be
registered properly with the factory, where we can then apply
overrides to create the correct base type in an instance of the agent.

While restructuring this code, I also renamed "alert_esc_type" to
"m_trans_type". It looked at first to me like it was a type that told
you whether this was an alert or an escalation, which is wrong: this
is actually the a type of transaction that can apply to either an
alert or an escalation.

Finally, I removed r_esc_rsp. This was used as a runtime indication
that an item was a response to an escalation, rather than an alert.
The information is now available in the data type. This also prompted
me to get rid of esc_receiver_esc_rsp_seq: it's completely identical
to esc_receiver_base_seq.

subject: [reggen] Make signals partition aware
body:
This is a preparation for the reggen/topgen tooling to support IPs split over two partitions, i.e.,
power domains.

This makes all signals (alerts, interrupts, inter-IP signals, etc) aware of to which partition /
power domain they are allocated. There are two partitions, the primary and the secondary. Both can
be mapped (later) to a power domain. Any signal defaults to the primary domain, which is the default
for any IP not specifying a split (the 'domain' attribute in the top hjson).

There is a limitation on how signals of different domains must be ordered in the lists in the hjson
files. To guarantee contiguous bit ranges per partition for things like alerts, any signals
allocated to the secondary domain (with the 'partition' attribute in the IP hjson) must come after
any signals for the primary domain. This is required because the order in these lists implicitly
define the bit ordering.

subject: [rules,bitstreams] Fall back to the system CA bundle
body:
Under Bazel this script runs on the hermetic CPython that rules_python
downloads, which bundles its own OpenSSL built with Debian-style CA
paths: `cafile` is unset and `capath` is `/etc/ssl/certs`.

RHEL-family distributions populate neither. `/etc/ssl/certs` does exist
there, as a symlink to `/etc/pki/tls/certs`, but holds only bundle files
and none of the `<subject-hash>.0` symlinks that OpenSSL's capath lookup
requires, and there is no `ca-certificates.crt`. The trust store is
therefore empty:

    ssl.create_default_context().cert_store_stats()['x509_ca'] == 0

so every request made by this script fails with

    [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] unable to get local issuer certificate

This breaks `util/prep-bazel-airgapped-build.sh`, where it surfaces well
away from its cause as

    no such package '@@+_repo_rules+bitstreams//':
    Bitstream cache not initialized properly.

Only this script is affected: `pip` vendors certifi, so wheel downloads
are fine, and Bazel's own downloader has its own trust store. Debian and
Ubuntu match the interpreter's compiled-in paths and are unaffected,
which is why this only shows up on some hosts.

Keep using the default context whenever it already trusts something, and
otherwise load the first system bundle we can find, covering the usual
Debian, RHEL, SUSE and BSD locations. `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR`
continue to take precedence, being honoured by `create_default_context`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Luís Marques <luismarques@lowrisc.org>

subject: [rram_ctrl,dv] Add scoreboard
body:
Adds the TL/CSR-monitoring scoreboard: process_tl_access() dispatches to
process_tl_core_access()/process_tl_prim_access() by RAL, and core-map
accesses split further into on_reg_access()/on_mem_access() by address
kind (an unmapped address is flagged inline instead, since predict_tl_err()
already makes that unreachable). The scoreboard owns and wires up the
uvm_reg_predictor that auto-predicts the core RAL model from bus traffic;
rram_ctrl_env connects the core TL monitor to it in a later commit, since
only the env has access to the TL agents.

configure_csr_check_exclusions() (called from connect_phase) enables
check_on_read on the RAL map: uvm_reg_predictor::write() compares observed
read data against the mirror before do_predict() overwrites it with that
same data, so this catches real mismatches unlike a scoreboard-side check.
It also walks every register/field and suppresses the compare wherever a
CsrExclCheck exclusion applies, for fields the RAL can never predict.

Also adds rram_ctrl_reg_predictor_filter, the uvm_subscriber that has to
sit upstream of that predictor: uvm_reg_predictor::write() calls
do_predict() unconditionally without checking status, so this drops any
d_error'd item first. See the in-file comments for why that matters.

Host reads/writes are not checked yet: process_tl_access()'s
host_ral_name branch is a no-op, pending a per-region config tracker that
doesn't exist in this reduced environment.
