subject: [rram_ctrl,dv] Add OTP key driver
body:
Adds rram_ctrl_otp_key_driver: a uvm_component bound to
rram_ctrl_otp_key_if, one instance per DUT request line (address and
data scrambling), both bound to the same interface (safe because they
are never asserted at the same time, backed by an assertion in the
interface itself). Each instance randomizes its own key/rand_key pair
once and answers every request on its line with that pair for the life
of the test, matching real key-derivation semantics.

Req/ack is sampled and driven through rram_ctrl_otp_key_if's host_cb
clocking block rather than raw signal edges: the clocking block's input
skew samples req in the Preponed region, just before the clock edge,
avoiding a race with the DUT's own same-edge always_ff update.

run_phase races provide_scrambling_keys() (handling one request) against
a reset event via fork/join_any/disable fork, so a mid-request reset
kills the in-flight handling and restarts cleanly instead of leaving
stale ack/seed_valid state. build_phase also asserts that
rram_ctrl_pkg::KeyWidth matches otp_ctrl_pkg::NvmKeyWidth, since
key/rand_key are sized by the former but drive fields sized by the
latter.

This answers the DUT's key requests from proper UVM driver code
instead of a sequence reaching through cfg to poke the interface
directly, per review feedback on the original otp_model() reactive
task embedded in the base vseq.

subject: [i3c] I3C fixes
body:
It is suspected that IBI Payload fetching must be done at a speed
commensurate with the declared tSCO for Private Read transfers; this
does not seem to be specified, but the design now appropriates the
AUTOCMD_MODE field for this purpose, and documents it. Its default value
of 0 leads to collection at SDR0 (full speed) so hopefully this is okay.

The signaling speed of the initial I3C Broadcast Address was lost in the
review process; this must be slow enough to allow I3C devices with spike
filters to see it.

Data length determination is moved into the command decoding, since this
is distinct from the FSM logic and current state.

The respin of the DAT Cache during review resulted in breakage; it must
also respond in the event of a miss.

Indicate whether the Target-side logic is connected to the bus and
monitoring, not just whether it is out of reset. There is a difference
and software will need to know.

Fix reset logic; identified an issue in the handling of HCI-specified
software reset. We need to modify or workaround our auto-generated
registers to handle this; possible solution available but deferred
until later.

Modify transceiver request generation to support Private transfers
that are prefixed with the I3C Broadcast Address; this is important in
ensuring a timely response to In-Band Interrupts.

Tidy the handling of the Half-Cycle SCL high extension; this shall be
dependent upon the specific timing being used.

Controller ACK/NACK monitoring and generation has been nailed down.

Add 'known value' checks to the other IP block outputs.

Software reset of the Standby Controller registers.

subject: [alert,dv] Remove fictional time-out (handshake_timeout_cycle)
body:
This timeout caused the driver to give up on sending an item, even if
there wasn't a response. The end result is that things end up out of
sync later.

Removing this fixes the adc_ctrl_clock_gating test, which was failing
because the clock gets gated.

In detail:

 - This gating doesn't gate the "async clock" on the interface, which
   was added in b620de35dbe to allow alerts/pings/acks that aren't
   synchronised with the main sender clock.

 - As such, a ping item might be sent when the clock is disabled.
   That's fine: the ping_p/ping_n signals change value, which is
   visible in receiver_cb and on the interface signals themselves.

 - A few cycles later, the driver gives up on waiting for a
   response. (BUG!)

 - When the clock gets re-enabled, the ping request becomes visible
   through monitor_cb (which is clocked on the clock that had been
   disabled).

 - The agent sees the ping request.

 - A couple of cycles later, the dut responds to the ping.

 - Nothing then acks the response. (The driver stopped waiting
   thousands of cycles ago).

 - Since the monitor doesn't see the full ping handshake, it reports a
   ping timeout.

 - Now the scoreboard fails: pings shouldn't time out.

subject: [alert_handler,dv] Split the alert and escalation agents
body:
These two agents were combined into an "alert_esc_agent", but it was
really complicated!

I think the reason that they had originally been combined is that both
protocols use differential signalling, have a possible "signal
integrity error", and have a ping mechanism.

But:

  - The alert and escalation interfaces don't actually share any
    signals.

  - The ping mechanisms work differently in the two interfaces.

  - Splitting up will make it much easier to replace the complicated
    dv_reactive_agent mechanism that the alert side of the agent was
    using.

  - Splitting things doesn't produce that many extra lines (look at
    the diff-stat: we're adding less than 200).

In the middle of writing this, I made a mistake and removed the
int_err_cyc_c constraint, which controlled whether alert items request
signal integrity errrors. The end result was a hanging
testbench (because the back-to-back items from the ping sequence would
be discarded in zero time). The version in this commit fixes my
mistake, but also makes the driver stop the test if this happens: it's
a bug in the stimulus.

Grepping for the constraint name, I strongly suspect that nothing ever
triggers signal integrity errors with this mechanism at all. But
that's a question for another commit.

key and add checks for if reset is asserted, exiting the task early
when that happens.

There are some loops that wait for an event by doing backdoor HDL
reads on negative edges of the clock. To do this tidily, I've added a
wait_n_clks_or_rst task to clk_rst_if (to match the wait_clks_or_rst
task that already existed).

One part of the changes in this commit is to add an "early exit on
reset" to aes_base_vseq::set_sideload. Since there are a couple of
equivalent tasks next to it, I've factored out the common code and
taught them about resets too.

Honestly, these tasks seem a bit strange to me: most of them have
their only call site in aes_base_vseq::setup_dut. This function
performs a chain of double-writes to the same register, one for each
field. This is a bit inefficient!

What's more, these sequence tasks do register prediction (presumably,
there was no scoreboard when it was originally written).

In both cases, the code is a bit awkward, but further changes to that
part of the sequence are probably out of scope for this commit.

subject: [sigverify/sphincsplus] Fix remaining word truncation in mgf1_sha256
body:
In `mgf1_sha256()`, the truncation size for each HMAC SHA-256 block
checked `out_len <= kHmacDigestNumWords` instead of checking the
remaining words needed for the current iteration. When `out_len`
exceeded 8 words, every block wrote 8 words regardless of how many
words remained in the final iteration.

Calculate the remaining words from `out_len - (ctr * kHmacDigestNumWords)`
and truncate the final digest block accordingly.

Additionally, add a static assertion in `hash_sha2.c` to verify that
`kSpxDigestWords` does not exceed a single HMAC SHA-256 block
(`kHmacDigestNumWords`).

Signed-off-by: Bastien Gillon <bgillon@google.com>

subject: [darjeeling,dv] Drop unsatisfiable unique MIO outsel map constraint
body:
chip_padctrl_attributes randomizes periph_to_mio_map[MioPadCount], the
peripheral output selected for each MIO pad's outsel register, under a
`unique {periph_to_mio_map}` constraint inherited from Earlgrey. On
Darjeeling there are 12 MIO pads but only MioOutCount = 5 peripheral
outputs (top_darjeeling_pkg.sv), so no unique assignment exists and
the test dies at time 0 with

  Error-[CNST-CIF] Constraints inconsistency failure
  UVM_FATAL (dv_base_test.sv) Check failed (test_seq.randomize())

before any stimulus is applied.

Drop the uniqueness requirement. pinmux_mio_outsel_checks() looks up
periph_to_mio[periph_to_mio_map[i]] independently for every pad, so
several pads sharing one peripheral output is a valid configuration and
is checked correctly. The other constraint (map != MioOutCount) is
kept.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [darjeeling,dv] Order DioToDioPadMap and DioPadType by dio_e
body:
chip_common_pkg::DioToDioPadMap and the DioPadType table in
chip_padctrl_attributes_vseq translate a pinmux / peripheral side DIO
index into the pad it is connected to. Both are indexed by
top_darjeeling_pkg::dio_e (the index space of the pinmux's
periph_to_dio_i / dio_to_periph_o ports), but their entries were listed
in pad order (SPI_HOST_D0-3, SPI_HOST_CLK, SPI_HOST_CS_L, SPI_DEV_D0-3,
SPI_DEV_CLK, ...), i.e. in dio_pad_e order.

dio_e is ordered inout, input, output: DioSpiHost0Sd0-3 = 0-3,
DioSpiDeviceSd0-3 = 4-7, DioI2c0Scl/Sda = 8-9, DioGpioGpio0-31 = 10-41,
DioSpiDeviceSck/Csb/TpmCsb = 42-44, DioUart0Rx = 45,
DioSocProxySocGpi0-11 = 46-57, DioSpiHost0Sck/Csb = 58-59,
DioUart0Tx = 60, DioSocProxySocGpo0-11 = 61-72. So indices 4-60 were
mapped to the wrong pad (only 0-3 and 61-72 line up): for example
chip_padctrl_attributes drives periph_to_dio_i[4] (DioSpiDeviceSd0) but
samples the SPI_HOST_CLK pad. The pad type was wrong at 15 indices:
seven input-only DIOs (DioSpiDeviceSck/Csb/TpmCsb, DioUart0Rx,
DioSocProxySocGpi0-2) were typed BidirStd, so the vseq drives their
periph side, and eight bidirectional DIOs (DioGpioGpio0-3, DioGpioGpio5,
DioSpiHost0Sck/Csb, DioUart0Tx) were typed InputStd. Both kinds of
mismatch break the pinmux_dio_insel_checks() comparisons. The same map
is used by chip_sw_sleep_pin_wake_vseq and
chip_sw_sleep_pin_mio_dio_val_vseq to find the pad for a SW-selected
DIO index.

Rewrite both tables in dio_e order. DioToDioPadMap is keyed by dio_e, so
a missing or duplicated entry is a compile error; the type table is
annotated with the dio_e name and the pad. The order and pad types are
derived from the `connection: direct` entries of pinmux.ios and
pinout.pads in hw/top_darjeeling/data/autogen/top_darjeeling.gen.hjson
and match the padring DioPadType parameter in chip_darjeeling_asic.sv.
This also corrects the I2C_SCL entry, which is BidirStd, not InputStd.
Earlgrey's DioToDioPadMap is already in dio_e order.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [darjeeling,dv] Force all DIO periph inputs in chip_padctrl_attributes
body:
The chip_if probe used by chip_padctrl_attributes to drive the pinmux's
peripheral side DIO inputs only covered periph_to_dio_i[11:0], and the
vseq only forced periph_to_dio[11:0]. This was carried over from
Earlgrey, which has 16 DIOs and splits the probe into [11:0] and
[15:14] around its two input-only SPI device pins. Darjeeling has
NDioPads = 73 DIOs, so bits [72:12] were never driven: the vseq
randomizes periph_to_dio for all DioCount entries and then compares
the pad against the value it believes it drove, so every bidirectional
DIO at index 12 and above with periph_to_dio_oe set fails
pinmux_dio_insel_checks() (pad reads back z / the pull instead of the
driven value).

Replace the partial probe with one that forces the full periph_to_dio_i
vector and pass the whole periph_to_dio array to it. Darjeeling's
input-only DIOs need no special casing: the vseq already treats
InputStd entries as "periph side has no effect" and only checks
dio_to_periph for them.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [sw,testutils] Fix alert crash dump parsing on Darjeeling
body:

last field. The index points one past the last bit read, so the check

is 288 bits, exactly 9 words, so every test that parses it fails at

computed from the alert handler parameters rather than hardcoded.

subject: [pwrmgr,dv] Scale MaxMainRstCycles to Darjeeling's slow clock
body:
pwrmgr_rstreqs_sva_if bounds its hardware reset checks with
MaxMainRstCycles = 400 cycles of clk_slow_i: 2 ms on Earlgrey's 200 kHz
AON clock, but 6.4 us on Darjeeling's 62.5 MHz one.

HwResetOff_A expects reset_cause to leave HwReq within that window after
the request drops. The fast FSM clears it on entering
FastPwrStateRomCheckDone, after the rstmgr/clkmgr handshakes, OTP init
and LC init. That is fast-clock work and takes about 11.8 us on
Darjeeling, so the assertion fails on both of its hardware reset
request sources, the aon_timer watchdog bite and the SoC reset request.

Give Darjeeling the same 2 ms budget (125_000 slow cycles), selected by
topname like FastToSlowFreqRatio; Earlgrey and Englishbreakfast keep
400. SwResetSetCause_A shares the macro but runs on clk_i, so give it
its own 400-cycle bound to keep it unchanged on every top.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [aes,dv] Teach parts of the base vseq to allow injected resets
body:
Doing this was a bit tricky, because the virtual sequence sometimes
wants to inject a reset (after it has seen a fatal fault). Doing that
under a sequence that itself wants to inject resets causes exciting
race conditions, so we don't want to do that.

The solution in this commit is to set a flag (m_external_reset) in the
sequence that says when the sequence is being run underneath another
sequence that will inject a reset.

In that situation, the part of the sequence that would have previously
generated a reset (the wait_for_fatal_alert_and_reset task) now just
waits for a reset to be asserted externally and then returns
immediately.

The sequence also gains a lot of early returns when reset is asserted.

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [chip,dv] Give jtag_rv_debugger its agent cfg in set_use_jtag_dmi()
body:
chip_env_cfg::initialize() creates the jtag_rv_debugger and calls
debugger.set_cfg(m_jtag_agent_cfg), but m_jtag_agent_cfg is only
created later, in set_use_jtag_dmi(), which chip_base_test calls after
super.build_phase() (and hence after cfg.initialize()) has run. The
debugger therefore always ends up with a null cfg handle in
+use_jtag_dmi mode. set_use_jtag_dmi() hands the new agent cfg to
m_jtag_riscv_agent_cfg and to the DMI register block, and hands the
register block to the debugger, but never hands the agent cfg to the
debugger.

Commit 1902280f8b moved the creation of m_jtag_agent_cfg (and the
debugger.set_ral() call) from initialize() into set_use_jtag_dmi() but
left the debugger.set_cfg() call behind, where it now only ever sees
null.

Everything that goes through the DMI RAL frontdoor still works, so the
abstract-command paths (halt, GPR/CSR reads) pass. The first path that
dereferences the debugger's own cfg is the system bus access path:
sba_access() -> sba_access_busy_wait() uses cfg.in_reset and
cfg.vif.wait_tck(). On Darjeeling,
chip_sw_rv_dm_ndm_reset_req_when_cpu_halted dies with

  Error-[NOA] Null object access
  jtag_rv_debugger.sv, 1108  (sba_access_busy_wait)

when the vseq reads lc_ctrl's device_id through
m_sba_access_reg_frontdoor. The same code exists on Earlgrey, and the
rom_e2e_jtag_inject tests are exposed too because mem_read()/
mem_write()/load_image() randomly pick the SBA route. The debugger's
do_trst_n() and finish()/call() also dereference cfg.

Drop the always-null set_cfg() call from initialize() and give the
debugger its agent cfg at the end of set_use_jtag_dmi(), next to the
existing set_ral() call, on both tops.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [soc_dbg_ctrl,dv] Exclude HW-driven trace regs from CSR checks

reset: the core and JTAG copies of TRACE_DEBUG_POLICY_CATEGORY and
TRACE_DEBUG_POLICY_VALID_RELOCKED, which follow the debug policy
derived from the LC, OTP, boot status and SW policy inputs, and
JTAG_BOOT_STATUS and JTAG_TRACE_SOC_DBG_STATE, which reflect the boot
status, the halt FSM state and the OTP debug state while lc_dft_en is
on. None was excluded, so the generic CSR tests compare them against
their reset values. The block bench ties those inputs to
reset-equivalent values and hides this; at chip level they differ once
lc_ctrl has initialised.

Tag them excl:CsrAllTests:CsrExclCheck, as lc_ctrl does for LC_STATE
and STATUS. Nothing else checks them yet; the next commit plans a
testpoint for that.

subject: [racl_ctrl,dv] Exclude policy registers from generic CSR writes
body:
The generic CSR tests (csr_hw_reset, csr_rw, csr_bit_bash and
csr_aliasing) write random values to every rw register. racl_ctrl's
POLICY_*_SHADOWED registers are rw: csr_wr writes a shadowed register
twice, so the random permission bitmap commits (csr_hw_reset's write
phase may instead poke it through the backdoor), and racl_ctrl
broadcasts it immediately to every subscribing IP. A policy carries a
read and a write permission bitmap, gated independently, so whenever
such a write clears ROT's bit from one of them, accesses of that kind
from ROT to a register under that policy are squashed with d_error for
as long as the bit stays clear (error_response is set in racl.hjson).
The CIP scoreboard has no RACL model, so it reports the d_error as
unexpected.

At chip level on Darjeeling, racl_ctrl shares the SoC mailbox address
space (chip_soc_mbx_reg_block) with ac_range_check and the SoC-side
mailbox interfaces, all of which are gated by the live policy vector.
chip_csr_hw_reset and chip_csr_rw fail a few microseconds after the CSR
sequence starts with

  On interface chip_soc_mbx_reg_block, item had unexpected d_error
  value(predicted 0, but saw 1) ... a_addr: 'h1464254

where the failing write targets an ac_range_check register from role
ROT, which every policy permits at reset. The policy write that
preceded it is not printed at UVM_LOW; the logged item rules out the
other d_error sources the scoreboard models.

Tag the policy registers with excl:CsrAllTests:CsrExclWrite so that no
CSR test writes them. csr_hw_reset still checks their reset values and
csr_aliasing still reads them back, but csr_rw and csr_bit_bash now
skip them entirely. racl_ctrl's own registers are gated by the static
ROT_PRIVATE policy, so these registers are the only way a CSR test can
change a live policy. The policy data path stays covered by the
block-level smoke test, which writes random values to randomly picked
policy registers while the scoreboard checks the broadcast value; that
bench needs a separate compile fix before it runs on current master.

Regenerated with util/topgen.py for top_darjeeling; only
hw/top_darjeeling/ip_autogen/racl_ctrl/data/racl_ctrl.hjson changes.

subject: [hw,csrng] Add GEN abort feature
body:
This commit adds the possibility to abort an ongoing GEN command.
This can be done by writing mubi4_true to one of the instances of
the GEN_ABORT_REGWEN protected register GEN_ABORT.

The command stage uses the existing UNI command to zero the state
and clears its own state. To use the instance again it has to
be reinstantiated.

If an abort is triggered while no GEN command is active, a
GEN_ABORT_INVALID_ALERT will be triggered.

Once the GEN command is aborted it will return an ACK with a
GEN_ABORTED status.

If the abort was triggered on an EDN instance this will cause
the EDN to raise an alert. The EDN then needs to be restarted.

For the SW app a successful abort triggers an interrupt and the
GEN_ABORTED status can then be read from CMD_STS.

as aes TRIGGER.START is. Both reset to zero and keep that value until a
counter is enabled, so the reset checks stay. In the control register

subject: [topgen] Handle intra-IP and inter-module signals for split IPs
body:
A split IP can have intra-IP connections which directly connect the two partitions. However, in the
config a split IP is a single instance. So any regular inter-module signal would have the same start
and end point, which is not supported by the current topgen.

This commit thus introduces an intra-IP signal handling which uniquifies inter-module signals per
partition. It does so by adding a partition qualifier to each inter-module signal of a split IP.
This allows the regular inter-module signal handling to connect the two partitions properly.

It also enables the partitions to use the same signal name, otherwise these would have to be unique.

Non-split IPs use no qualifier.

subject: [i3c] Target reset generation
body:
This small module handles the generation of the asynchronous
reset into the SCL-clocked Target transceiver logic.
It works in conjunction with the `i3c_timers` module to produce
a sustained reset assertion in response to:

 - IP block reset.
 - Software-initiated reset.
 - Serious errors reported by the Target-side logic.

It also generates the enable to the Target-side input buffers,
after a Bus Available condition is observed following reset.
This ensures that the Target transceiver logic is connected to
the I3C bus only when it is in a known state, not mid-transfer.

subject: [reggen] Support a list of reinit signals
body:
Modify reggen and prim_subreg to support an optional list
of reinitialization inputs into the autogenerated register RTL.

Each register/multi_register may be bound to one of these
reinit signals and its contents thus restored to the post
reset state, with higher priority than any write operations
from either software or hardware.

The requirement for this change comes from the introduction
of the I3C IP block which implements the MIPI Alliance
Host Controller Interface (HCI) specification. The HCI
specification mandates that the registers shall be set to their
reset values via the software reset mechanism provided by the
register field `RESET_CONTROL.SOFT_RST`.

Such functionality may be more generally useful and it is not
possible simply to provide an extra stimulus to the `rst_ni`
asynchronous input of the autogenerated registers externally
because the generated logic also includes TL-UL components and
could cause a bus hang.

It is important that the block level asynchronous reset signal
remains the means of ensuring a guaranteed, clean initial
state for the whole IP block, and that this reinitialization
mechanism shall be used sparingly, as required for specific
cases only.

Signed-off-by: Adrian Lees <a.lees@lowrisc.org>

reset state, which is a mandatory requirement of the I3C
IP block implementation but is also likely to be useful in
other IP blocks later.

These unused inputs will impact coverage results slightly,
so UNR will need to be re-run later.

Also fix up the manual instantiations of this module.

subject: [dv,xcelium] Enable Constant Object Marking in coverage flow
body:
Add `set_com -on -log` to the project-wide Xcelium coverage
configuration file (common.ccf, included by both cover.ccf and
cover_reg_top.ccf). This enables Cadence's Constant Object Marking
(COM), which detects coverage items driven by constants inside the DUT
during elaboration, marks them IGN and omits them from the coverage
figures.

This is the Xcelium equivalent of the VCS `-cm_seqnoconst` switch that
the VCS flow already applies. It prevents statically-tied inputs -- such
as the reinit inputs newly added to the generated register blocks, which
are tied to zero for all existing integrations -- from being reported as
false coverage holes. The `-covdut` interface already set in the build
step keeps genuine DUT ports variable, so only constants within the DUT
are marked.

body:
This commit adds the Adaptive Proportion Symbol Test as defined in the
NIST SP 800-90B specification. Previously, only a lane-based variant of
this test was supported which can meet the NIST spec when using a
health test window size of 1024 bits. For parameterizations with a
symbol size lower equal 4 bits, the already supported bucket test can
be viewed as a super set of the Adaptive Proportion Symbol Test.
However, this test is more complex and will eventually be made optional.

Besides the RTL, this commit also adds DV and SW support for the newly
added test and extends the OTP_CTRL memory map such that ROM can first
configure the bypass and later the continuous mode threshold value
for this new test.

subject: [chip,dv] Define sw_logger_if::wait_for_log_message
body:
This was triggered by warning messages when building chip-level
testbenches. The original motivation was messages generated when
building chip_sw_keymgr_dpe_key_derivation_vseq, but I've also used
the new task in some of the other chip_sw_keymgr_dpe_* virtual
sequences.

The existing code had lines like the following:

    `DV_WAIT(cfg.sw_logger_vif.printed_log ==
        $sformatf("KeymgrDpe generated AES output from DPE context in slot %0d", derived_key_slot_idx))

This generates warnings because cfg.sw_logger_vif.printed_log is a bit
vector, so the EDA tool suggests the comparisons should be cast to
strings, giving something like this:

    `DV_WAIT(string'(cfg.sw_logger_vif.printed_log) ==
        $sformatf("KeymgrDpe generated AES output from DPE context in slot %0d", derived_key_slot_idx))

This is rather ugly, and would end up with users having to reason
about the implementation of the interface. With the new version of the
code, this can be simplified to

    cfg.sw_logger_vif.wait_for_log_message(
      $sformatf("KeymgrDpe generated AES output from DPE context in slot %0d", derived_key_slot_idx))

The wait_for_log_message task has a default timeout, which I've
actually copied manually from csr_utils_pkg: it doesn't feel like
sw_logger_if should depend on that core.

It also has the option of describing the thing that's being waited
for, which lets the caller be a bit more specific about what should be
in an error message.

The change described above squashes some warnings, which is nice, but
the code is still rather hard to read (a long string literal and a
call to $sformatf). To improve things further, this commit pulls some
of that repeated code into some helper tasks. The example above
eventually becomes:

    wait_for_keymgr_dpe_gen_output_slot_msg("AES", derived_key_slot_idx);

The helper tasks are specific to this virtual sequence because the
precise wording of the messages is different for the other virtual
sequences, but they can still use wait_for_log_message().

Signed-off-by: Rupert Swarbrick <rswarbrick@lowrisc.org>

subject: [otp_ctrl,dv] Model the Zeroize marker in DAI accesses
body:
Several otp_ctrl tests fail on Darjeeling. For example, partition_walk
fails on every seed at the first Zeroize marker. One of its failures
is:

  otp_ctrl_base_vseq.sv:215 [otp_ctrl_partition_walk_vseq] Check failed
  rdata0 == exp_data0 (0 [0x0] vs 16080 [0x3ed0]) dai addr 3ed0 rdata0
  readout mismatch

On Darjeeling, the SECRET partitions can be zeroized. Each of them ends
with a Zeroize marker, which comes right after the digest. Software
cannot write the marker directly. It can always read it, even when the
partition is locked, and it gets back the stored bits unchanged.

The testbench handled only part of this. It wrote to the marker and the
digest as if they were normal data. It also expected the wrong result
when it read the marker.

Teach the testbench about the marker. Expect writes to it to fail, and
expect reads to succeed and return the stored bits. Also keep the smoke
test's random accesses away from the digest. Earlgrey has no zeroizable
partitions, so nothing changes there.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [i3c] I3C Pattern Detectors
body:
The I3C bus uses three special signaling patterns to perform
special actions at the request of the Active Controller:

 - Target Reset
 - HDR Restart
 - HDR Exit

These two modules detect those patterns and signal to the
core IP and to other system-level IP (reset/power) that they
have occurred.

The detector logic runs entirely on the I3C signals directly
(SCL and SDA). In the case of the reset detector this reduces
power consumption in 'Deepest Sleep' state by obviating the
need for a high frequency clock.

subject: [dv] Only clone jtag_riscv_map from the main RAL model
body:
When a test asks for a JTAG map, cip_base_env_cfg clones the default
map of every RAL model. All clones go into the same jtag_riscv_map
handle, so the handle keeps only the last one. Only that map gets the
JTAG RISC-V sequencer.

This is fine with one RAL model. The Darjeeling bench has three, so
the handle ends up with the mailbox model's map. Every access to the
main chip registers then goes through a map without a sequencer:

  UVM_FATAL [SEQ] neither the item's sequencer nor dedicated
  sequencer has been supplied to start item in default_parent_seq

Clone the map for the main RAL model only. In the Darjeeling chip_env,
make it the default map of that model only. Benches with a single RAL
model, such as the Earlgrey chip and lc_ctrl, do not change.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [darjeeling,dv] Keep the JTAG DTM connected for jtag_riscv tests
body:
chip_jtag_csr_rw and chip_jtag_mem_access fail on Darjeeling at about
131 us:

  UVM_ERROR (jtag_riscv_driver.sv:221) Check failed
  sbcs_val[SbAccess32] == 1 (0 [0x0] vs 1 [0x1])

In stub-CPU mode the bench drives the debug TL port from its own TL
agent, which disconnects the JTAG DTM. The DTM never gets a response,
so the JTAG agent reads stale data. Keep the DTM connected whenever a
test uses jtag_riscv_map, as the bench already does for the JTAG DMI
agent.

With the DTM connected, the scoreboard checks the DTM's reads of the
debug module registers as if they were memory, and reports false
mismatches. Both tests compare the data they read back themselves.
Turn off their scoreboard memory check, as chip_rv_dm_lc_disabled
does.

is a host on the main crossbar only. The soc_dbg and mailbox register
blocks sit on separate crossbars, reached only from the JTAG DTM and
the SoC side.

Narrow the CSR test down to chip_reg_block, which is also what the
Earlgrey test covers. Stop with a fatal error if a caller asks for
register blocks that leave it out.

subject: [darjeeling,dv] Shorten the JTAG CSR and memory tests
body:
chip_jtag_csr_rw and chip_jtag_mem_access spend all their simulated
time on JTAG. Each access through the rv_dm system bus takes about
11 JTAG scans, or about 11 us of simulated time. The sizes were taken
from Earlgrey, which simulates about ten times faster. On Darjeeling
the CSR test took 67 minutes on a local machine, past the default 60
minute run timeout, and the memory test took 48.

Test at most 100 CSRs per iteration instead of 500. The CSR sequence
picks one random chunk of the chip's registers per iteration, so any
register can still be picked on some seed, but each run tests fewer.
Write and read back 32 random words per memory instead of 128. Every
memory the test selects is still tested on every run.

subject: [otbn,dv] Pick BadDeepLoop loop ends from the valid set
body:
OTBN tests that use the random instruction generator (RIG) sometimes
fail before they simulate, while generating the program:

  bad_deep_loop.py, line 67, in _pick_bodysize
    assert bodysize is not None

Each loop that BadDeepLoop nests must end at an existing instruction or
above the top of IMEM, so that it never completes. The generator picked
a random body size and gave up after 50 tries. Since IMEM grew to
16 KiB, a loop head at a low address with little code above it has few
valid body sizes, and all 50 tries can miss.

List the valid body sizes and pick one of them. For seeds where the old
re-roll succeeded, the loop end is drawn from the same distribution as
before. Seeds that reach BadDeepLoop now generate a different program
from the same seed. The largest body size always ends above IMEM, as
long as IMEM is at most 16 KiB, so the list is never empty. An assert
checks this before the list is built.

Fixes #31096

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [otbn,dv] Accept ELF segments that end at the top of IMEM or DMEM
body:
The OTBN standalone simulator refuses to load a program whose code
reaches the last word of IMEM. Programs from the OTBN random
instruction generator (RIG) sometimes do:

  RuntimeError: Segment has LMA range 0x7ff8..0x8000, which intersects
  the IMEM range (0x4000..0x7fff), but is not fully contained in it.

Since 510f1c8301 the memory top in _get_elf_mem_data() is the last
byte of the memory, but the segment top is still one past the last
byte of the segment. Comparing the two rejects a segment that ends
exactly at the top. The same happens to data that ends at the top of
the bus-visible part of DMEM.

Compute the segment top as its last byte too. A segment that goes one
byte past the top is still rejected. A segment that starts right after
IMEM is still treated as DMEM. That is the case 510f1c8301 fixed.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [racl_ctrl,doc] Say what clearing the error log does
body:
The theory of operation only says that writing 1 to ERROR_LOG.VALID
clears the log. The register descriptions are more precise: the write
clears ERROR_LOG and ERROR_LOG_ADDRESS. VALID is rw1c, so a write of 0
must leave the log alone.

State both points in the theory of operation, so that the block spec
says what the next commit implements.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [racl_ctrl,rtl] Clear the whole error log when software clears it
body:
The register description says that writing 1 to ERROR_LOG.VALID
clears the log, including ERROR_LOG_ADDRESS. In fact only VALID goes
to zero. The other fields and ERROR_LOG_ADDRESS keep their old
values. If OVERFLOW was set before the clear, the next error still
reads back with OVERFLOW set.

The clear logic fires on VALID.q and VALID.qe together. But the qe
that reggen generates is flopped: it rises one cycle after the write,
when the rw1c write has already cleared VALID. So a write of 1 never
clears the other fields. A write of 0 to a set VALID does fire it,
and then clears the whole log, VALID included.

Clear the other fields on a write to ERROR_LOG that leaves VALID
clear. VALID itself is left to the rw1c register. The other fields
clear one cycle after VALID. A TL read cannot land in that cycle. An
error that arrives in it is still logged as a first error.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [racl_ctrl,dv] Check the error log registers in the racl_ctrl tests
body:
The scoreboard predicts ERROR_LOG and ERROR_LOG_ADDRESS, but no test
read them, so the prediction was never checked. It was also wrong.
The arbiter predictor clones each item, but racl_error_log_item had
no do_copy. So the predicted role, UID, access type and address were
always zero.

Read both registers before clearing the log in the base vseq, and
read them again after the clear, so the scoreboard can check that the
clear emptied them. Sometimes write 0 to ERROR_LOG first, which must
not change it. Enable the racl_error interrupt in the smoke vseq so
that the interrupt check is not trivially zero.

Add the missing do_copy to the item. In the scoreboard, model the log
as the spec describes it. A second error only sets OVERFLOW. The
address is stored without its bottom two bits. A clear empties the
whole log. Take the expected value of a read when the read is
accepted, because the log can change before the response.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

response to the appropriate software reset signals;

the TTI registers. The Standby Controller registers respond to
the either or both reset signals based upon the current

appropriately, as required by both the HCI and the TTI.
Initialize the read and write pointers (and thus FIFO state) for
each of the FIFOs in response to the asynchronous reset; this
aids CSR testing and results in the register state after a
software reset matching the post-reset state of the registers in
the event that the default configuration is used.

subject: [otbn,dv] Sample the BN.NOT source from read port B in coverage
body:
enc_bnan_cg samples the source of BN.NOT from bignum read port A.
BN.NOT encodes its only source in the rs2 field, and the RTL reads it
on port B. Port A is not enabled for BN.NOT, so since the blanking
change (e150160a6c) it reads as zero. The coverage therefore never
sees a source bit set to one, and the nonzero-shift coverpoint and
its cross can never be hit.

The BN.LID and BN.SID coverage treats every positive address as bad,
because its check reads "0 < addr" where it means "addr < 0". The
multi-error crosses that pair a bad address with another error are
then hit by accesses to valid addresses.

Use "addr < 0", as the LW/SW covergroup does.

added this mapping in the same commit, with a typo in the address.

access to 0x7D8 lands in the invalid bin of insn_csrrs_cg and
insn_csrrw_cg. Conversely, an access to the invalid address 0xFC8 is

subject: [csrng/dv] Rework processing of CMD_REQ accesses in the scoreboard
body:
Prior to this commit, the scoreboard modeled SW commands inline, in the
CMD_REQ and GENBITS register handlers, while also duplicating the
command processing that the HW apps go through in
process_csrng_cmd_fifo().

There were two problems with this approach, besides needless code
duplication:

1) The two copies had drifted apart: The SW copy sampled commad coverage
once per register write rather than once per command.
2) A lot worse: The old approach blocked `process_tl_access()` while
waiting for entropy, and it never recorded the FIPS bits of the
generated blocks.

This commit fixes both problems by unifying the command processing for
SW commands with the existing one for HW commands:
Assemble the SW command from the CMD_REQ writes (and, for GEN, the
GENBITS reads) into an item and pass it to the SW app's command FIFO,
such that all apps share one command processing path. This also implies
that the SW app gets the reseed and generate command status checks and
the per-app FIPS transition coverage that only the HW apps had before.

Note that items for the SW app are only assembled during processing of
the CMR_REQ accesses and hence carry no status, so the status check in
process_csrng_cmd_fifo() is skipped for the SW app. The status that SW
observes is instead checked when SW_CMD_STS is read.

To fix the issue with blocking `process_tl_access()`, replace the
handle_disable() polling loop by a call from the CTRL write handler plus
a reset watcher, which no longer relies on observing the disable via a
backdoor CSR read.

Signed-off-by: Florian Glaser <glaserf@lowrisc.org>

subject: [csrng/dv] Stop the stress_all vseq when under reset
body:
`csrng_env_cfg` sets `can_reset_with_csr_accesses`, so
`run_seq_with_rand_reset_vseq` injects its reset whenever it feels like
it and then requires the sequence it raced against to have run to
completion by the time the reset is de-asserted, rather than killing it.

The sub-sequences do stop promptly once they see the reset, but
`csrng_stress_all_vseq` then simply started the next one, so the
enclosing sequence was still running when the reset was released and
`csrng_stress_all_with_rand_reset` failed with
"Check failed (vseq_done)" for every iteration that happened to draw a
short reset delay.

This commit fixes this by consulting `under_reset` before starting each
sub-sequence.

Signed-off-by: Florian Glaser <glaserf@lowrisc.org>

subject: [rom_ctrl,dv] Fix the rom_ctrl_max_throughput_chk test
body:

46f5ef0. The result of that change is that tl_host_driver will take an
extra cycle to sync up with the clock if it receives the first item
after a gap.

This commit fixes the timing expected by the sequence by loosening the

cycle here and there *really* doesn't matter.

It also extends the documentation comment at the top of the file to
explain the sequence more fully.

Minor changes (since I was touching the file):

  - Use a more conventional order for items in the class (data
    members, functions, constraints).

  - Avoid the (non-UVM!) uvm_object_new macro.

  - Don't randomize a rand class variable (num_trans) an extra time at
    the start of body.

  - Don't run a loop with multiple bunches of ROM reads. There's not
    much point, given that they will just go back-to-back anyway. The
    test previously waited for a once-per-reset event to have happened
    on each iteration: maybe the original author imagined that there
    would be a reset between iterations.

    Instead of doing that, scale the number of reads in the single
    iteration to be similar (slightly bigger, actually).

  - Make the check at the end of the test give a slightly more
    informative failure message and explain the number we expect in
    detail in a comment above.

  - Expand out use of DV_SPINWAIT_EXIT. The result is two lines
    longer, but dramatically easier to understand (and doesn't use a
    magic macro).

subject: [crypto/aes] Fix padded decryption above security level Low
body:
Decrypting padded data with otcrypto_aes() and a High security key
traps at the fault check that compares the two passes:

  aes_functest.c:382] Starting test decrypt_high_test...
  ottf_isrs.c:105] FAULT: Illegal Instruction. MCAUSE=00000002

Above security level Low, otcrypto_aes() runs the inverse operation
on its output and checks that both passes saw the same blocks. The
inverse call reuses the caller's padding mode. For a decryption the
inverse encrypts whole blocks, so the padding mode makes it append a
full padding block. That block and its ciphertext only enter the
second checksum. Unless they happen to cancel out, the two checksums
differ and the call traps. Encryption and unpadded decryption are not
affected.

The output of the first pass is always whole blocks, so run the
inverse operation without padding. Extend aes_functest with a one-shot
decryption of every test vector using a High security key.

subject: [aes/rtl] Overwrite GHASH state when clearing instead of XORing
body:
Previously, the design XORed the current, unmasked cipher core output
qualified by CTRL_GCM_SHADOWED.NUM_VALID_BYTES into the current GHASH
state for clearing the GHASH state. Even though the unmasked cipher
core output is over steered using the clearing PRNG while clearing the
GHASH state, this was non optimal for the following reasons:

1. How many bytes of the GHASH state got cleared depended on
   CTRL_GCM_SHADOWED.NUM_VALID_BYTES. If software mis-configured this
   register, it would have been possible that the GHASH state isn't
   modified at all.
2. Knowing two secret netlist permutations applied to the output of the
   clearing PRNG, and assuming that software did not fully clear the
   GHASH module, it was possible to re-trigger the generation of the
   final tag computation and thereby recovering the intermediate state
   of the GHASH module. This could be leveraged for subsequent
   cryptanalysis attacks on the hash subkey.

This commit changes the implementation as follows:
- The cipher core is modified to output the AES state whenever idle.
  This is fine as before entering the idle state, the AES state is wiped
  using the clearing PRNG.
- For clearing, the GHASH state is overwritten with the current, masked
  cipher core output (i.e. the cleared AES state when the cipher core is
  idle).

Since now the hash subkey registers and the GHASH state are cleared with
the same data, it means the two GF multipliers effectively compute the
square of the two individual shares afterwards. This is fine from an SCA
perspective, because the cleared AES state (i.e. the output of the
clearing PRNG) isn't secret anyways (it is also used to clear the data
output registers readable by software).

Thanks to Dino Mehmedagić @nodix95 for reporting this!

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

subject: [otbn,dv] Handle WFI instructions in coverage collection
body:
The nightly runs with functional coverage on. There, otbn_wfi_smoke
and otbn_wfi_back_to_back fail at the first RESUME on every run:

  otbn_scoreboard.sv:440 Check failed model_status == 1 (5 [0x5] vs 1
  [0x1]) Saw instruction when not in BUSY_EXECUTE operational state.

A WFI instruction retires in the cycle that OTBN resumes, but STATUS
only leaves PAUSED two cycles later. So the model reports the WFI and
the next instruction while the scoreboard still has PAUSED. Accept
exactly that while PAUSED: a WFI, then at most one more instruction.

otbn_wfi_sec_wipe often fails on an illegal bin in pairwise_insn_cg.
The coverage model does not know the wfi mnemonic. Add it, sample it
in the covergroup that ECALL uses, and add it to both sides of the
pairwise cross.

The pair tracking also restarted on every STATUS change, so a WFI
pause dropped the pairs around the WFI. Keep tracking pairs while
OTBN is executing or paused. Most WFI pairs still stay unhit, because
only directed tests run WFI.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

body:

subject: [chiplevel] Tie lc_dft_en off explicitly
body:
Prior to this commit, building the English Breakfast simulation with
Verilator 5 failed, because it rejects the implicit conversion to
`lc_ctrl_pkg::lc_tx_t` in `assign lc_dft_en = '0;` (`ENUMVALUE`).
Verilator 4 accepted it.

This commit assigns `lc_ctrl_pkg::Off` instead, which is how the rest
of the code base ties a multi-bit life cycle signal off.  The driven
value changes from `4'b0000` to the `Off` encoding.  Both read as "not
On" to every multi-bit check, and the only consumer is the behavioral
AST model of English Breakfast, which takes the bits as they are, so
nothing observable changes.

The chip level templates of Earl Grey and English Breakfast are copies
of each other, so both are changed, even though only the latter
generates this assignment.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [rram_ctrl/rtl] Drive macro request from one process
body:
Prior to this commit, the fields of `rram_macro_req_o` were driven by
four submodule ports and one `always_comb`, and five expressions that
feed those drivers read other fields back out of the struct.  A
simulator that tracks dependencies per variable sees one variable that
the same processes both read and write, so they appear to form a
combinational loop.  Settling that loop is not guaranteed.  Verilator 4
settles it; Verilator 5 does not and leaves `addr` at its default for
the cycle in which `wr_req` rises.  The RRAM macro latches the offset
within the page in exactly that cycle, so every write lands at offset 0
of its page, which `rom_epmp_test` catches on the read-back.

This commit collects the fields in signals of their own and drives the
struct from a single assignment.  Every field keeps its source, the
defaults of the multiplexer are unchanged, and the widths are the same.
`wr_page_addr` and `wr_part_i` now come from the write side directly
instead of from the output of the multiplexer, which saves a level of
logic: both are used only while `wr_req` holds, and the multiplexer
selects the write side then.

See verilator/verilator#8377, where the advice is to let a single
process write a packed struct, as splitting the drivers "will not
schedule correctly in all cases".  The optimizer half of that issue is
fixed by verilator/verilator#8397, which no release contains yet.

Verified with Verilator 5.048: `rom_epmp_test` passes on the Earl Grey
simulation, where it failed before.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [dv,lint] Fix waivers for Verilator 5
body:
Prior to this commit, building the OTBN simulation with Verilator 5
failed on four warnings, which are fatal in that target:

  - `UNUSEDSIGNAL` on the immediate of two functions in the vendored
    `dm_pkg.sv`.  A waiver for these exists, but Verilator 5 changed
    the message from "Bits of signal are not used" to "Bits of function
    variable are not used", so it stopped matching.  The waiver now
    matches both wordings.
  - `PROCASSINIT` on two variables that are meant to have a value from
    time zero.  Verilator 5 reports an initial value together with a
    procedural assignment, in case a reset was meant instead.

This commit updates the waiver of the vendored code in place, which
also silences the warning in the chip simulations, and waives the two
`PROCASSINIT` in the waiver file of the OTBN simulation.  Both are
scoped to the file and the message, so that other instances of the same
rules keep being reported.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [dv,verilator] Ignore AST delays under Verilator 5
body:
Prior to this commit, building a chip simulation with Verilator 5
failed with six `NEEDTIMINGOPT` errors.  The behavioral AST models
`vio_pgd` and `vcc_pgd` drive their outputs through delays, and
Verilator 5 requires the caller to state whether delays are modelled or
ignored, whereas Verilator 4 had no support for them and ignored them.

This commit passes `--no-timing` in the simulation target of all three
tops, which keeps the behavior of Verilator 4.

`--no-timing` applies to the whole design, so a delay added elsewhere
would be ignored as well.  Verilator reports each one as `STMTDLY` or
`ASSIGNDLY`, but `-Wno-fatal` demotes those to a warning in the build
log.  This commit therefore waives the two models in
`ip/ast/lint/ast.vlt`, which the simulation already reads, and raises
both rules to an error with `-Werror-STMTDLY` and `-Werror-ASSIGNDLY`,
so that a delay anywhere else stops the build.

The Darjeeling simulation still times out with a silent console.  That
is unrelated to this commit: its UART clock and its CTN RAM preload are
wrong, which #31570 fixes.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [hw,ci] Require Verilator 5.048
body:
Prior to this commit, the minimum version was 4.210 and CI installed
exactly that from a prebuilt tarball, while the development shell
provided 5.048.  The simulation targets now pass `--no-timing`, which
Verilator 4 does not know.

This commit raises the minimum to 5.048 and lets CI take Verilator from
the development shell, so that its version cannot drift from the one
`flake.nix` pins.  The jobs that need Verilator gain `prepare-nix` and
run through `nix run .#eda`, as `lint_bazel` already does, and their
timeouts grow by the time it takes to restore the Nix store.

`dj_sw_build_test` builds Verilator-dependent targets without needing
the simulation itself, so it now sets `DISABLE_VERILATOR_BUILD` like
the other software build jobs, rather than entering the shell.

This commit also drops the note on building Verilator with GCC 11,
which was a limitation of 4.210.

The OTBN smoke test now runs inside the shell while the RISC-V
toolchain it needs is installed outside it.  That works because the
shell bind-mounts the directories of the host.

Resolves: #28696

body:

pinmux output select of IOB0 to 54 and that of IOB3 to 53.  These were
the selects of SPI_HOST1 CSB and SCK until `e6b79d449d` ("[top_earlgrey]
Remove pattgen") shifted the MIO peripheral outputs by four.  Since
then, they select `sensor_ctrl` AST debug outputs 2 and 1.  As a
result, the case analysis disabled the path from the SPI_HOST1 SCK flop
to IOB3, on which `SPI_HOST1_CLK` is generated.

This commit sets the selects to the current values: 50 (CSB) for IOB0
and 49 (SCK) for IOB3, and updates the comments accordingly.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [earlgrey] Move SPI_HOST1 to the IO clock domain
body:
Prior to this commit, `spi_host1` was clocked by `io_div2` (48 MHz).
For Earl Grey 2, a reduced pinmux matrix should make it feasible to
close timing for SPI_HOST1 at the full IO clock frequency (96 MHz),
like SPI_HOST0.

This commit moves `spi_host1`, its reset node and its `xbar_main` port
from `io_div2` to `io` in `top_earlgrey.hjson` and regenerates the top.
SPI_HOST1 now shares the `clk_io_peri` gate and its alert LPG clock
enable with SPI_HOST0, so `CLK_ENABLES.CLK_IO_PERI_EN` gates both SPI
hosts.  The `Main` domain of the `lc_io_div2` reset is no longer used
and is not generated anymore.

Like SPI_HOST0, SPI_HOST1 now runs at half its nominal frequency in
the low-speed external clock mode and during the life cycle clock
bypass, where `io` drops to 48 MHz.  Previously, its frequency stayed
constant in these modes, because the `io_div2` divider steps down.
This commit documents this in the Earl Grey design document.

The xbar port was the only non-software-gated consumer of `io_div2`.
Since clkmgr only measures clock sources with such consumers, the
regenerated clkmgr no longer has an IO_DIV2 measurement: this removes
`IO_DIV2_MEAS_CTRL_EN`, `IO_DIV2_MEAS_CTRL_SHADOWED`, the countermeasure
`CLKMGR.MEAS_CTRL.IO_DIV2` and the IO_DIV2 bits in `RECOV_ERR_CODE`,
whose remaining fields shift down.  `io_div2` still clocks the scan
clock of `spi_device` (via `clk_io_div2_peri`) and rstmgr.

This commit also updates the hand-written collateral:
- SDC: SPI_HOST1 constraints now refer to `IO_CLK`, and the SPI_HOST1
  clocks are in the `IO_CLK` asynchronous clock group.  The blanket
  `IO_DIV2_CLK` I/O delays on the muxed pads are removed, since no
  logic on `IO_DIV2_CLK` uses muxed pads anymore.  As a consequence,
  SPI_HOST1 inputs from pads not in `SPI_HOST1_DATA_PORTS` are no
  longer timed, in line with SPI_HOST1 I/O timing being closed only on
  its constrained pads.
  The non-`spec_constr` SPI_HOST1 I/O delays now equal those of
  SPI_HOST0, since SPI_HOST1 is intended to be usable at the same
  frequencies as SPI_HOST0.
- FPV connectivity CSVs and `chip_conn_testplan.hjson`.
- RDC scenario and AST CDC abstract model: drop the removed
  `clk_io_div2_infra`.
- clkmgr AscentLint waiver: waive `NOT_READ` and `HIER_NET_NOT_READ`
  on `clk_io_div2_root`, which is no longer read because the remaining
  `io_div2` consumer `clk_io_div2_peri` only uses `clk_io_div2_en`.
- clkmgr templates: the sec_cm testplan and the DV scoreboard take the
  measured clocks from `get_rg_srcs()` instead of listing all clocks.
  This removes `clk_io_div2` from the `MEAS.CLK.BKGN_CHK` and
  `TIMEOUT.CLK.BKGN_CHK` testpoints and the `io_div2_meas_ctrl_*`
  scoreboard case items.  Darjeeling and English Breakfast do not
  measure `io_div2` either, so their output changes accordingly.
- `chip_clkmgr_testplan.hjson`: drop the IO_DIV2 measurement features
  and `CLKMGR.ENABLE.IO_DIV2` from `chip_sw_clkmgr_off_peri`.
- `dif_clkmgr.h`: renumber the Earl Grey recoverable error types and
  drop the IO_DIV2 ones; update the DIF unit test and the Rust HAL.
- `clkmgr_testutils.c`: derive the expected IO count for a low-speed
  external clock from the IO count, as IO_DIV2 is not measured anymore.
- `clkmgr_off_peri_test.c`: skip `clk_io_div2_peri`, which no longer
  clocks a CSR-accessible peripheral.
- `alert_handler_lpg_clkoff_test.c`: SPI_HOST1 is gated by
  `clk_io_peri`.
- SPI_HOST1 users (`spi_host_tx_rx_test`, `spi_host_config_test`, pmod
  flash tests, teacup demo) now use `kClockFreqHiSpeedPeripheralHz` as
  the peripheral clock frequency.
- Pentest library comments.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [earlgrey,syn] Constrain SPI_HOST1 SD2 and SD3
body:
Prior to this commit, the SDC constrained only SPI_HOST1's CSB, SCK,
SD0 and SD1 pads (IOB0 to IOB3).  SD2 and SD3 had no I/O timing
constraints, and the false paths from SPI_HOST1 to all other pads
covered them.  In addition, the PrimeTime case analysis modelled SD0 as
output-only and SD1 as input-only, which only fits standard SPI mode.
SPI_HOST1 is intended to be usable in quad mode in Earl Grey 2.

This commit assigns SD2 to IOB4 and SD3 to IOB6 and constrains them
like the existing SPI_HOST1 data pads:
- `SPI_HOST1_DATA_PORTS` includes IOB4 and IOB6, so they get the same
  input and output delays relative to `SPI_HOST1_CLK`.
- The false paths from `IO_CLK` and `SPI_HOST1_INTERNAL_CLK` through
  SPI_HOST1 to IOB4 and IOB6 are removed, and loopback false paths
  through IOB4 and IOB6 back to `IO_CLK` are added.
- The hold false paths on the pad output enable cover IOB4 and IOB6.
- The PrimeTime case analysis selects SD2 and SD3 as outputs on IOB4
  and IOB6, and IOB4 and IOB6 as the SD2 and SD3 inputs.  The select
  values are those of the current pinmux.

This commit also models SD0 and SD1 as bidirectional in PrimeTime: the
case analysis additionally selects SD1 as output on IOB2 and IOB1 as
the SD0 input, and the false path for SPI_HOST1 outputs to IOB2 is
removed.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [earlgrey] Give SPI_HOST1 its own clock gate
body:
Prior to this commit, SPI_HOST1 and SPI_HOST0 shared the `clk_io_peri`
clock gate, since both are clocked by `io` and in the `peri` clock
group.  Software could therefore not turn off the clock of one SPI host
while using the other one, although both SPI hosts are rarely needed at
the same time.

This commit adds a software-gated clock group `spi_host1` and moves
SPI_HOST1 into it.  SPI_HOST1 is now clocked by `clk_io_spi_host1`,
which `CLK_ENABLES.CLK_IO_SPI_HOST1_EN` (bit 4) gates.  The existing
`CLK_ENABLES` bits are unchanged.  The alert handler LPG of SPI_HOST1
uses the clock gate indication of the new clock.

The clkmgr templates assumed at most one software-gated clock per source
clock, which led to duplicate feature names and DV identifiers.  This
commit adds `get_sw_clk_keys()` to `clkmgr_gen.py`, which returns the
source name for each software-gated clock, or the clock name if several
software-gated clocks share a source, and asserts that these names are
unique.  The templates use it for feature names (`CLKMGR.ENABLE.IO_PERI`
and `CLKMGR.ENABLE.IO_SPI_HOST1` instead of `CLKMGR.ENABLE.IO`) and DV
identifiers, and use the clock name for `CLK_ENABLES` fields and SVA
bind instances.  The generated output of Darjeeling and English
Breakfast is unchanged, except for the DV README and the formatting
of `clkmgr_if.sv`, which wraps a line that exceeds 100 characters for
`clk_io_spi_host1`.  The DV README now derives the number of
peripheral and hintable clocks from the configuration instead of
hardcoding four of each, which was wrong for Darjeeling and English
Breakfast and would now also be wrong for Earl Grey.

This commit also updates the hand-written collateral:
- FPV connectivity CSVs, `chip_conn_testplan.hjson` and
  `chip_clkmgr_testplan.hjson`.
- RDC waivers and scenario, and the AST CDC abstract model.
- `clkmgr_off_peri_test.c` tests SPI_HOST1 via the new clock again, and
  `alert_handler_lpg_clkoff_test.c` gates SPI_HOST1 via the new clock.
- The pentest library has a new `kPentestPeripheralSpiHost1` to turn off
  the clock of SPI_HOST1.  Like other Earl Grey-only code in that
  library, it is excluded for English Breakfast, which lacks that clock.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [crypto/gcm] Shred the GCM context and shares after use
body:
The one-shot AES-GCM functions return without clearing their context on
the stack. The context holds the GHASH tables for both shares of the
hash subkey H. The two tables reveal H. With H and one valid tag, an
attacker can forge tags for other messages under the same nonce. The
streaming functions leave their local contexts behind in the same way.
Finalisation clears only the caller's context.

The setup code also leaves both shares of H and the encrypted initial
counter block on the stack. An error return can skip the existing shred
of the unshared H.

Add aes_gcm_context_shred and attach it as a cleanup guard to every
local GCM context in the library. Guard the setup blocks the same way.
The guards also run on error returns.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [crypto/gcm] Shred the GHASH temporaries after use
body:
ghash_process_block leaves three blocks on the stack. One is the input
to both multiplications. The other two are its products with the two
shares of the hash subkey H. The products XOR to the input times H. One
field division then gives H back.

Other GHASH helpers leave secrets behind in the same way. The counter
block setup keeps both shares of the encrypted initial counter block S.
The subkey remask keeps its random mask next to S0 and S1 multiplied by
that mask. The redundant update can return early before it shreds its
copy of the context.

Attach cleanup guards to these blocks and to the redundant context.
The block update keeps its temporaries in a buffer owned by its caller,
so they are shredded once per update instead of once per block. The
field multiplication writes its product through a pointer. A returned
block would leave an unshredded copy in the caller's stack frame. On
the first block, each share's product is written straight into its
state share instead of being copied there.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [crypto/gcm] Shred the expected tag after decryption
body:
After a failed tag check, the expected tag stays on the stack. For a
forged message it is the tag the forger needs. The decryption
finaliser and both tag-generation helpers leave copies on the stack.
ghash_final also leaves the tag combined with the S1 share.

Attach cleanup guards to these blocks.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [crypto/mlkem] Fix secret key size and check buffer lengths
body:
The ML-KEM header gives the secret key size as 3168 bytes, the FIPS 203
encoding, but the cryptolib stores a 4736-byte key blob with two share
slots each for s and z. Keygen writes the whole blob without checking
its length, so a blob sized from the header overflows by 1568 bytes.
Decapsulation then reads the same amount past its end.

Make the header give the real blob size, as the ML-DSA header does, and
reject key, ciphertext and randomness buffers of the wrong length in
the public operations. The shared secret blob only needs room for the
32-byte secret, because nothing past it is written and the pentest
firmware passes a larger blob. Output lengths are checked after OTBN
finishes, so the wrapper can still wipe DMEM when a check fails.

Update the cryptotest and pentest firmware for the new size, and add
functest cases for a round trip with the public sizes and for wrong
lengths.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [pentest] Fix stack overflow in AES SCA handlers
body:
`sca_aes_fpga_cw340_sival_rom_ext` times out on `BatchFvsrData`
because of a stack overflow.

`handle_aes_sca()`. Their large stack buffers (mainly the GCM batch

stack is 16 KB. So every AES command overflows the stack. Until

grown `.bss` to just below the stack:

subject: [crypto/hmac] Check tag and context lengths
body:
otcrypto_hmac() writes a full digest into the caller's tag buffer
without checking the buffer's length. A caller that sizes its tag for a
truncated MAC gets a write past the end of the buffer, and the call
still returns OK. The header promises a bad-argument error for this.
otcrypto_hmac_final() and the SHA-2 one-shot functions already check
it. Reject a tag whose length differs from the digest size of the key
mode.

Callers also hold the streaming context between update and final calls.
The driver sizes copies into its fixed buffers from the context's
length fields without bounding them. An oversized block, partial-block
or key length can make it write past those buffers. A zero block length
is used as a divisor. The SHA-2 API checks the block and digest lengths
first. HMAC finalization only compares the tag length with the stored
digest length. Add one check of the four context lengths in the driver.
It runs at the start of update, final and the redundant final, so it
covers both APIs.

Add tag-length cases to hmac_functest and cases for each context length
to hmac_test. I ran both on the Earlgrey Verilator model. I also ran
sha256_functest and the HMAC functional tests for SHA-256, SHA-384 and
SHA-512, which cover all three security levels. All passed. Without the
source changes, the first new case in each test fails.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [lc_ctrl,dv] Fixed nvm_rma_error injection
body:
The error was not being seen by the FSM because
the combination of the ack signal being toggled
On/Off every cycle from the virtual sequencer
+ scrambling from CDC instrumentation and
lc_tx_and_hi() would sometimes result in the
combined ack signal (which is what the FSM sees)
being sampled as Off for a couple of cycles,
allowing enough time for the FSM to leave the
TransProgSt state due to receiving an ack from
OTP after it sent the request when it first
entered TransProgSt.

Corrected sequence ensure that an nvm_rma_error is
flagged in either the TokenCheck0St,
TokenCheck1St, or TransProgSt states, which is
where the FSM is expected to flag the error.

Disabled OTP program interface assertions for the
duration of the error injection. These assertions
are disabled if cdc instrumentation is enabled,
but they are not disabled if cdc instrumentation
is disabled. The issues faced with the assertions
are that they are not aware of the error injection
and will flag an error when the FSM sends an OTP
program request before catching the nvm_rma_error.
I've reviewed the assertions and they are not needed for
this test, so they are disabled when injecting an
nvm_rma_error.

Signed-off-by: Mohammed Tayyab Khalid <mohammed.khalid@lowrisc.org>

subject: [top_earlgrey] Increase retention SRAM to 8 KiB
body:
Prior to this commit, `sram_ctrl_ret` in `top_earlgrey.hjson` had the
Earl Grey 1 size of 4 KiB (`InstSize` 4096, memory size `0x1000`).
Earl Grey 2 requires an 8 KiB retention SRAM, which the EG2 datasheet
already states.

This commit sets `InstSize` to 8192 and the `ram_ret_aon` memory size
to `0x2000`.  The base address `0x40600000` stays 8 KiB-aligned and
the region does not overlap any other device.  All top-level autogen
files are regenerated with `util/topgen.py`.

This commit does not change the layout of `retention_sram_t`.  It still
covers the first 4 KiB, and the upper 4 KiB are not allocated yet.  The
comments in `retention_sram.h` now say so instead of describing the
creator area as "the first half" of the retention SRAM.

This commit also updates the hard-coded `ram_ret_aon` ranges in
`mapfile_to_json.py` and the `object_size` tool, and two comments that
stated the old size (`chip_sw_data_integrity_vseq` and `ibex_fi.h`).

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [sram_ctrl,dv] Use 8 KiB for the retention variant
body:
Prior to this commit, the block-level `sram_ctrl_ret` DV variant used a
4 KiB memory to emulate the Earl Grey retention SRAM.  Earl Grey now has
an 8 KiB retention SRAM, so the variant no longer matched the top.
Darjeeling also ran this variant, and its retention SRAM is 4 KiB.

This commit sets `SRAM_SIZE_BYTES` to `2**13` in
`sram_ctrl_ret_sim_cfg.hjson`, which Earl Grey keeps using.  It adds a
`ret_4kB` variant in `sram_ctrl_ret_4kB_sim_cfg.hjson` with the previous
4 KiB configuration, and switches `top_darjeeling_sim_cfgs.hjson` to
it.  It also updates the DV README, and makes the comments in `tb.sv`,
`sram_ctrl_lc_escalation_vseq` and `sram_ctrl_base_sim_cfg.hjson` that
named specific sizes or variants apply to all variants.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [top_earlgrey,dv] Raise data integrity test reseed
body:
Prior to this commit, `chip_sw_data_integrity_escalation` had a default
`reseed` of 6.  Each seed picks one of three fault targets (main SRAM
data, retention SRAM data and main SRAM instruction) uniformly, so a
regression with the default seeds missed a given target with a
probability of (2/3)^6, about 9 %.

This commit sets `reseed` to 12, which lowers that probability to below
1 %.  The nightly regression runs every test with a single seed, so this
affects weekly and manual runs only.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [top_earlgrey,doc] Remove stale content from spec

referred to the `chip_earlgrey_cw310` target, which no longer exists.

subject: [top_earlgrey,doc] Describe EG2 Ibex in spec
body:
Prior to this commit, the "Main processor" section of the detailed
Earl Grey chip specification described Ibex as an RV32IMC core with a
2-stage pipeline.  This did not match the Earl Grey 2 configuration in
`top_earlgrey.hjson` and did not mention CHERIoT (see #30941).

This commit describes the Ibex configuration as set by the
`rv_core_ibex` parameters: the 3-stage pipeline, the ISA extensions,
ePMP, the instruction cache, the debug triggers and the `SecureIbex`
security features.  It adds a "CHERIoT" subsection that covers the
write-once switch that selects CHERIoT or locks RV32I, the
`cheriot_mem_sys` memory subsystem and its background revocation engine.
It removes the history of Ibex as "Zero-riscy" and, with it, the
"References" section, whose only entry was the Zero-riscy paper.  It
notes that Zbc implies Zbkc, which the Ibex documentation does not name.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [top_earlgrey,doc] Describe EG2 memories in spec
body:
Prior to this commit, the "Memory" section of the detailed Earl Grey
chip specification described only the ROM, the RRAM and a single
128 KiB SRAM.  It lacked the Secondary SRAM, the Retention SRAM, the
CHERIoT meta SRAM and the OTP emulated in RRAM.  It also contained
stale sentences about an RSA check whose details would "come at a
later date" and were "TBD" (see #30941).

This commit adds a table of all memories with their sizes, controllers,
power domains and intended uses, and splits the section into ROM, RRAM,
OTP and SRAM subsections.  It describes the Retention SRAM as 8 KiB, the
Earl Grey 2 requirement.  It describes the layout of the CHERIoT meta
SRAM and the OTP region at the top of the RRAM.  It replaces the stale
RSA-check sentences with a reference to the "Secure boot" section.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [top_earlgrey,doc] Fix ROM key slots in spec
body:
Prior to this commit, the "Secure boot" section of the detailed Earl
Grey chip specification stated that the ROM had 3 key slots, while its
table listed 7 (see #30941).  Neither number matched the ROM code: the
ROM has no hard-coded keys and reads 4 ECDSA-P256 and 4 SPHINCS+ key
slots from the `ROT_CREATOR_AUTH_CODESIGN` OTP partition
(`sigverify_otp_keys.h`).

This commit states that Earl Grey supports post-quantum secure boot with
ML-DSA-87 signatures accelerated by OTBN.  It describes the OTP key
slots, which signatures the ROM checks, the life cycle states in which
it accepts each key type (from `sigverify_otp_keys.c`), and the key
states in the `ROT_CREATOR_AUTH_STATE` OTP partition.  It removes the
inconsistent slot table.  It describes ML-DSA-87 key slots and
signatures where the ROM currently uses SPHINCS+, because ML-DSA-87
replaces SPHINCS+ in Earl Grey 2.  It replaces the note at the top of
the document with the wording of the Earl Grey README and datasheet, and
adds that the document describes the hardware design while the software
(ROM, ROM_EXT) is still under development and may not yet implement
all features of the hardware.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [top_earlgrey,doc] Add security IPs to spec

security-relevant IPs of Earl Grey 2 (see #30941).

This commit adds short sections for KMAC, OTBN, the key manager DPE, the
life cycle controller, the OTP controller, the ROM controller, the SRAM
controller and sensor control.  Each section summarizes the IP's role in
Earl Grey, its connections to other IPs as instantiated in

section names the hardened ML-DSA and ML-KEM support.

more details "in a later specification update", and stated that "more
than one I2C host module might be instantiated" (see #30941).
`top_earlgrey.hjson` instantiates three I2C peripherals, which support
both controller and target modes.

This commit renames the section to "I2C" and describes the three
instances, their controller and target modes, the supported speeds,
their connection through the pinmux, their virtual open-drain outputs
and the pad type needed for a pull-up above the pad supply, and their
software-controllable resets.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

subject: [top_earlgrey,doc] Document watchdog in spec
body:
Prior to this commit, the "Timer(s)" section of the detailed Earl Grey
chip specification described only `rv_timer` and stated that a
watchdog timer "will be provided in the future" (see #30941).  The
watchdog exists in `aon_timer`, which `top_earlgrey.hjson`
instantiates in the `Aon` power domain.

This commit describes `rv_timer` and `aon_timer`.  For the watchdog,
it covers petting, the bark (interrupt, NMI to Ibex and wakeup

configuration lock and the pause during sleep.

`top_earlgrey.hjson` sets `NumEndPoints` of `edn1` to 1, so there are
no tied-off endpoints (see #30941).

body:
Prior to this commit, the ISA string in the Earl Grey datasheet
omitted Zbkc, although the bit manipulation list below it included
Zbkc.  Ibex implements Zbkc: with `RV32BFull`, its decoder implements
`clmul` and `clmulh` (`ibex_decoder.sv`), which make up Zbkc.  The list
also gave version 1.0.0 for Zbkb, Zbkc and Zbkx, which are defined by
version 1.0.1 of the scalar cryptography specification (see #30941).

This commit adds Zbkc to the ISA string and lists Zbc (version 1.0.0)
separately from Zbkb, Zbkc and Zbkx (version 1.0.1).

subject: [otbn,rtl] Raise ILLEGAL_INSN for WSR indices with bits 7:5 set
body:
BN.WSRR and BN.WSRW take an 8-bit WSR index. An index that doesn't
name a WSR should raise an ILLEGAL_INSN error, and the ISS does that.
The predecoder and the controller only decode the low 5 bits, so an
index such as 0x20 reads or writes MOD instead. With the RIG fix in the
next commit, the block-level DV sees this as an RTL/ISS mismatch:

  Mismatch between RTL and ISS trace entries: RTL had a write to
  `w08', but the ISS doesn't have a write to that location.

Treat an index with any higher bit set like the other invalid indices:
raise the error and select MOD as the ISPR. Do this in both the
predecoder and the controller, so that their ISPR enables still agree.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [otbn,dv] Generate invalid WSR accesses in the RIG
body:
The RIG's BadIspr generator ends a program with an access to a CSR or
WSR that doesn't exist. It picks its instructions by mnemonic, but it
has the wrong names for the two WSR instructions. So it has only ever
generated invalid CSR accesses, never invalid WSR accesses.

It also picks its address from the gaps between the registers that the
RIG model knows. The model only lists the registers the RIG accesses,
so the gaps also hold the KMAC, MAI, URND control and INSN_CNT
registers. These are real registers, so an access to one of them
doesn't raise ILLEGAL_INSN. It usually succeeds, and the program then
runs past its end into unwritten IMEM.

Look for the WSR instructions as bn.wsrr and bn.wsrw. Pick the invalid
address from the whole index range of the instruction's CSR or WSR
operand, avoiding every register that csr.yml or wsr.yml defines.
Remove the pick_bad_addr helpers in the model and in KnownMem, which
now have no caller.

Related to #8082

subject: [mbx,rtl] Reject sub-word writes to the SoC WDATA and RDATA windows

February 2026:

return an error for a narrower write. The two windows have their own

subject: [crypto/gcm] Speed up AES-GCM about 2x with carry-less multiply
body:
GHASH multiplies each block by both shares of the hash subkey with
4-bit product tables. This takes about half of the time of each block,
and building the tables costs about 16,000 cycles per AES-GCM call.

Ibex on Earlgrey and Darjeeling has the Zbc carry-less multiply
instructions. Use clmul and clmulh to multiply the state by the subkey
one 32-bit word at a time and reduce after each word. Keep the GHASH
context in the bit order of clmul and convert blocks only where they
enter or leave it.

The arithmetic stays in registers, with and without Zbc. The register
file is cleared after each multiplication. Builds without Zbc, such as
the host unit test, use a C loop. AES-GCM encryption is 1.8 to 2.2
times faster on the Earlgrey Verilator model.

subject: [otbn] Reject unsupported vector element lengths
body:
The vector instructions have a 2-bit element length (ELEN) field.
Each instruction supports only some values and should raise
ILLEGAL_INSN for the others. The RTL gets this wrong in two ways.
The ISS also crashes on one encoding.

The decoder only looks at bit 25 for BN.MULV and its variants. With
ELEN set to 2'b10, the RTL runs the multiply as .8s.

When the decoder does reject an ELEN, the predecoder still enables
the register reads and the write. The CTRL.REDUN checks see these
accesses without a valid instruction and raise a fatal error, so
OTBN locks instead of stopping with only ILLEGAL_INSN.

The ISS asserts on the reserved value 2'b11 before the instruction
can check the length.

Check both ELEN bits in the decoder for the multiply instructions.
In the predecoder, flag an unsupported ELEN and disable its register
accesses. Map the reserved value in the ISS to a length that no
instruction supports. Update the copy of that helper in the ISA doc.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [keymgr_dpe,rtl] Check the KMAC output only when KMAC is done
body:
keymgr_dpe raises the KMAC_OUT fatal fault when a KMAC digest share is
all zeros or all ones. The check runs whenever an operation completes
or updates a slot. Disable, erase and load-root do both in a single
cycle without any KMAC transaction.

In that cycle the KMAC interface drives decoy data. Each share is one
32-bit LFSR word repeated across the key. If the LFSR output is
uniform, about one such operation in 2^30 sees an all-zero or all-ones
share. The key manager then wipes its slots and raises a fatal fault
that no KMAC output caused.

Qualify the check with kmac_done_i. Advance and generate operations
complete when kmac_done_i is set, so their KMAC output is still
checked.

Signed-off-by: Kulan Palanichamy <kulan.palanichamy@opentitan.org>

subject: [keymgr_dpe,dv] Hold the decoy data constant in some smoke operations

and all-ones shares are rare, so normal smoke runs are unlikely to

Randomly hold the decoy data at all zeros or all ones during erase and

subject: [doc,i3c] Documentation of OT I3C TTI

Introduce an initial version of the Target Transaction Interface
documentation of this OT I3C IP block.

The Target Transaction Interface is a proprietary extension,
allowing the HCI-specified Standby Controller to support Private
Read and Private Write Transfers also, as well as supporting
independent pure-Target operation on the I3C bus(es).

This documentation is at the level of the 'Theory of Operation'
found for more conventional OpenTitan IP blocks and does not
encompass content akin to the typical Programmer's Guide, such
as procedures for enabling/disabling Virtual Targets or streaming
longer transfers.

It should be viewed as a specification/statement of requirements
rather than a description of what is already present/complete.
Target-side implementation has suffered from being incompletely-
specified and stalled for a long time.

Minimal changes to the RTL to reflect the redefinition of the
TTI PRN structure; this logic is presently incomplete and has
been changed just to ensure that the `len` check is not
overlooked since not all values are now valid.
